["Increasing corn yield trough appropriate Nitrogen fertilization based on drone based vegetation index", "", "Increasing Corn Yield Through Appropriate Nitrogen Fertilization Based on Drone-Based Vegetation Index\\\" focuses on optimizing corn yield by utilizing drone technology to assess crop health and determine the ideal nitrogen fertilization levels. ["Validating Drone based vegetation Index model in predicting growth and yield of cotton", "", "Validating Drone-Based Vegetation Index Model in Predicting Growth and Yield of Cotton\\\" focuses on assessing the effectiveness of using drone technology to monitor cotton crop health and predict its growth and yield. ["Good Fungi, Better Shallots: A Natural Ally for Sustainable Farming", "Shallots are one of the most important kitchen ingredients in Indonesia. They are used almost every day, not only as a spice but also as a crop with high economic value for farmers. As demand continues to rise, farmers need practical ways to maintain and increase shallot production without depending too heavily on synthetic inputs. A study published in Yuzuncu Yil University Journal of Agricultural Sciences explored one promising solution: beneficial fungi. These are fungi that can support plant growth, improve root activity, help plants absorb nutrients, and in some cases protect crops from pests or disease. The researchers tested four shallot varieties—Maserati, Sanren F1, Lokananta, and Tuk-Tuk—combined with four types of beneficial fungi: Trichoderma asperellum , Beauveria bassiana , Metarhizium anisopliae , and Glomus sp. The fungi were applied at three doses: 0, 7, and 14 g. The results showed that variety selection was very important. Among the tested varieties, Tuk-Tuk stood out for several production traits. It produced the tallest plants, largest bulb diameter, heaviest fresh and dry bulb weight, and highest yield per hectare. Sanren F1 showed strength in leaf number and stomatal density, while Lokananta had the largest stomatal opening area. The type of fungus also mattered. Beauveria bassiana produced the highest average plant height, while Trichoderma asperellum supported the highest number of leaves. For yield, some combinations were especially promising. Sanren F1 combined with Glomus sp. produced the highest yield per hectare, while Tuk-Tuk with a 7 g fungal application also showed very high production. This means that beneficial fungi are not “one-size-fits-all.” Their effect depends on the shallot variety and the application dose. Interestingly, the full interaction among variety, fungus type, and dose was significant only for chlorophyll index. The best chlorophyll response appeared in Maserati treated with Metarhizium anisopliae at 7 g. Chlorophyll is important because it helps plants capture light and produce energy through photosynthesis. This research supports Sustainable Development Goal 15: Life on Land . Using beneficial fungi can help promote healthier soil biology, reduce excessive reliance on synthetic agricultural inputs, and support more sustainable crop production. These fungi act as natural partners in the farming system, helping plants grow while maintaining ecological balance. The main message is clear: better shallot farming is not only about fertilizer or variety alone. It is about finding the right combination of plant genetics and biological support. Beneficial fungi, when matched with suitable varieties, can become a practical tool for improving shallot production while protecting land-based agricultural ecosystems."]

["A Small Cut for a Stronger Start: Pruning Shallot Seedlings Before the Field", "For many shallot farmers, good production begins with good planting material. Traditionally, shallots are grown from bulbs, but this method requires a large amount of planting material and may carry diseases from one season to the next. True shallot seed offers a promising alternative because it needs less planting material, is easier to transport, and can produce healthier crops. However, seed-grown shallots also bring a challenge: seedlings need a nursery period before transplanting, and weak seedlings may not survive well in the field. A study published in the Journal of Agriculture Faculty of Ege University investigated a simple question: can pruning improve the growth of shallot seedlings grown from seeds? The researchers tested three shallot varieties, Sanren F1, Lokananta, and Maserati, and compared three pruning frequencies. Seedlings were pruned once at 25 days after sowing, twice at 25 and 30 days, or three times at 25, 30, and 35 days. The pruning method was simple: about 25% of the leaf length was cut in the morning using scissors. The results showed that pruning mattered. Seedlings pruned three times had better growth than those pruned once or twice. They produced more leaves, thicker pseudostems, longer roots, more root tips, and higher fresh and dry seedling weight. In practical terms, repeated pruning helped seedlings become stronger both above and below the soil surface. The response also depended on the variety. Maserati produced the highest number of leaves and root tips. Lokananta had the largest pseudostem diameter and the heaviest fresh and dry seedling weight. Sanren F1 produced the longest roots. These differences show that genetics still play an important role, but pruning can improve seedling performance across varieties. Why can cutting leaves make seedlings stronger? Pruning may encourage new leaf growth and help balance the relationship between shoots and roots. When seedlings have better root development, they may absorb water and nutrients more effectively after transplanting. A thicker pseudostem may also help seedlings become more robust before they are moved to the field. This research supports Sustainable Development Goal 1: No Poverty . For smallholder farmers, stronger seedlings can mean fewer losses after transplanting, better crop establishment, and more reliable production. A simple nursery practice such as scheduled pruning does not require expensive equipment, making it suitable for practical use by farmers and seedling producers. The main message is clear: sometimes a small cut can lead to stronger growth. By pruning shallot seedlings three times during the nursery period, farmers may produce healthier seedlings that are better prepared for field conditions. Better seedlings can become the first step toward better harvests and more stable farmer livelihoods."]

["From Compost to Stronger Melons: Why Seedling Media Matters", "A good melon harvest does not begin when fruits appear. It begins much earlier, in the nursery, when a small seed becomes a seedling. At this stage, the growing medium is more than just something that holds the plant upright. It supplies water, air, nutrients, and space for roots to grow. If the medium is poor, seedlings may look weak before they ever reach the field. A study published in Italus Hortus examined how different growing media affect the growth and quality of melon seedlings. The researchers tested seven media: soil, rice husk biochar, compost, soil mixed with rice husk biochar, soil mixed with compost, compost mixed with rice husk biochar, and a mixture of soil, compost, and rice husk biochar. Melon seedlings of the ‘Golden Langkawi F1’ variety were grown for 21 days after sowing without additional fertilizer. The results showed that no single medium was best for every growth trait. Soil mixed with rice husk biochar produced the tallest seedlings, with an average height of 16.5 cm. It also supported the longest roots, reaching 31.5 cm, and produced high fresh shoot weight. This suggests that adding rice husk biochar to soil can improve the growing environment, especially by supporting root extension and early shoot growth. Compost mixed with rice husk biochar gave the best results for total leaf area, root volume, and fresh biomass. Larger leaves are important because they help seedlings capture more light and produce more energy through photosynthesis. Better root volume also means the seedling has a stronger underground system to absorb water and nutrients. However, when overall seedling quality was considered, compost alone gave the best performance. It produced the highest dry biomass and the highest seedling quality index. This quality index is important because it combines several traits, including shoot and root balance, rather than looking at only one measurement. In simple terms, compost produced seedlings that were not just big, but better balanced and potentially more ready for transplanting. This finding is practical for farmers and nursery operators. Strong seedlings can reduce transplant shock, improve field establishment, and support better crop performance later. Choosing the right medium is therefore not a small technical detail; it is a key decision in melon production. This research supports Sustainable Development Goal 15: Life on Land . Using organic materials such as compost and rice husk biochar can help recycle agricultural waste, improve nursery practices, and support more sustainable plant production. Instead of depending only on soil, farmers can use locally available organic materials to build healthier seedling systems. The message is clear: better melons start with better roots. Compost and rice husk biochar are not just waste materials; when used wisely, they can become valuable tools for producing stronger, healthier melon seedlings."]

["Stronger Seeds, Better Bulbs: How Zinc Priming Can Improve Shallot Farming", "Shallots are a daily need in many Indonesian kitchens, but producing them is not always easy. One of the biggest challenges for farmers is obtaining good planting material. Traditionally, shallots are planted using bulbs, but this method can be costly, bulky, and risky because bulbs may carry diseases. True shallot seed offers another option. It is easier to store, easier to transport, and can support healthier crop production. However, seed-grown shallots also face a problem: seedlings may grow unevenly and some may fail to survive after transplanting. A study published in the International Journal of Horticultural Science and Technology explored a simple technique to improve shallot seed performance: seed priming. Seed priming is a pre-sowing treatment where seeds are soaked in water or nutrient solutions and then dried before planting. This process helps seeds prepare for growth and can improve seedling strength. The researchers tested two shallot varieties, Lokananta and Maserati, and six priming treatments: no priming, hydropriming, IAA priming, zinc oxide priming, zinc sulfate priming, and zinc-EDTA priming. The study was conducted at Hasanuddin University, Makassar, using true shallot seeds that had been stored for 15 months. The results showed that zinc-based priming improved shallot growth and production. Among the treatments, zinc-EDTA gave the strongest overall results. It increased the percentage of surviving seedlings, plant fresh and dry weight, bulb fresh and dry weight, bulb diameter, bulb height, yield, and productivity. Zinc sulfate also performed well, especially in improving leaf number, bulb fresh weight, and yield. In practical terms, seeds treated with zinc were more likely to become stronger plants and produce better bulbs. Why does zinc help? Zinc is a micronutrient, meaning plants need it only in small amounts, but its role is important. It supports enzyme activity, chlorophyll formation, protein metabolism, and plant growth regulation. When seeds receive zinc before planting, they may begin growth with a better nutritional start. This can help seedlings adapt after transplanting and produce more biomass, which later supports bulb development. The study also found that seed priming affected bulb quality. Treatments such as zinc-EDTA and zinc sulfate helped reduce bulb shrinkage and improve bulb characteristics. This matters because better bulb quality can support postharvest handling and market value. This research supports Sustainable Development Goal 1: No Poverty . For smallholder farmers, better seedling survival and higher productivity can reduce crop failure and improve income stability. A simple, low-cost seed treatment may help farmers get more reliable harvests from true shallot seed systems. The main message is clear: better shallot production can begin before the seed is even planted. Zinc-based seed priming, especially zinc-EDTA and zinc sulfate, offers a practical step toward stronger seedlings, better bulbs, and more resilient farmer livelihoods."]

["Local Chilies, Global Lessons: Why Seed Ripeness Matters for Better Harvests", "Chili is more than a spicy ingredient. In many Indonesian households, especially in Gorontalo, local chili is part of daily food culture, farmer livelihoods, and regional identity. Behind its strong flavor, however, lies an important agricultural question: which local chili genotypes should be developed, and when should fruits be harvested for the best seed quality? A study published in Yuzuncu Yil University Journal of Agricultural Sciences evaluated four local Capsicum frutescens genotypes from Gorontalo: Diti, Malita FM, Samia, and Siropu. The researchers studied their morphology, germination performance, plant growth, and yield. They also tested seeds taken from fruits at three ripeness stages: 50%, 75%, and 100% maturity. The results showed that local chili genotypes are not all the same. Each has unique traits that can be useful for farmers and breeders. Diti had strong vegetative growth and produced many branches, but it showed weak reproductive performance and low seed vigor. Malita FM had potential, but only when seeds were taken from fully ripe fruits. Meanwhile, Samia and Siropu consistently performed better across many traits, including germination and yield. Seed ripeness was also very important. Seeds from 50% ripe fruits generally produced weaker plants and lower yields. In contrast, seeds from 100% ripe fruits produced the best overall performance, including taller plants, more fruits, and heavier fruit yield per plot. This means that harvesting fruits too early can reduce seed quality and later crop productivity. For farmers, this finding is practical. A fruit that looks almost ready may not produce the best seed. Waiting until full maturity can give seeds more time to accumulate food reserves and complete physiological development. Better seeds then become stronger seedlings, and stronger seedlings can become more productive plants. The study also highlights the value of local genetic resources. Samia and Siropu were identified as promising genotypes for commercial cultivation and future breeding programs. This is important because local varieties often carry traits adapted to local environments. Protecting and studying them can help farmers face changing climate, pests, and market demands. This research supports Sustainable Development Goal 15: Life on Land . By identifying and using local chili genotypes wisely, agriculture can help conserve plant biodiversity while improving productivity. Sustainable farming is not only about increasing yield; it is also about protecting valuable genetic resources that may support future food systems. The message is simple: better chili production starts with better seed decisions. Choosing the right genotype and harvesting fruits at full maturity can improve seed quality, plant growth, and yield. Local chilies from Gorontalo are not only part of cultural heritage—they may also hold important answers for sustainable agriculture."]

["Tiny Nutrient, Big Seeds: How Zinc Can Strengthen Shallot Seed Production", "Shallots are an everyday ingredient in Indonesian kitchens, but producing them is not always simple. One of the biggest challenges in shallot farming is the supply of healthy planting material. Many farmers still use bulbs from previous harvests. This method is familiar, but it has weaknesses. Bulbs can carry diseases, lose quality after repeated use, and need a dormancy period before they can be planted again. A published study in the International Journal of Horticultural Science and Technology explored another path: botanical seed production, also known as true shallot seed. These seeds can help reduce dependence on seed bulbs because they are easier to store, easier to transport, and less likely to carry bulb-borne diseases. However, producing true shallot seed is not easy. Some shallot varieties flower poorly, and even when flowers appear, they may not always produce strong, viable seeds. The researchers studied three Indonesian shallot varieties: Lokana, Rubaru, and Ambassador 3 Agrihorti. They tested different doses of zinc, a micronutrient needed in small amounts but important for plant metabolism, flowering, and seed development. Zinc was applied as a foliar spray at 0, 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 kg ha⁻¹ under highland conditions in Bantaeng Regency, South Sulawesi. The results showed that variety mattered. Ambassador 3 Agrihorti produced the strongest seed yield components, including the highest number of capsules per umbel, number of seeds per umbel, seed weight, seed production per hectare, and germination rate index. This means that genetic background plays a major role in determining whether a shallot variety is suitable for botanical seed production. Zinc also played an important role, especially in seed quality. The highest zinc dose, 1.5 kg ha⁻¹, gave the best results for seed weight per clump, faster germination time, higher coefficient velocity of germination, and higher germination rate index. In simple terms, zinc helped the seeds become more vigorous and germinate faster. The Rubaru variety treated with 1.5 kg ha⁻¹ zinc also showed the highest germination percentage. This research is closely linked to Sustainable Development Goal 17: Partnerships for the Goals . Improving shallot seed systems cannot be done by farmers alone. It requires collaboration among universities, seed laboratories, extension workers, government programs, and farming communities. Research findings like this can guide practical recommendations, while farmers’ field experience can help test and improve them under real conditions. The key message is clear: a tiny nutrient can make a big difference. Zinc is not a magic solution, but when combined with the right variety, it can help improve true shallot seed production. Stronger seeds mean stronger planting systems, and stronger planting systems can support more stable shallot farming in Indonesia."]

In Indonesia, they are an important horticultural crop that supports household cooking, food businesses, and farmer income. However, shallot production often faces one basic problem: not all seeds germinate well. However, shallot production often faces one basic problem: not all seeds germinate well. When seeds germinate slowly or unevenly, farmers may get weak seedlings, delayed planting, and lower crop performance in the field. A study published in Advances in Horticultural Science explored a simple way to improve shallot seed germination: seed priming with boron. Seed priming means soaking seeds in a solution before planting, then drying them again. This process helps seeds “prepare” for germination before they meet the soil. It supports cell wall formation, membrane function, and early metabolic activity. During germination, these processes are important because the seed must absorb water, activate enzymes, and begin growing into a seedling. The study also showed strong relationships between boron concentration and germination percentage, indicating that boron played an important role in improving seed performance. ["Eight Weeks to Wake Up: The Simple Storage Secret Behind Stronger Shallot Seedlings", "For many shallot farmers, the next harvest begins not in the field, but in storage. After harvest, shallot bulbs cannot always be planted immediately because they enter a natural resting phase known as dormancy. During this period, the bulb looks alive but is not yet ready to grow. If planted too early, it may sprout slowly, root poorly, or produce weak seedlings. If stored too long, the bulb may lose quality, dry out, or become more vulnerable to damage. A study published in Advances in Horticultural Science examined a practical question: how long should shallot bulbs be stored before planting to achieve strong early growth? The researchers focused on the Super Philips variety, a shallot cultivar widely used by farmers in Enrekang, South Sulawesi. The bulbs were stored under ambient room conditions for five different durations: 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 weeks. After storage, the researchers observed sprouting, rooting, plant height, leaf number, root length, and root volume. The result was clear: eight weeks was the best storage duration. Bulbs stored for eight weeks had the highest sprouting rate, reaching 98%, and the highest rooting rate, reaching 99%. They also sprouted and rooted faster than bulbs stored for shorter periods. This means that after eight weeks, the bulbs were physiologically ready to “wake up” and begin active growth. The same pattern appeared in seedling growth. Bulbs stored for eight weeks produced taller plants, more leaves, longer roots, and greater root volume. In simple terms, they did not only start growing faster; they also grew better. Their roots and shoots developed in a more balanced way, which is important because roots help absorb water and nutrients, while shoots support photosynthesis and early plant establishment. The study also showed why timing matters. At two or four weeks, many bulbs were likely still dormant, so their growth was slow and uneven. At ten weeks, performance began to decline, possibly because longer storage can cause water loss, aging, or quality deterioration. Therefore, storage is not just about waiting; it is about finding the right physiological window. This research directly supports Sustainable Development Goal 1: No Poverty . For smallholder farmers, better seed storage management can reduce planting failure, improve crop establishment, and support more stable production. When farmers know the right time to plant stored bulbs, they can make better decisions, reduce losses, and protect their income. The message is simple but powerful: shallot bulbs need enough time to rest before they are ready to grow. For Super Philips shallots under local ambient conditions, eight weeks of storage may be the key to stronger seedlings, better field establishment, and more reliable harvests."]

["Growing More Potatoes from Small Cuttings: A Practical Step for Farmers", "Potato is one of the world’s most important food crops after rice and wheat. It is rich in carbohydrates, calories, minerals, and vitamins, making it valuable not only as a vegetable but also as a potential staple food. In Indonesia, potato farming supports many highland communities. However, one major problem remains: farmers often struggle to access healthy and high-quality seed potatoes. A recent study published in the Journal of Agriculture Faculty of Ege University explored a simple but promising solution. Instead of relying only on seed tubers, the researchers tested potato propagation using stem cuttings. This method can help produce more planting material in a shorter time and with less space. The study focused on two important factors: the size of the cutting, based on the number of nodes, and the concentration of NAA, a synthetic auxin commonly used to stimulate root growth. The research tested cuttings with two, three, and four nodes, combined with four NAA concentrations: 0, 100, 200, and 300 mg L⁻¹. The cuttings were soaked in NAA solution for 15 minutes before planting. The researchers then observed plant growth, root development, tuber formation, and yield. The results showed that cuttings with four nodes tended to perform better, especially in producing more leaves. This makes sense because more nodes mean more growing points. More leaves can also support better photosynthesis, allowing plants to produce more energy for growth and tuber formation. However, the most powerful result came from the NAA treatment. Among all concentrations, 200 mg L⁻¹ NAA gave the best overall performance. It increased leaf number, chlorophyll index, root length, root volume, root fresh weight, number of tubers, tuber size, tuber weight, and estimated yield per hectare. In practical terms, this concentration helped the potato cuttings grow stronger roots and produce better tubers. The study reported that 200 mg L⁻¹ NAA produced the highest root length, root volume, tuber number, tuber length, tuber diameter, tuber weight per plant, and yield per hectare. This suggests that the right dose of plant growth regulator can make a real difference. Too little may not be effective, while too much may not improve results further. The key is using the right concentration. This research is closely related to Sustainable Development Goal 1: No Poverty . For smallholder farmers, better planting material can reduce production failure, improve harvest quality, and increase income opportunities. If farmers can multiply potato seed material more efficiently through cuttings, they may depend less on expensive or low-quality seed tubers. The main message is clear: small cuttings can create big opportunities. With proper cutting selection and the right NAA concentration, potato propagation can become faster, healthier, and more productive. For farming communities, this simple technique may support better harvests and stronger rural livelihoods."]

["Stronger Seedlings, Safer Harvests: A Simple Key to Better Shallot Farming", "For many farmers, the success of a shallot crop begins long before harvest. It begins with a tiny seedling being moved from the nursery to the field. This step may look simple, but it is one of the most stressful moments in a plant’s life. After transplanting, shallot seedlings can suffer from “transplant shock,” a condition where growth slows because roots are disturbed, water uptake becomes difficult, and the plant needs time to recover. A published study in Revista Colombiana de Ciencias Hortícolas explored an important question: which seedling traits help shallots recover faster after transplanting? The researchers studied three shallot varieties grown from true seed: ‘Lokananta’, ‘Merdeka F1’, and ‘Sanren F1’. They observed several traits, including leaf number, pseudostem diameter, seedling biomass, root length, root volume, number of root tips, and recovery time after transplanting. The most important finding was clear and practical: seedlings with thicker pseudostems recovered faster. The pseudostem is the lower stem-like part of the shallot plant. In simple terms, it works like a small storage tank. A thicker pseudostem can hold more energy and water, helping the seedling survive the stress that happens after transplanting. The study found that pseudostem diameter was the strongest predictor of recovery time, explaining much of the difference in how quickly seedlings returned to normal growth. Among the tested varieties, ‘Merdeka F1’ performed best. It had higher biomass, stronger root development, and recovered faster than the other varieties. Its recovery time was around 5.77 days, compared with about 6.33 to 6.53 days in the other varieties. Although this difference may sound small, for farmers it matters. Faster recovery means seedlings can resume growth sooner, reduce the risk of death, and establish better in the field. Interestingly, root traits such as root length and root volume were less useful in predicting recovery time. This may be because roots are often damaged during transplanting, even when seedlings initially have good root systems. Therefore, while healthy roots are still important, the study suggests that farmers and nursery managers should pay special attention to visible seedling strength, especially pseudostem thickness. This research supports Sustainable Development Goal 1: No Poverty . Better seedling selection can reduce crop failure, lower production losses, and improve farmers’ income stability. For smallholder farmers, even simple decisions—such as choosing stronger seedlings before transplanting—can make farming less risky and more profitable. The message is easy to understand: not all seedlings are equally ready for the field. A strong shallot seedling, especially one with a thicker pseudostem, has a better chance to recover quickly and grow well. In practical farming, small observations at the nursery stage can lead to safer harvests and stronger rural livelihoods."]

["Small Bulbs, Big Impact: Rethinking Shallot Seed Production for Sustainable Farming", "Shallots may look small on the kitchen table, but behind every bulb lies a major challenge for farmers: how to produce healthy, uniform, and affordable planting material. In many shallot-growing areas, farmers commonly use bulbs as seed. This method is familiar, but it can be costly, bulky to transport, and risky because diseases may be carried from one planting season to the next. A recent study published in Notulae Botanicae Horti Agrobotanici Cluj-Napoca offers a practical alternative: producing mini shallot bulbs from true shallot seed. The study explored two simple questions. First, can farmers control bulb size by changing how densely shallots are planted? Second, can paclobutrazol, a plant growth regulator, help make the bulbs smaller and more suitable as planting material? The researchers tested three planting densities, 100, 200, and 300 plants per square meter, and several paclobutrazol concentrations applied through root dipping before transplanting. The answer was surprisingly clear: crowding mattered more than chemistry. Paclobutrazol briefly reduced plant height and leaf number in the early growth stage, but its effect did not last until harvest. It did not significantly change bulb size, bulb weight, or leaf pigment composition. In contrast, planting density strongly shaped the final harvest. When more plants were grown in the same space, individual bulbs became smaller, lighter, and more likely to fall into the mini-bulb category. This finding is important because mini bulbs are not “failed” bulbs. In seed systems, they can be valuable. Mini bulbs are easier to handle, store, transport, and plant uniformly. For farmers and seed producers, this means that a simple agronomic adjustment—planting more seedlings per square meter, may help produce practical seed bulbs without relying heavily on chemical growth regulation. The study also found that leaf pigments remained stable across treatments. In simple terms, the plants did not show clear signs of physiological stress even when planted at higher density. This makes high-density planting an attractive strategy: it encourages smaller bulb formation while maintaining plant health. This research directly supports Sustainable Development Goal 15: Life on Land , especially through more efficient and sustainable crop production. By improving shallot seed systems, farmers can reduce dependence on large seed bulbs, improve planting material efficiency, and potentially lower losses linked to poor-quality seed. A stronger seed system also supports healthier agricultural land use because farmers can produce more planting material in limited space. The message for farmers is simple but powerful: sometimes innovation does not require a complex technology. In shallot mini-bulb production, arranging plants closer together may be one of the most practical steps toward sustainable seed production. Small bulbs, when produced wisely, can bring big benefits for farming systems, food supply, and land-based livelihoods."]

["One Maize Hybrid, Many Environments: Finding the Right Seed for Sustainable Farming", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia July 7, 2025/CORN-RG/– Farmers know that a maize variety that performs well in one location may not always perform equally well somewhere else. Differences in soil, rainfall, temperature, altitude, and other environmental conditions can significantly affect crop productivity. This creates an important challenge for plant breeders: how can we identify maize hybrids that combine high yields with stable performance across different growing environments? A 2025 study by Muhammad Azrai and colleagues provides important insights into this challenge. Published in Open Agriculture , the study entitled “Stability and Adaptability Analyses to Identify Suitable High-Yielding Maize Hybrids Using PBSTAT-GE” evaluated promising maize hybrids across diverse environments in Indonesia. The researchers evaluated eight candidate maize hybrids together with two commercial check varieties across eight locations in Indonesia during 2023 . The testing environments represented remarkably different growing conditions, ranging from lowlands at only 31 meters above sea level to highlands reaching 997 meters above sea level . Why test the same hybrids in so many different places? Because yield alone does not tell the whole story. A hybrid may produce exceptionally high yields in one environment but perform poorly when conditions change. For farmers, breeders, and the seed industry, a valuable hybrid needs either stable performance across a broad range of environments or strong adaptation to a specific target environment . To investigate this, the researchers used PBSTAT-GE , a web-based statistical platform for analyzing genotype-by-environment interactions. Rather than simply asking which hybrid produced the highest yield, the analysis addressed two critical questions: Which hybrids remain stable across environments, and which hybrids are particularly well adapted to specific locations? The results demonstrated substantial variation among testing environments. The overall average maize productivity reached 10.55 tonnes per hectare . Among the test locations, Klaten recorded the highest average productivity at 12.75 tonnes per hectare , while Bone recorded the lowest at 9.01 tonnes per hectare . These differences demonstrate precisely why multi-environment testing is essential. The performance of a maize genotype is shaped not only by its genetic potential but also by how that genetic potential interacts with the environment in which it is grown. Most importantly, MAI-UH 08 and MAI-UH 03 emerged as promising hybrids , combining high productivity with favorable stability and adaptability across the evaluated environments. Based on these characteristics, the researchers recommended both hybrids for further variety-release procedures . Other hybrids demonstrated more specific adaptation. MAI-UH 01, MAI-UH 02, and MAI-UH 05 showed potential for particular environments, including locations such as Tomohon and Boyolali . These findings highlight another important principle of modern plant breeding: not every successful variety needs to perform identically everywhere. Some genotypes may be particularly valuable when matched with the environments where they perform best. The research contributes to the broader goals of sustainable agriculture and responsible land use . It is particularly relevant to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger , through efforts to develop productive and resilient crop varieties, and SDG 15: Life on Land , by supporting more efficient and environmentally appropriate use of agricultural land. Identifying maize hybrids that are well matched to their growing environments can help farmers make better use of existing agricultural land while reducing the uncertainty associated with deploying varieties under unsuitable conditions. For Indonesia, where maize is cultivated across highly diverse agroecological environments, this information is particularly valuable. The study carries a simple but powerful message: The best maize seed is not merely the one that produces the highest yield—it is the one that delivers the right performance in the right environment. Through multi-environment testing and analytical tools such as PBSTAT-GE, maize breeding can move beyond selecting for yield alone toward identifying hybrids that combine productivity, stability, and environmental adaptability . For the Corn Research Group at Hasanuddin University , this research represents an important step toward developing maize varieties that are scientifically selected not only for their yield potential, but also for their ability to perform under the diverse growing environments encountered by Indonesian farmers. Reference Azrai, M. et al. (2025). Stability and Adaptability Analyses to Identify Suitable High-Yielding Maize Hybrids Using PBSTAT-GE . Open Agriculture, 10 (1), 20250447. De Gruyter. DOI: 10.1515/opag-2025-0447 Contact: Prof. Dr. Muhammad Azrai Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University azrai@agri.unhas.ac.id"]

["Breeding Maize for a Drier Future: Identifying Stable and Drought-Tolerant Hybrids", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, April 1 2026/CORN-RG/– Maize is more than an important crop. It supports food systems, livestock production, and agricultural industries, while providing livelihoods for millions of farming households. Yet maize production is highly dependent on water availability, making drought one of the major challenges to maintaining stable yields. As climate variability increases the risk of water shortages during critical stages of crop growth, plant breeders face an increasingly important question: Can we develop maize hybrids that maintain high and stable yields even when water becomes limited? A 2026 study entitled “Yield Stability in Maize (Zea mays L.) Using GGE Biplot and Selection Indices Under Irrigated and Drought-Stress Conditions” provides important insights into this challenge. Published in the SABRAO Journal of Breeding and Genetics , the research evaluated the performance and stability of maize hybrids under contrasting water conditions. The researchers tested eight experimental maize hybrids and two commercial varieties across four environments in Indonesia . Two environments represented irrigated conditions, while the other two exposed the plants to drought stress. This experimental design allowed the researchers to look beyond a simple question of which hybrid produced the highest yield. Instead, they could ask something more important for future maize production: Which hybrids can remain productive and reliable when water availability changes? The impact of drought was substantial. Across the evaluated environments, average grain yield under drought stress was 42.4% lower than under irrigated conditions . This sharp decline illustrates how strongly water limitation can affect maize productivity. However, the hybrids did not respond equally. Using several drought-tolerance and selection indices, the researchers identified G05 (R0641), G03 (R0211), and G08 (R0020) as promising drought-tolerant hybrids. Among them, G05 performed particularly well across several selection indices, while G03 demonstrated strong yield stability under drought conditions. The researchers also applied GGE biplot analysis , a statistical approach commonly used by plant breeders to visualize genotype performance and genotype-by-environment interactions. The analysis revealed an important pattern: G06 performed particularly well under irrigated conditions, G03 showed strong potential under drought stress, while G05 demonstrated good stability across contrasting water conditions . In practical terms, maize hybrids can behave differently depending on their environment. Some may perform exceptionally well when water is readily available, while others are better able to maintain productivity under drought. A particularly valuable hybrid may combine both attributes—competitive yield potential and greater stability when environmental conditions change. This distinction matters for farmers. Selecting maize solely on the basis of maximum yield under favorable conditions may overlook genotypes that offer greater reliability when rainfall becomes uncertain. The study therefore demonstrates the importance of combining yield evaluation, drought-tolerance indices, and genotype-by-environment analysis in modern maize breeding. Together, these approaches can help breeders distinguish between hybrids adapted to specific conditions and those capable of maintaining more stable performance across contrasting environments. The findings are particularly relevant to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger , as drought-tolerant and stable crop varieties can contribute to more resilient agricultural production under increasing environmental stress. The research is also relevant to SDG 13: Climate Action . Developing crop varieties capable of maintaining productivity under water-limited conditions represents an important component of agricultural adaptation to increasing climate variability. In addition, the study supports the broader objectives of SDG 15: Life on Land by promoting crop improvement strategies that can help sustain agricultural productivity on existing farmland under increasingly challenging environmental conditions. For maize breeding, the message is clear: The maize of the future should not only produce high yields when conditions are favorable—it must also remain productive when water becomes scarce. By combining multi-environment testing, drought-tolerance indices, and analytical approaches such as GGE biplot, maize breeders can identify genetic materials that offer both productivity and resilience . Such information provides an important scientific foundation for developing maize varieties better prepared for increasingly variable growing environments. Reference Bimantara, Y.M., Suwarno, W.B., Sobir, S., & Maharijaya, A. (2026). Yield Stability in Maize (Zea mays L.) Using GGE Biplot and Selection Indices Under Irrigated and Drought-Stress Conditions . SABRAO Journal of Breeding and Genetics, 58 (2), 643–654. Contact: Prof. Dr. Muhammad Azrai Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University azrai@agri.unhas.ac.id"]

["Finding Maize That Thrives When Water Runs Short", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sep 03 2025 /CORN-RG/– Climate change is making drought an increasingly serious challenge for maize production. For farmers, especially in tropical regions, a shortage of water during critical growth stages can result in smaller plants, reduced kernel development, and significantly lower harvests. But what if breeders could identify maize hybrids that continue producing well even when water becomes scarce? A recent study led by Muhammad Azrai and colleagues provides promising answers. Published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems , the study entitled “Integrating Multi-Trait and Multi-Index Approaches for Identifying Drought Tolerant Tropical Maize Genotypes” explored how multiple drought-tolerance indicators and advanced selection methods can be combined to identify resilient tropical maize hybrids. The researchers evaluated 33 tropical maize hybrids under both normal irrigation and controlled drought conditions at two locations in South Sulawesi, Indonesia: Maros and Bajeng . Water was withheld from 40 days after planting until approximately the milk stage , covering a critical period that includes flowering and early grain development. Rather than focusing only on grain yield, the researchers evaluated multiple characteristics related to plant growth, physiology, and productivity . This multi-trait approach provides a more comprehensive picture of how different maize genotypes respond when water becomes limited. The results clearly demonstrated the impact of drought on maize performance. Water stress reduced plant height by 12% , leaf area by 20.7% , chlorophyll-related SPAD values by 12.9% , and 1,000-kernel weight by 10.8% . Most importantly, average grain yield declined by approximately 23% compared with plants grown under normal irrigation. But not every maize hybrid responded in the same way. To identify the most promising materials, the researchers combined four drought-tolerance indices— Stress Tolerance Index (STI), Stress Susceptibility Index (SSI), Yield Stability Index (YSI), and Harvest Index (HI) —with the Multi-Trait Genotype-Ideotype Distance Index (MGIDI) . MGIDI can be understood as a tool for identifying plants that come closest to an “ideal maize.” Instead of selecting a genotype based on a single characteristic such as grain yield, the method considers several desirable traits simultaneously. This allows breeders to identify genotypes that combine productivity with characteristics needed to perform under stressful environmental conditions. Using the drought-tolerance indices, the researchers identified six promising hybrids: GE13, GE17, GE21, GE26, GE29, and GE32 . When these results were combined with the MGIDI analysis, GE13, GE21, and GE32 consistently emerged as the strongest candidates across both selection approaches. These findings demonstrate an important principle in modern maize breeding: the highest-yielding genotype under favorable conditions is not necessarily the best genotype when environmental conditions become stressful . By integrating multiple traits and selection indices, breeders can identify maize hybrids that offer a better balance between productivity and drought resilience. This approach is particularly important for tropical agriculture, where variability in rainfall and water availability can strongly influence crop performance. Developing maize hybrids capable of maintaining productivity under water-limited conditions can provide farmers with more resilient options for increasingly unpredictable growing environments. The research contributes directly to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by supporting the development of resilient crop varieties that can help sustain agricultural production under challenging environmental conditions. It also contributes to SDG 13: Climate Action , as developing drought-tolerant crops is an important component of adapting agricultural production systems to increasing climate variability. In addition, the study is relevant to SDG 15: Life on Land by supporting more efficient use of existing agricultural land. Improving crop adaptation to water-limited environments can help maintain agricultural productivity without relying solely on the expansion of cultivated areas. The message is simple but increasingly important: The maize of the future should not only produce high yields when conditions are favorable—it must also keep producing when water becomes scarce. By integrating multi-trait evaluation with advanced selection tools such as MGIDI, this research provides a scientific foundation for identifying tropical maize hybrids that combine productivity and drought resilience , supporting the development of more sustainable and climate-resilient maize production systems. Reference: Azrai, M., et al. (2025). Integrating Multi-Trait and Multi-Index Approaches for Identifying Drought Tolerant Tropical Maize Genotypes . Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 9 , 1608307. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2025.1608307 Contact: Prof. Dr. Muhammad Azrai Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University azrai@agri.unhas.ac.id"]

["Smarter Maize for Higher Yields: Finding the Right Plant Density", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Oct 31 2025 /CORN-RG/– How can farmers produce more maize without continuously expanding farmland? One promising answer is surprisingly simple: grow more plants on the same area—but make sure the plants are designed to handle the crowd. A 2025 study led by Muhammad Azrai and colleagues explored this idea by investigating how maize canopy architecture and physiological traits influence productivity when plants are grown at higher densities. The study, entitled “Canopy Architectural and Physiological Traits for Optimizing Maize Yield under High Planting Density,” was published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems . The researchers evaluated 13 maize hybrids at the Bajeng Experimental Station in Gowa Regency, South Sulawesi, Indonesia , using three planting densities of approximately 71,000, 81,000, and 95,000 plants per hectare . Why does planting density matter? When maize plants are grown closer together, competition for sunlight, water, nutrients, and space becomes more intense. Leaves can increasingly shade one another, limiting the amount of light reaching deeper layers of the crop canopy and potentially reducing photosynthetic efficiency. However, not all maize plants are built the same way. Maize hybrids with a more compact canopy and relatively upright leaves can distribute sunlight more effectively throughout the canopy. This architecture can help reduce excessive shading and potentially allow more plants to grow within the same area while maintaining efficient light interception and grain production. The results revealed an important finding: more plants do not automatically mean higher yield. The intermediate density of approximately 81,000 plants per hectare produced the highest average grain yield, reaching 12.85 tons per hectare . In comparison, the density of approximately 71,000 plants per hectare produced 11.54 tons per hectare, while increasing the population further to approximately 95,000 plants per hectare resulted in an average yield of 11.79 tons per hectare. This means that the intermediate planting density increased average grain yield by approximately 11% compared with the lower density . Increasing the population beyond this level did not provide an additional yield advantage. The finding highlights an important principle for maize production: the goal is not to maximize the number of plants, but to optimize the relationship between plant population, canopy structure, and available resources. The researchers also applied the Multi-Trait Genotype-Ideotype Distance Index (MGIDI) to identify maize hybrids that combined several desirable characteristics. MGIDI can be thought of as a way of searching for an “ideal maize plant.” Rather than selecting hybrids based on grain yield alone, the method considers multiple traits simultaneously. This allows breeders to identify plants that combine high productivity, desirable canopy architecture, physiological performance, and adaptation to increased planting density . Through this approach, G4, G2, and G5 emerged as promising hybrids with broad adaptability across the evaluated planting densities. These genotypes provide valuable breeding materials for developing maize hybrids better suited to more intensive production systems. The study demonstrates that increasing maize productivity does not necessarily require expanding agricultural land. Instead, productivity can be improved by combining better-adapted hybrids with optimized planting density and more efficient canopy architecture . This concept is known as sustainable intensification —producing more from existing agricultural land while using resources more efficiently. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by providing scientific approaches for increasing crop productivity and supporting more efficient food and feed production. It is also relevant to SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production , as optimizing plant density and crop architecture can contribute to more efficient use of agricultural resources. In addition, the study supports SDG 15: Life on Land . Increasing productivity on existing farmland can contribute to sustainable land use and potentially reduce pressure to expand agricultural production into natural ecosystems. The message is clear: Future maize productivity is not simply about planting more—it is about designing smarter plants and finding the right space for them to thrive. By combining optimized planting density with maize hybrids that possess favorable canopy and physiological traits, breeders and farmers can move toward production systems capable of generating higher yields from existing farmland while using available resources more efficiently . Canopy Architectural and Physiological Traits for Optimizing Maize Yield under High Planting Density . Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 9 , 1469305. ["Understanding the Genetic Clues Behind Better Maize", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, August 6, 2026/CORN-RG/– Why can one maize hybrid perform well in one location but differently in another? The answer lies in a complex interaction between genetics and the environment . For plant breeders, understanding this relationship is essential because developing a superior maize variety requires more than simply selecting the plant with the highest yield. But which plant traits are reliably inherited, and which ones can help breeders identify more productive maize? A 2026 study by A. M. Aditya Wardana, Muhammad Azrai, and colleagues explored this question by examining genetic diversity, heritability, and relationships among important agronomic traits in hybrid maize. The study, entitled “Genetic Diversity, Heritability, Trait Correlation of Hybrid Maize Evaluated in Two Contrasting Topologies,” was published in the Gunung Djati Conference Series , Volume 66, as part of the Proceedings of the International Conference on Perennial Crops . The researchers evaluated eight maize genotypes , consisting of five experimental hybrids and three commercial varieties , in two contrasting environments in Indonesia. Field experiments were conducted from July to September 2025 in Sinoa, Bantaeng Regency, South Sulawesi, at 512 meters above sea level , and Tomohon, North Sulawesi, at 1,006 meters above sea level . Testing the same maize materials in contrasting environments allowed the researchers to investigate how genetic differences and growing conditions influence important plant characteristics. One of the key concepts examined was heritability —the extent to which differences in a particular trait are associated with genetic variation rather than environmental influences. For breeders, traits with higher heritability can provide useful information because their expression may be more consistently passed from one generation to the next. Several traits showed high heritability , including ear height, leaf width, number of kernels, ear length, and ear diameter . Among these characteristics, ear length showed particularly high heritability , indicating its potential value as a selection criterion in maize breeding. The researchers also investigated how different plant characteristics were related to grain yield. One result stood out: fresh ear weight showed a very strong positive correlation with grain yield (r = 0.95) . This means that, within the materials and environments evaluated in the study, plants with greater fresh ear weight also tended to produce higher grain yields. Other characteristics, including ear length, ear diameter, kernel-related traits, and several leaf characteristics , were also positively associated with productivity. These relationships provide breeders with useful clues when identifying promising maize materials. However, the study also revealed an important limitation: genetic variability among the evaluated hybrids was relatively narrow . Genetic diversity is one of the foundations of crop improvement. When breeding materials contain greater useful genetic variation, breeders have more opportunities to combine desirable characteristics and generate improved varieties. The narrow variability observed in this study therefore highlights the importance of maintaining and broadening genetic diversity in future maize breeding programs. The contrasting environments also reinforced another important lesson: grain yield cannot be understood from genetics alone . Environmental conditions can substantially influence how genetic potential is expressed. A hybrid that performs well in one location may respond differently when grown at another altitude or under different environmental conditions. For this reason, evaluating promising maize materials across multiple environments remains essential before breeders can determine whether a genotype is broadly adapted or better suited to particular growing conditions. The study contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by strengthening the scientific foundation for developing productive and better-adapted crop varieties. It is also relevant to SDG 15: Life on Land , particularly through the sustainable use of plant genetic resources. Understanding genetic diversity, heritability, and environmental responses can help breeding programs use available maize germplasm more effectively while developing varieties suited to diverse agroecological conditions. The message for maize breeding is clear: Better maize does not come from yield alone—it comes from understanding which genetic traits consistently help plants perform better. By examining the genetic clues hidden in ears, kernels, leaves, and plant architecture , breeders can make more informed selections and build a stronger foundation for developing productive and adaptable maize varieties for the future. ["Reading Maize Leaves: Simple Clues to Drought Tolerance", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, April 2026 /CORN-RG/– Drought is becoming an increasingly serious challenge for maize production. When water becomes scarce, plants cannot escape the stress—they must adjust. Interestingly, maize plants provide visible and measurable signals of how well they are coping. Their leaves may roll, lose their green color, and ultimately produce less grain. But can these simple changes in maize leaves help scientists identify plants that are better able to withstand drought? A 2026 study by Suwardi, Muhammad Azrai, and colleagues investigated this question by examining two physiological indicators that can be measured relatively easily in the field: leaf rolling and leaf greenness measured using the SPAD chlorophyll index . The study, entitled “Evaluation of Leaf Rolling and SPAD Chlorophyll Index as Physiological Indicators for Drought Tolerance in Maize,” was published in IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science as part of the 7TH-ICAGRI-2025 proceedings. The researchers evaluated 12 maize genotypes under three water conditions: normal irrigation, moderate drought, and severe drought . By comparing plant responses across different levels of water stress, they investigated whether changes in leaf characteristics could provide useful clues about drought tolerance and grain productivity. One of the indicators was leaf rolling . When maize experiences water stress, its leaves may roll inward, reducing the leaf surface exposed to sunlight and the surrounding air. This response can help limit water loss, although severe leaf rolling can also indicate that the plant is experiencing substantial stress. The second indicator was the SPAD chlorophyll index , a rapid and non-destructive measurement of leaf greenness associated with chlorophyll status. Maintaining greener leaves during drought may indicate that a plant is better able to preserve its photosynthetic machinery and continue supporting growth and grain development. The results clearly demonstrated the impact of water limitation on maize productivity. Under normal irrigation, grain yields among the evaluated genotypes ranged from approximately 6.4 to 12.2 tonnes per hectare . As drought stress intensified, yields declined substantially. However, not all maize genotypes responded in the same way . One of the most informative findings was the relationship between leaf greenness and grain productivity. The SPAD measurement at 75 days after sowing showed a positive correlation with grain yield (r = 0.61) . This suggests that genotypes capable of maintaining greener leaves later in the growing period tended to maintain better productivity under the conditions evaluated. Leaf rolling showed a different pattern. Greater leaf rolling was generally associated with lower grain yield. In practical terms, maize plants that remained relatively green and exhibited less severe leaf rolling tended to perform better under drought. Using these physiological responses together with yield performance, the researchers identified several promising drought-tolerant materials, particularly CH-4, CH-5, CH-6, CH-8, and Bisi-2 . The study also revealed an interesting exception. NK 22 maintained relatively high grain yield despite showing severe leaf rolling , suggesting that drought tolerance cannot always be explained by a single visible characteristic. Other physiological or genetic mechanisms may also help certain maize genotypes maintain productivity under water stress. This finding highlights an important principle for plant breeding: simple physiological indicators are valuable screening tools, but they are most powerful when interpreted together with yield and other plant characteristics . For breeders, measurements such as leaf rolling and SPAD offer a practical advantage. They can provide relatively rapid and non-destructive information about how plants respond to water stress, helping researchers screen breeding materials and identify promising genotypes for more detailed evaluation. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by supporting efforts to develop maize varieties capable of maintaining agricultural productivity under increasingly challenging growing conditions. It is also strongly connected to SDG 13: Climate Action , as identifying and developing drought-resilient crops is an important strategy for adapting agricultural systems to increasing climate variability and water scarcity. In addition, the study supports SDG 15: Life on Land through the development of crop varieties better adapted to water-limited agricultural environments, contributing to more resilient and sustainable use of existing farmland. The message is simple: Sometimes, the color and shape of a maize leaf can tell scientists an important story about how well the plant is coping with drought. By combining accessible physiological indicators such as leaf rolling and SPAD chlorophyll measurements with grain-yield evaluation, breeders can improve drought screening and accelerate the identification of maize materials better prepared for increasingly water-limited environments. ["DNA Fingerprinting: Giving Indonesian Maize Its Genetic Identity", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Dec 06 2025 /CORN-RG/– A maize seed may look ordinary, but hidden inside it is a unique genetic identity. Just as fingerprints can distinguish one person from another, DNA can help scientists distinguish maize varieties, trace their parental lines, and safeguard valuable genetic resources. But why does a maize hybrid need its own genetic “identity card”? A 2025 study by Slamet Bambang Priyanto, Lesty Ayu Bidhari, Roy Efendi, Bunyamin Zainuddin, Nining Nurini Andayani, and Muhammad Azrai explored this question using DNA fingerprinting. The study, entitled “DNA Profiling of Indonesian Maize Hybrids and their Parental Lines Using SSR Markers,” was published in Agriculture (Poľnohospodárstvo) . For hybrid maize, maintaining genetic identity and purity is essential. Hybrid seed production depends on specific parental lines, and unintended contamination or genetic changes during seed multiplication can compromise the consistency of seed stocks. Identification based solely on visible plant characteristics can also be challenging because many traits are influenced by environmental conditions. DNA markers provide another layer of information—one that comes directly from the plant's genetic material. The researchers examined four Indonesian maize hybrids— JH 27, JH 45, JH 37, and NASA 29 —together with their parental lines. They used 57 Simple Sequence Repeat (SSR) markers , short and highly variable regions of DNA that can reveal genetic differences among maize genotypes. Across the evaluated materials, the SSR analysis detected 230 alleles , with an average of approximately four alleles per marker. These genetic differences allowed the researchers to distinguish relationships among the hybrids and their parental lines. The analysis was somewhat like constructing a genetic family tree . At a similarity coefficient of 42% , the evaluated maize genotypes were separated into four major groups , revealing patterns of genetic similarity and diversity among the materials. More importantly, the researchers identified distinctive SSR profiles that could serve as genetic fingerprints for individual maize hybrids. For example, JH 27 could be distinguished using a combination of 12 SSR markers , while informative marker profiles were also identified for JH 45, JH 37, and NASA 29 . These DNA fingerprints are more than scientific labels. For maize breeders and seed producers, reliable molecular profiles can help verify varietal identity, monitor genetic purity, characterize parental lines, assess genetic relationships, and support the selection of genetically diverse breeding materials . This information can also help breeders design crosses more strategically by providing a clearer understanding of the genetic relationships among potential parents. The study therefore demonstrates how molecular tools can complement conventional plant breeding. While field evaluation remains essential for determining how maize performs in real growing environments, DNA markers provide information about genetic identity that cannot always be obtained reliably from plant appearance alone. This is particularly important for foundational seed stocks , where maintaining the identity and genetic purity of parental materials is critical for producing consistent hybrid seed. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by strengthening the scientific foundation for reliable crop improvement and quality seed production. It is also particularly relevant to SDG 15: Life on Land , which includes the conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources. Characterizing maize diversity at the DNA level can help researchers document, manage, and utilize valuable genetic materials more effectively for future breeding programs. The message is clear: Every maize seed carries more than the potential to become a plant—it also carries a genetic identity that can be read, documented, and safeguarded. By using SSR-based DNA fingerprinting, researchers can help protect the genetic identity of Indonesian maize hybrids and their parental lines, strengthen seed purity management, and provide breeders with valuable information for developing the next generation of improved maize varieties. ["When Artificial Intelligence Learns to Read a Maize Fie", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Jul 15 2026 /CORN-RG/– What if farmers and agricultural researchers could predict maize yield before harvest by allowing artificial intelligence to “read” the plants and their management conditions? This possibility is becoming increasingly realistic as artificial intelligence helps researchers uncover complex relationships among crop characteristics, cultivation practices, and productivity. But can artificial intelligence really learn which combinations of plant traits and management practices are most closely associated with maize yield? A 2026 study by Muhammad Aqil, Muhammad Azrai, Nining Nurini Andayani, and colleagues explored this question by applying advanced machine-learning approaches to maize production data. The study, entitled “Transformer-based modeling of maize yield and biomass using integrated agronomic and management traits,” was published in the Journal of Agriculture and Food Research . The research brought artificial intelligence directly into the maize field. Conducted at the Maros Experimental Station in South Sulawesi, Indonesia , the experiment evaluated different planting arrangements and nano-fertilizer application times while collecting information on plant growth, leaf characteristics, chlorophyll status, canopy condition, grain yield, biomass, and crop management. These data were then used to train artificial intelligence models to recognize complex patterns that may be difficult to identify through individual observations alone. The researchers compared four prediction approaches: Tab-Transformer, FT-Transformer, Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Random Forest . The results were promising. For grain-yield prediction, the Tab-Transformer achieved the best performance, with an R² value of 0.93 . This was followed by the FT-Transformer (R² = 0.91) , Random Forest (R² = 0.88) , and ANN (R² = 0.77) . In practical terms, the high predictive performance of the Transformer-based models demonstrates their ability to capture relationships between maize characteristics, management practices, and final productivity within the conditions represented by the study data. Predicting biomass proved more challenging. Nevertheless, the Transformer-based approaches still outperformed the conventional models evaluated in the study, demonstrating their potential for analyzing complex agricultural datasets. But perhaps one of the most interesting contributions of the research was that the models did more than generate predictions. They also helped reveal which groups of variables contributed most strongly to grain-yield prediction . Biomass-related traits accounted for 45.2% of the importance in predicting grain yield , while management factors contributed 39.8% . This highlights the substantial role of crop-management decisions alongside measurable plant characteristics. The finding carries an important message: artificial intelligence does not make good agronomy less important—it can help researchers understand it better. Planting arrangements, fertilizer timing, plant growth, canopy development, and other crop characteristics interact in complex ways. Machine-learning approaches can help analyze these relationships simultaneously, turning large amounts of agricultural data into information that may support better decision-making. AI should therefore not be viewed as a replacement for farmers, plant scientists, or agronomists. Instead, it can serve as a decision-support tool , complementing field experience and scientific knowledge with the ability to detect patterns across many interacting variables. This research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by advancing data-driven approaches that can support more productive and efficient crop-production systems. It is also relevant to SDG 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure , particularly through the integration of artificial intelligence and digital analytical methods into agricultural research and innovation. In the longer term, such technologies may also contribute to SDG 1: No Poverty by supporting innovations that improve agricultural decision-making, resource-use efficiency, and productivity. However, realizing these benefits will depend on translating research models into practical and accessible tools for agricultural users. The future of maize production may therefore combine two complementary forms of intelligence: the experience of people who understand the field and artificial intelligence capable of finding patterns hidden within agricultural data. By bringing together agronomic knowledge, crop-management information, and Transformer-based modeling, this research demonstrates how agricultural data can be transformed into more powerful insights for the future of maize production. Reference: Aqil, M., Azrai, M., Andayani, N. N., et al. (2026). Transformer-based modeling of maize yield and biomass using integrated agronomic and management traits . Journal of Agriculture and Food Research, 30 , 103136. Contact: Prof. Dr. Muhammad Azrai Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University azrai@agri.unhas.ac.id"]

["From Breeding to Market: Accelerating the Commercialization of UNHAS Hybrid Maize", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, 2025 /CORN-RG/– Developing a promising maize hybrid in a research field is only the beginning. For a new hybrid to benefit farmers, it must move through a much longer pathway—from breeding and selection to multi-location testing, variety release, seed production, and eventually commercialization. But how can university-developed maize innovations move more quickly from research plots into the national seed industry and farmers’ fields? This challenge is being addressed through the research project entitled “Accelerating the Downstream Development and Commercialization of UNHAS Hybrid Maize through the Release of New Superior Varieties,” led by Dr. Muhammad Azrai, S.P., M.P. from Universitas Hasanuddin (UNHAS) . The project is implemented under the 2025 Priority Research Downstreaming Scheme of the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, and Technology (Kemdiktisaintek), Indonesia . Its central objective is to accelerate the transformation of maize breeding results developed through research into new superior hybrid varieties that can progress toward official release, seed production, and commercialization . A key element of the project is collaboration between Universitas Hasanuddin and PT Agrosid Manunggal Sentosa , a national seed company engaged in the production of food crop and horticultural seeds. This university–industry partnership connects scientific expertise in maize breeding with the facilities, seed-production capacity, and market experience needed to move promising genetic materials closer to practical agricultural use. The process begins long before a hybrid reaches farmers. The breeding pipeline starts with the development of base populations , followed by the development and selection of lines until sufficiently homozygous parental materials are obtained. Combining ability is then evaluated to determine which parental lines have the greatest potential for producing superior hybrid combinations. General Combining Ability (GCA) is used during the earlier stages of selection to identify parental lines with strong overall breeding value, while Specific Combining Ability (SCA) becomes increasingly important at intermediate and advanced stages to identify particular parental combinations capable of producing promising hybrids. The strongest hybrid candidates then move through a progressive downstreaming pathway involving multi-location and adaptation trials, variety release, variety protection, seed production, and commercialization . This stepwise process is essential because a promising hybrid must offer more than high performance in a single research environment. Before commercialization, candidate varieties need to demonstrate sufficient performance and adaptation across relevant growing environments while meeting the requirements for variety release and seed development. The project has already generated several important breeding outputs. To date, four sets of promising hybrid maize candidates have been identified for further adaptation trials toward the development and release of new superior varieties . The breeding and selection program has also identified 25 promising dent-type maize hybrids with high starch quality . These materials provide opportunities for developing maize varieties that combine agronomic performance with grain characteristics relevant to downstream utilization. In addition, 32 selected maize hybrids with high biomass potential have been identified, broadening the potential value of the breeding program beyond grain yield alone and providing genetic materials for further evaluation and development. These achievements illustrate an important principle of agricultural innovation: successful breeding does not end when a promising genotype is identified . Research creates greater impact when promising genetic materials can move through validation, regulatory processes, seed multiplication, and industry partnerships until improved varieties become accessible to users. The collaboration between UNHAS and PT Agrosid Manunggal Sentosa therefore integrates multiple stages of the innovation pathway—from breeding and selection to multi-location evaluation, variety release and protection, seed production, and commercialization . The initiative contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by supporting the development and delivery of improved maize varieties that can strengthen agricultural productivity and national seed systems. It is also closely connected to SDG 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure , particularly through the translation of university research into agricultural innovation and the strengthening of collaboration between research institutions and the seed industry. The university–industry partnership further supports SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals , demonstrating how collaboration between academic research and private-sector expertise can help move agricultural innovations toward wider application. The message behind this research downstreaming initiative is clear: A superior maize hybrid creates its greatest value not when it remains in a research plot, but when scientific innovation can be transformed into a reliable variety, quality seed, and a product that reaches farmers. Through the integration of maize breeding, rigorous selection, multi-location testing, variety release, seed production, and commercialization , the project is building a pathway for UNHAS maize innovations to progress from scientific research toward competitive products for Indonesia’s maize seed industry.
