["Planting Smarter: Finding the Right Density for Higher Maize Yield", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Oct 31 2025 /CORN-RG/– As the global population grows, agriculture faces a fundamental challenge: How can we produce more food from limited farmland without putting greater pressure on the environment? For maize, one promising solution may lie not in expanding farmland, but in arranging plants more efficiently and selecting hybrids that can thrive when grown closer together. But does planting more maize plants in the same field always produce more grain? A 2025 study led by Muhammad Azrai and colleagues investigated this question by examining how maize canopy architecture and physiological characteristics influence productivity under different planting densities. The study, entitled “Canopy Architectural and Physiological Traits for Optimizing Maize Yield under High Planting Density,” was published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems on 31 October 2025 . The researchers evaluated 13 maize hybrids at the Bajeng Experimental Station in Gowa Regency, Indonesia . The experiment compared three planting densities: approximately 71,000 plants per hectare (standard density), 81,000 plants per hectare (intermediate density), and 95,000 plants per hectare (intensive density) . The goal was to determine whether increasing the number of plants per hectare could improve productivity and, importantly, which types of maize plants were best suited to increasingly crowded growing conditions. When maize plants grow closer together, competition becomes more intense. Individual plants must compete for sunlight, water, nutrients, and growing space . Excessive crowding can increase shading within the canopy and trigger changes in plant growth that may ultimately limit grain production. This is where canopy architecture becomes important. Maize hybrids with more upright leaves can improve light distribution within dense crop canopies by reducing excessive shading. This allows sunlight to penetrate deeper into the canopy, helping maintain photosynthetic activity across a larger proportion of the plant. Such characteristics can make certain maize genotypes better suited to high-density production systems. The results revealed an important lesson: More plants do not automatically mean more grain. The intermediate density of approximately 81,000 plants per hectare produced the highest average grain yield at 12.85 tons per hectare . In comparison, the standard density of approximately 71,000 plants per hectare produced 11.54 tons per hectare , while the intensive density of approximately 95,000 plants per hectare produced 11.79 tons per hectare . This means that the intermediate density increased average yield by approximately 11% compared with the standard density . However, increasing the population further to 95,000 plants per hectare did not produce an additional yield advantage. The finding illustrates a fundamental principle of crop management: there is an optimum balance between plant population and competition . Too few plants may leave available resources underutilized, while too many can intensify competition to the point that the productivity of individual plants declines. The researchers also used the Multi-Trait Genotype-Ideotype Distance Index (MGIDI) to identify maize hybrids combining multiple desirable characteristics. Rather than selecting plants based on grain yield alone, MGIDI allows breeders to consider several traits simultaneously and identify genotypes that come closest to a desired plant type or “ideotype.” Using this approach, G4, G2, and G5 emerged as promising hybrids with broad adaptability across the evaluated planting densities. These genotypes demonstrated characteristics that make them valuable candidates for developing maize better suited to more intensive production systems. The study demonstrates that increasing maize productivity is not simply a matter of fitting as many plants as possible into a hectare. Plant density, canopy architecture, physiology, and genetics must work together. This approach is closely aligned with the concept of sustainable intensification —increasing agricultural productivity from existing farmland while improving the efficiency with which land and other resources are used. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by providing scientific strategies for increasing maize productivity and supporting more efficient crop production. It is also relevant to SDG 15: Life on Land , as improving productivity on existing agricultural land can contribute to more efficient land use and potentially reduce pressure for agricultural expansion into natural ecosystems. The message is clear: The future of maize production is not simply about planting more—it is about planting smarter. By combining the right planting density with maize hybrids possessing suitable canopy architecture and physiological characteristics , breeders and farmers can make better use of every hectare and move toward more productive and sustainable maize production systems. Reference: Azrai, M., Aqil, M., Efendi, R., Zainuddin, B., Syam’un, E., Anshori, M. F., Riadi, M., Priyanto, S. B., Andayani, N. N., Yasin, M., Laurenze, R., & Syam, A. (2025). Canopy architectural and physiological traits for optimizing maize yield under high planting density . Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 9 , 1469305. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2025.1469305 Contact: Prof. Dr. Muhammad Azrai Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University azrai@agri.unhas.ac.id"]

["Maize That Can Do More with Less Water", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sep 03 2025 /CORN-RG/– Imagine a maize field under the blazing tropical sun. The soil is drying, rainfall has become unpredictable, and every drop of water matters. For farmers, drought can mean more than stressed plants—it can mean lower harvests and greater uncertainty in crop production. Maize is particularly vulnerable when water becomes scarce during critical growth stages such as flowering and grain development. This makes drought tolerance an increasingly important target for maize breeding. But can scientists identify maize hybrids that continue producing well even when water becomes limited? A 2025 study led by Muhammad Azrai and colleagues provides promising answers. The study, entitled “Integrating Multi-Trait and Multi-Index Approaches for Identifying Drought Tolerant Tropical Maize Genotypes,” was published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems on 3 September 2025 . The researchers evaluated 33 tropical maize hybrids under both normal irrigation and water-limited conditions at two locations in South Sulawesi, Indonesia . The objective was not simply to identify the highest-yielding hybrids, but to determine which genotypes could combine productivity with greater resilience when water became scarce. To achieve this, the researchers examined multiple characteristics related to plant growth, leaf development, chlorophyll status, ear characteristics, kernel development, and grain yield . This broader approach is important because drought tolerance is not controlled by a single characteristic. It results from multiple plant responses working together. The impact of drought was clearly visible. Under water stress, plant height decreased by approximately 12% , while chlorophyll-related SPAD values declined by 12.9% and 1,000-kernel weight fell by 10.8% . Most importantly, average grain yield decreased by approximately 23% compared with plants grown under normal water conditions. Yet the results also revealed something encouraging: Not all maize hybrids responded to drought in the same way. This variation gives plant breeders an opportunity to identify genetic materials that can better maintain performance under water-limited conditions. The researchers used several drought-tolerance indices to compare hybrid performance under normal and drought conditions. These included the Stress Tolerance Index (STI), Stress Susceptibility Index (SSI), Yield Stability Index (YSI), and Harvest Index (HI) . Using these indices, six promising hybrids—GE13, GE17, GE21, GE26, GE29, and GE32—were identified as potential drought-tolerant materials . But drought tolerance involves more than grain yield alone. To obtain a more comprehensive assessment, the researchers also applied the Multi-Trait Genotype-Ideotype Distance Index (MGIDI) , a selection approach that allows breeders to evaluate several desirable plant characteristics simultaneously. MGIDI can be thought of as a way of searching for an “ideal maize plant.” Instead of selecting a hybrid because it performs well for only one characteristic, breeders can identify plants that combine multiple desirable traits needed to perform under challenging conditions. When the results from the drought-tolerance indices and MGIDI analysis were considered together, GE13, GE21, and GE32 emerged as particularly promising hybrids , as they were consistently selected by both approaches. This finding demonstrates an important principle for modern crop improvement: breeding for drought tolerance requires looking at the whole plant, not just its final yield . By combining grain-yield performance with physiological, morphological, and other agronomic characteristics, breeders can make more informed decisions about which genetic materials should advance in a breeding program. The research contributes directly to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by supporting the development of resilient crop varieties that can help sustain agricultural production under water-limited conditions. It also strongly supports SDG 13: Climate Action , as developing drought-tolerant crops is an important strategy for helping agricultural systems adapt to increasing climate variability. In addition, the study is relevant to SDG 15: Life on Land by supporting more resilient and efficient use of existing agricultural land under increasingly challenging environmental conditions. The message is powerful: The future of maize may depend not only on giving plants more water, but on developing plants that can do more with less. By combining multiple drought-tolerance indices with advanced multi-trait selection, researchers can identify tropical maize hybrids that offer a better balance between productivity and drought resilience , providing valuable genetic materials for the development of maize varieties better prepared for a changing climate. Reference: Azrai, M., et al. (2025). Integrating Multi-Trait and Multi-Index Approaches for Identifying Drought Tolerant Tropical Maize Genotypes . Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 9 , 1608307. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2025.1608307 Contact: Prof. Dr. Muhammad Azrai Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University azrai@agri.unhas.ac.id"]

["From Innovation to Farmers: Accelerating Jagung Jago Unhas Seed Production", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia /CORN-RG/– Developing a superior maize variety is an important scientific achievement, but the impact of innovation is only fully realized when quality seed can be produced at scale and made accessible to farmers. The initiative contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2): Zero Hunger by supporting access to improved maize seed and strengthening the technological foundation for productive maize cultivation. The collaboration between UNHAS and its commercialization partner further reflects SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals , demonstrating the importance of university–industry partnerships in accelerating the adoption and dissemination of agricultural innovation. Through the downstreaming of Jagung Jago Unhas (JJUH) , Hasanuddin University is strengthening the connection between maize breeding, seed production, commercialization, and agricultural application —helping transform scientific innovation into tangible value for farmers and Indonesia’s maize seed industry. ["One Hybrid, Many Landscapes: Finding Maize That Can Thrive Anywhere", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Aug 31 2026 /RICE-RG/– Maize is a vital crop for food, animal feed, and industry, but farmers face a familiar problem: a hybrid that performs well in one place may disappoint in another. ["Development and Updating of the WeRise Web System Based on Rice Plant Modeling to Support Climate Change Resilience Efforts in South Sulawesi (2023-2024)", "South Sulawesi, Indonesia\\'s top rice-producing province, has been tasked by the president to bolster rice production, especially in Eastern Indonesia. However, climate change poses significant challenges, necessitating resilience efforts to maintain stable output. Hasanuddin University (Unhas) plays a key role in these efforts, collaborating with international partners like Taiwan’s International Cooperation and Development Fund (ICDF) and the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) to develop agronomic solutions for smallholder farmers. A focal point of this collaboration is the digitalization of rice farming, particularly through IRRI’s WeRise system, which predicts rice productivity and optimal planting times to mitigate climate change impacts. However, the system’s data in South Sulawesi is outdated, limited to 2018 and one location, and relies on older rice varieties less effective against climate change. To address this, the WeRise system requires updating with refined climatological data from Maros and Gowa Regencies and field experiments using IRRI’s Oryza v3 crop model for early maturing rice varieties. This research, part of ICDF-Unhas’ roadmap, aims to enhance climate resilience in rice production. ICDF provides weather data, IRRI offers guidance, and Unhas hosts the research. Expected outcomes include international publications, crop data for early maturing varieties, and strengthened collaboration between Unhas and IRRI, positioning Unhas as a contributor to global rice development."]

["Development of Superior Early Rice Varieties in Support of IP 400 at Various Nitrogen Doses Based on Vegetation Index (2023-2024)", "Rice development is a critical priority for ensuring food security in Indonesia. Hasanuddin University (UNHAS), as a leading higher education institution, is actively engaged in agrocomplex tridarma activities aimed at enhancing rice productivity. One of the key strategic initiatives in this domain is the IP 400 concept, which promotes planting rice four times in a single season on the same land. This approach is designed to boost production through the use of early-maturing rice varieties. However, the IP 400 concept faces challenges, including increased resistance to plant pests, soil degradation due to excessive inorganic fertilizer use, and potential environmental harm. To address these issues, the development of a sustainable agricultural system is essential. This includes optimizing fertilization methods by integrating compost and organic-inorganic fertilizers, alongside the use of early-maturing rice seeds. Nitrogen (N) fertilizer application plays a crucial role in determining rice productivity and grain quality, influencing starch structure, gene expression related to grain quality, and amino acid metabolism. However, the effectiveness of N fertilizer depends on precise and careful evaluation. Smart farming technologies, such as drone-based crop monitoring, offer a promising solution. While drones have been widely adopted in modern agriculture, their application in the context of sustainable IP 400 systems remains underexplored. This research aims to bridge this gap by optimizing the IP 400 concept through improved fertilization strategies and the integration of early-maturing rice varieties, supported by smart farming techniques. By leveraging drone technology for precise crop evaluation, this study seeks to enhance the productivity and sustainability of the IP 400 system, ensuring long-term food security and environmental resilience in Indonesia."]

["Screening Rice Tolerance to Drought and/or Salinity Through Development Methods Image-Based Phenotyping (2021-2023)", "Phenomics is an emerging field focused on characterizing a species\\' complete set of phenotypes. Image-based phenotyping, a key tool in this domain, enables the analysis of plant traits such as anatomy, growth, shape, and surface features across various organs like leaves and roots. This method significantly accelerates the screening and selection process, reducing the time required from weeks to mere minutes or even seconds. As a result, identifying drought- and salinity-tolerant plants becomes more efficient. This study aims to develop a simple, user-friendly, image-based phenotyping method in Indonesia for screening drought- and salinity-tolerant rice varieties. The research will evaluate eight rice varieties over three years: Year I involves hydroponic cultivation, Year II includes pot testing, and Year III focuses on field trials in dry, saline, and normal conditions. The goal is to identify key morphological, physiological, and phenotypic traits that contribute to stress tolerance, which will then inform the development of image-based phenotyping selection methods for rice."]

["Development of Early-maturing Rice Model with IRRI (2024)", "The Development of an Early-Maturing Rice Model in collaboration with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in 2024 aims to create a high-yielding, fast-growing rice production system that enhances food security, optimizes resource use, and improves climate resilience . This initiative focuses on accelerating rice growth cycles while maintaining stable yields, pest resistance, and adaptability to diverse environmental conditions . The project integrates advanced breeding techniques, precision agriculture, and climate-smart technologies to develop a scalable model for early-maturing rice varieties . Key research activities include genetic selection, field trials, and digital modeling to optimize growth parameters such as planting density, irrigation efficiency, and nutrient management . Additionally remote sensing tools, and data analytics support real-time monitoring of rice growth and environmental impacts. Farmer engagement, capacity-building programs, and technology transfer workshops are conducted to facilitate the adoption of this efficient rice production system . The collaboration with IRRI provides cutting-edge research expertise, enabling the development of sustainable rice farming practices that enhance productivity, resilience, and long-term food security in Indonesia and beyond."]

["Mutation induction of double haploid strains for high production, early maturing, and abiotic tolerant (2024)", "The mutation induction of double haploid (DH) strains in 2024 aims to develop high-yielding, early-maturing, and abiotic stress-tolerant rice varieties through advanced breeding techniques. This research focuses on improving rice adaptability to climate change, soil limitations, and water stress , ensuring sustainable rice production in challenging environments. Using mutation breeding and doubled haploid technology , selected rice strains undergo mutation induction to enhance genetic diversity and desirable agronomic traits . This process accelerates the development of homozygous rice lines , allowing researchers to rapidly select varieties with superior yield potential, early maturity, and tolerance to drought, salinity, and extreme temperatures . Field trials and controlled experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of these mutant DH lines across different agroecological zones. Key phenotypic and physiological traits such as growth duration, grain quality, pest resistance, and yield stability are assessed under stress conditions. Additionally, molecular and genomic analysis supports the identification of promising genetic traits for further breeding programs. The findings from this study contribute to rice breeding innovation, food security, and climate resilience strategies . The development of these high-performing rice varieties provides new opportunities for farmers, researchers, and policymakers to enhance rice production efficiency and sustainability in the future."]

["Evaluation of adaptive early maturing rice in South Sulawesi (2022-2023)", "The evaluation of adaptive early maturing rice in South Sulawesi (2022-2023) was conducted to assess the performance of rice varieties that can mature in a shorter period while maintaining high productivity and adaptability to local environmental conditions. During the evaluation, multiple early maturing rice varieties were tested across various locations in South Sulawesi , including Sidrap, Bone, Luwu Utara, Pinrang, and Wajo . The research focused on key agronomic parameters such as growth duration, yield potential, resistance to pests and diseases, and tolerance to climatic stresses like drought and flooding . Regular field observations, data collection, and farmer participatory assessments were conducted to measure the adaptability of these varieties under different agroecological conditions. The study also incorporated smart farming technologies such as drone , including automatic weather stations and precision farming tools , to optimize the evaluation process. Results from this study provided valuable insights for future rice breeding programs and the development of climate-resilient agriculture in the region. The findings have contributed to improving seed selection, guiding farmer adoption strategies, and supporting government initiatives in sustainable rice production in South Sulawesi."]

["Cooperation of Rice Seed Assistance in South Sulawesi with ICDF Taiwan from 2017-2023", "The Cooperation of Rice Seed Assistance in South Sulawesi between the Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University (Unhas) and the Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund (ICDF) from 2017 to 2023 has significantly contributed to enhancing rice seed production and food security. ["Deteksi Asam Klorogenik menggunakan Pelarut NADES (Natural Deep Eutectic Solvent) pada Daun Kopi sebagai Atraktan terhadap Imago Penggerek Buah Kakao (Conopomorpha cramerella Snellen)", "Penggerek buah kakao merupakan hama utama yang dapat menimbulkan kerusakan/masalah besar jika tidak dikelola/dikendalikan padahal tanaman kakao merupakan penghasil devisa negara. ["Industrial-scale production of the ‘Mikrobat’ biofertilizer as a stimulant for rice plant productivity and health", "2022", "Industrial-scale production of the 'Mikrobat' biofertilizer emphasizes the use of plant growth–promoting microbes—particularly various strains of Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Azotobacter, Lactobacillus, and Paenibacillus polymyxa —in formulating a biofertilizer rich in benefits for rice plants."]

["Exploration and Identification of Indigenous Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi in Bulukumba Rubber Agroforestry Plantations as Starter Agents", "2023", "This project focuses on exploring and identifying native arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) in rubber-based agroforestry systems in Bulukumba—specifically within plantations intercropped with species like cloves and durian—and evaluating their potential as starter bioagents for enhancing tree health and soil fertility."]

["Rice Farmers’ Adoption and Economic Benefits of Integrated Pest Management in South Sulawesi Province, Indonesia", "2023", "The study examined the adoption levels and economic benefits of IPM among rice farmers in South Sulawesi Province, Indonesia. The research was conducted in two main rice producing areas of the province, Soppeng and Maros Regencies. Simple random sampling was employed in selecting 20% of the total populations, resulting in sample sizes of 69 repondents in Soppeng and 52 respondents in Maros. A structured questionnaire was used in direct interview with the selected respondents to obtain data on their socio-economic profile, IPM implementation, and profit gained from IPM. Percentage was used to present the data. In both regencies, overall IPM adoption rates were high with most respondents were categorized as medium and high IPM adopters with adoption rates of 85.1% in Soppeng and 88.5% in Maros. The medium and high IPM adopters gained more economic profits of 26.9% in Soppeng and 16%% in Maros in comparison to the low IPM adopters. The high adoption rates indicated that although the nationwide IPM Program has ended in late 1990’s, there was a continuous technological transfer from older farmers who participated in IPM-FFS to younger farmer generation. In order to improve IPM implementation by the younger farmers, they need to be provided with intensive extension support for IPM innovations."]

["Breeding of High-Yield Potential Hybrid Maize Variety (13.75 t/ha) Resistant to Major Pests and Diseases", "2022", "This project centers on the breeding of a high-yield hybrid maize variety , targeting an impressive potential yield of 13.75 t/ha , while simultaneously ensuring resistance to major pests and diseases. By leveraging hybrid breeding approaches—such as exploiting heterosis through strategic crosses between inbred parental lines—this initiative aims to achieve both superior yield and agronomic resilience. Hybrid maize advantages include increased uniformity, vigor, and improved response to inputs, along with the ability to incorporate resistance traits for enhanced adaptability and productivity"]

["Study of the Genetic Diversity of the Fungus Pyricularia oryzae Cav. and Exploration of Rhizosphere Microbes as Biological Control Agents Against Rice Blast Disease", "2022", "Blast disease is the main disease that reduces the quality and quantity of rice production and can attack at the beginning of plant growth in the vegetative to generative phases. Control of blast disease can be done in various ways, including cultivation techniques, planting resistant varieties, and the use of fungicides. Chemical control of the disease which is often carried out by farmers using fungicides can have a negative impact on the sustainability of rice production because it will affect the high levels of toxicity in the environment around the planting area. The aim of this research is to find out the percentage of resistance of rhizosphere microbes to the pathogen Pyricularia oryzae and to know the technique for isolating rhizosphere microbes from rice plant tissue and how to test their antagonism against the P. oryzae pathogen and to find out the antagonistic mechanism of several rhizosphere microbes from rice plants against the P. oryzae pathogen. This research method uses a Completely Randomized Design (CRD), namely the treatment of rhizofer microbes in rice plants, each consisting of three replications with dilution levels of 104, 103, and 102. The stages of this research consist of purification, antagonism testing, microbial identification, inhibition testing, observation of antagonistic mechanisms including (competition, antibiosis, parasitism) and data analysis using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) to determine whether there is an influence of fungi. The results showed that in treatments E02 and E09 were identified as Trichoderma sp., isolate E05 was identified as Aspergillus niger., and E08 was identified as Penicillium sp. The percentage of microbial inhibitory power is 83% which can inhibit the growth of the pathogen P. oryzae. The antagonistic mechanisms that occurred were competition in treatments E02, E08 and E09 and parasitism occurred in treatment E05."]

["Application of Molecular Technology for Early Detection of CVPD (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus) in Selayar Mandarin (Keprok) Nurseries", "2022", "CVPD disease is caused by the bacterium Cand. Liberobacter asiaticum which belongs to the subdivision of Proteobacteria. This bacterium lives in the phloem tissue of citrus plants. The molecular detection technique that can be used for the diagnosis of this disease is PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction). The study aimed to detect the presence of CVPD disease early in nurseries, rootstock sources, and citrus plantations as well as the percentage of attacks in the Selayar Islands Regency. This research was carried out in the Districts of Bontomanai and Bontoharu and the PCR test was carried out at the Laboratory of Biotechnology and Tree Breeding, Faculty of Forestry, Hasanauddin University. Observations were made visually on citrus plants that showed typical symptoms, namely, there were symptoms of chlorosis between the leaf bones while the leaf bones were still green, especially in the leaf shoots. The percentage of plants affected by CVPD is the number of plants showing symptoms of chlorosis divided by the number of plants observed and multiplied by 100%. The results showed that the percentage of plants with CVPD-like symptoms in Bontonasaluk Village, Bontomatene District for the Selayar variety was 21%, Selayar – Selayar (S-S) was 13%, and JC – Selayar (JC – S) was 10%. The percentage of citrus seedlings with CVPD-like symptoms in 2 nurseries were 0.27% and 0.09%. The PCR technique was not successful in amplifying DNA fragments of Cand bacteria. Liberobacter asiaticum measuring 1160 bp and also no vector from CVPD (Diaphorina citri) at the rootstock source location or in nurseries during field observations. For further testing, optimization of the PCR process is needed so that the results are more accurate and it is better to use real-time PCR."]

["Isolation and Characterization of Rhizosphere Microbes from Kajang as Superior Local Microorganisms for Controlling Rice Stem Rot Disease in Bulukumba Regency and South Sulawesi", "2022", "Rhizosphere is a layer of soil in the roots area which are still influenced by root activitily. It is good habitat for microbial growth because roots can provide various organic materials needed by microbes in that area. This study aims to determine the diversity of microbes in the rhizosphere of rice (Oryza sativa L.) in Bulukumba. This research was conducted in September 2020 until March 2021 in Kajang district of Bulukumba Regency and Plant Disease Laboratory, Department of Plant Pests and Diseases, Faculty of Agriculture, Hasanuddin University. The study was divided into three activities; (1) survey which included disease incidence measurment and collected plant spesiment, (2) isolation and morphological identification and (3) data analysis. The study found 23 native fungal isolates in different species including Rhizopus sp., Phytopthora sp., Fusarium sp., Rhizoctonia sp., Geotrichum sp., Aspergillus sp., Gliocladium sp. and Gongronella sp. The others were 14 unknown fungal isolates. The finding suggested that the more diverse rhizospher microbes occupied the rice farm, the lower rice disease incidence occurred"]

["Exploration and Efficacy of Endophytic Fungi Against the Pathogen Causing Citrus Stem Rot (Botryodiplodia theobromae) In Vitro", "2021", "Stem rot disease (also known as \"blendok\")—caused by the fungus Botryodiplodia theobromae —is a major issue in citrus cultivation, as it infects the stem tissue, disrupts metabolic processes, and significantly reduces plant productivity. Biological control is preferred to minimize residual effects from chemical fungicides that can harm soil health. This study explores environmentally friendly control strategies by investigating endophytic fungi capable of acting as antagonists to manage stem rot in pomelo ( Citrus maxima ) orchards. Endophytic fungal isolates were obtained from healthy citrus leaves and stems, yielding 14 isolates with diverse characteristics. Following purification and morphological and microscopic characterization, eight isolates were identified as belonging to the genera Trichoderma , Penicillium , and Aspergillus , while four remained unidentified due to the absence of conidia. Dual culture assays revealed varying levels of antagonistic effectiveness; isolates PK6, PK13, PK14, PK11, and PK1 demonstrated high inhibition rates (exceeding 70%), with PK6, PK13, and PK14 achieving complete (100%) inhibition against all three tested B. theobromae isolates. The least effective isolate, PK9, inhibited pathogen growth by only 18.91%, 24.81%, and 19.81%, respectively. Observed antagonistic mechanisms included competition and antibiosis."]

["Quantitative analysis of rhizosphere microbial population obtained from main-croplands in South Sulawesi", "2021", "The study aims to investigate microbial species and quantify population richness associated with main crop rhizosphere in South Sulawesi. Survey was conducted in two areas including healthy and infected croplands. In each area about 1 ha, samples were collected to consist of 250 g bulk soil of rhizosphere in healthy and infected farms 1 month after transplanting. For analysis, those samples were carried out at the Plant pathology Lab, Department Plant Pest and Disease, Faculty of Agriculture. 10 g bulk soil separation out of 250 g obtained from rhizosphere was sterilized into water 25 mL and sieved 50-100 mesh prior to transfer to growth medium. After that, 4 % (g/mL) potato dextrose agar (PDA) in the petri dish was earlier prepared. The soil mixture (1g/10 mL) was diluted and transferred into a series dilution and parallelly loaded into solid media kept in dark room with at room temperature. Microbiota successfully growing in the solid media were split and transferred into petridish contained PDA for morphological identification and quantified through a series dilution. The study found 23 native fungal isolates consisting of Genera: Rhizopus sp. Phytophthora sp., Fusarium sp., Rhizoctonia sp., Geotrichum, Aspergillus sp., Gliocladium sp., Gongronella sp., and 14 unknown groups of fungi. Three bacterial isolates were discovered as gram-positive bacteria (GPB) in the infected cropland and the other two were gram-negative bacteria (GNB) found in healthy farm. The finding evidenced that population of microbiota 'bacterial and fungal' richness was twofold much higher in the healthy farm than infected farm. Bacterial population was the highest in both healthy and infected farms. There is a tendency of the higher fungal population richness, the lower rice disease incidence in croplands, vice versa."]

["Genetic Diversity of Citrus in South Sulawesi and the Application of In Vitro Micrografting Technique to Produce Virus-Free Oranges", "2021", "Citrus is a crucial commodity in South Sulawesi with numerous varieties. However, its production faces a major challenge due to the spread of CVPD disease. The objectives of this research are to determine the diversity of local citrus in South Sulawesi; detect the presence of Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus bacteria through PCR in citrus cultivation centers in South Sulawesi; and identify the appropriate concentration of the growth regulator BAP for in vitro growth of local citrus varieties in South Sulawesi. To achieve these objectives, the study employs clustering analysis using the UPGMA, PCoA, descriptive analysis, and SPSS analysis. The study reveals that the genetic diversity of citrus in South Sulawesi is moderate. Different genetic variations in citrus varieties can lead to variations in plant responses to disease infections. Molecular detection results indicate the presence of citrus varieties positive for Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus bacteria, with DNA fragments appearing at 1160 bp. These varieties include lime, siam orange, keprok batu 55, and keprok selayar, each originating from Sidrap, North Luwu, and Bantaeng districts. However, field observations did not find Diaphorina citri insects in five citrus cultivation locations. CVPD inoculum possibly originated from infected shoots which spread through budding or grafting. Despite efforts to control CVPD, the disease is still found in various citrus cultivation centers. A holistic control strategy is required for CVPD management. One strategic approach is the production of pathogen-free citrus plants through in vitro culture. Plant regeneration through in vitro culture involves the use of plant growth regulators (PGRs) to stimulate plant growth. The addition of BAP as a PGR in the tissue culture medium significantly influences the growth of red pamelo pangkep citrus shoots at a concentration of 1.5 ppm and the growth of the number of shoots and leaves of selayar keprok at a concentration of 2 ppm."]

["Determination of Paddy Field Quality Through Analysis of Soil Microbial Diversity Using Metagenomic Techniques", "2021", "This study aimed to 1) analyze the relationship of soil property parameters to the soil quality field, 2) analyzing the quality of paddy fields based on the function of the soil, and 3) analysis and clustering, and microbial abundance and diversity in rice fields in natural farming systems using a metagenomic technique. Data analysis with statistical analysis using the JAPS 014.6 application (open source). The soil quality index was calculated based on the modified criteria of Mausbach and Seybold (1998), with slightly modified criteria of Hadija (2022). Analysis of abundance and diversity of soil microbes using metagenomic techniques. The results of this study showed that five main component variables, namely PC1 (25.2%), PC2 (43.4%), PC3 (56.5%), PC4 (66.9%), and PC5 (76.1%), explained the total variance of 53.62%. These five main components are the factors that affect the quality of paddy fields in the study area. Rice fields in years 0 (0.60), 2 (0.61), 4 (0.65), and 6 (0.65) showed good soil quality based on the weighting results of the three soil functions. The decline in soil quality was established in the 8th year (0.51) after the application of compost for the last eight years, with moderate criteria. In this study, the composting management system affected the number of paddy fields and diversity of soil microbes. Based on the number of bacterial features detected, 1567 bacterial sequence features were found only in conventional agricultural systems, and 2337 others were found in systems agriculture. Based on the number of Fungal Features available, 478 fungal sequence features were found only in agricultural systems and 632 were found in natural farming systems. Land management affects the number and diversity of paddy soil microbes."]

["Exploration and Determination of Pyricularia oryzae Races Causing Blast Disease in Maros Regency", "2020", "Blast disease caused by the fungus Pyricularia oryzae (Teleomorph: Magnaporthe oryzae ) is one of the most important diseases causing significant yield losses on rice worldwide. The fungus has a high degree of virulence and adaptation as evidenced by the large number of its races. The study was conducted to identify the race of P. oryzae isolates and their distribution in eight sub-districts in Maros Regency. Race identification was determined based on bioassay using seven differential rice varieties, i.e. Asahan, Cisokan, IR 64, Krueng Aceh, Cisadane, Cisanggarung and Kencana Bali varieties. Observation of disease severity followed the Standard Evaluation System for Rice by IRRI. Susceptibility of host plant was assessed based on leaf spot symptom on the scale of 5 to 9. As many as 30 isolates of P. oryzae were found with the distribution as follows, 4 isolates from Bantimurung, 8 isolates from Simbang, 4 isolates from Maros Baru, 3 isolates each from Moncongloe, Tanralili, Tompobulu, Mandai, and 2 isolates from Lau. A total of 17 P. oryzae races were identified, namely race 000, 001, 011, 020, 023, 031, 033, 041, 061, 101, 103, 111, 141, 173, 221, 301 and 373. Race 001 is the dominant race in which it was found at five locations where P. oryzae isolates were collected."]

["Induction of Plant Resistance by Endophytic Bacteria and Salicylic Acid against Downy Mildew Disease in Maize", "2020", "Control of downy mildew using synthetic fungicides has proven ineffective in the field, leading to the development of alternative approaches—namely, induction of plant resistance. This study aimed to evaluate the potential of rhizosphere bacterial isolates and/or salicylic acid for inducing resistance in maize against downy mildew ( Peronosclerospora philipinensis ). The benefits of this research include providing induced-resistance technologies to enhance resistance in three maize varieties. The experiments were conducted from March to July 2020 in a greenhouse, plant pathology, and biomolecular laboratories at the Indonesian Cereal Research Institute (Balitsereal). Rhizosphere bacteria used were Bacillus paramycoides Ga3 and B. cereus Si4, both sourced from Balitsereal’s collection. A combination of rhizobacteria and salicylic acid was tested for its effectiveness in reducing downy mildew progression in maize under greenhouse conditions. This was followed by analysis of endogenous salicylic acid levels across the three maize varieties, and measurement of the expression of Pathogenesis-Related (PR) protein genes. The experiments employed a completely randomized design and were repeated six times. Results indicated that both B. paramycoides Ga3 and B. cereus Si4, when combined with salicylic acid, synergistically induced resistance against downy mildew in the Bima 20 variety and enhanced productivity in Bima 3. The combination of B. cereus Si4 with salicylic acid positively enhanced resistance in Bima 3. Meanwhile, B. paramycoides Ga3, both alone and combined with salicylic acid, effectively induced resistance in maize and promoted plant height growth in the Anoman variety."]

["Integrated Implementation of Environmentally Friendly Technological Innovations for Siem Malangke Oranges in North Luwu Regency", "2020", "This project focuses on the integrated implementation of environmentally friendly technological innovations aimed at improving the cultivation of the local citrus variety Siem Malangke orange in North Luwu Regency , South Sulawesi. By combining sustainable farming techniques, low-impact agronomy, and ecological best practices, this initiative enhances productivity while preserving environmental integrity. ["Severity of Rice Blast Disease (Pyricularia oryzae Cav.) and Genetic Analysis of Virulence-related Genes Using the SCAR (Sequence Characterized Amplified Region) Method", "2020", "Rice ( Oryza sativa L., Poaceae) is the world’s most important cereal crop and serves as the primary source of starch for over half of the global population. Rice blast disease, caused by the fungus Pyricularia oryzae (teleomorph: Magnaporthe oryzae ), is one of the most significant threats to rice cultivation worldwide. Cultivating resistant varieties is widely regarded as a cost-effective, efficient, and environmentally safe strategy to manage this disease, as it avoids the risks associated with pesticide contamination. However, such resistance often remains effective for only a few years due to the pathogen’s genetic complexity, particularly when resistance is governed by a single dominant gene. This study aims to assess the severity of blast disease and examine the genetic diversity of P. oryzae isolates from Maros District. Disease severity was evaluated using the IRRI Standard Evaluation System for Rice (2013). Genetic diversity was analyzed using primers specific to virulence-associated genes ( Pwl2 , Erg2 , and Cut1 ). Significant variation in disease severity was observed among locations: the highest severity occurred in the Mekongga variety—42.12% in Simbang sub-district and 23.33% in Maros Baru—while Tanralili (Inpari 7) and Mandai (Ciherang) registered lower severities of 7.6% and 7.88%, respectively. A total of 15 P. oryzae isolates were collected from eight sub-districts in Maros. Genetic analysis using the three primers revealed five distinct haplotypes: A-000 (four isolates), C-011 (three isolates), D-111 (two isolates), F-110 (three isolates), and G-100 (three isolates)."]

["The Hidden Diversity of Plant Destroyers: What Scientists Found Inside Phytophthora Clade 10", "2022", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia 10 May 2026/PRG – Plant diseases are often invisible threats that quietly damage forests, crops, and natural ecosystems around the world. ["The Secret World Inside a Plant Pathogen: Exploring the Virome of Phytophthora cinnamomi", "2025", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia 10 May 2026/PRG – When we think about threats to forests and agriculture, we often imagine pests, climate change, or deforestation. ["Hidden Threats in Our Forests: Why Newly Discovered Pathogens Matter for Our Planet (SDG 15: Life on Land)", "2024", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia 10 May 2026/PRG – Forests are often seen as stable and timeless ecosystems, yet recent scientific discoveries reveal a very different reality. ["Hidden Viruses, Global Threats: What Lies Beneath a Devastating Plant Pathogen", "2025", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia 9 May 2026/PRG – In today’s interconnected world, threats to agriculture and ecosystems often come from unexpected places. ["Resilient RuralAI for Rice Farming and Future Cocoa Village", "2025", "Background Precision agriculture is vital for food security and climate resilience, yet rural Indonesia faces connectivity gaps, noisy sensor data, and privacy concerns. Current digital farming systems assume stable infrastructure, leaving smallholders behind. To address this, we propose Resilient RuralAI , an AI-driven system using Hierarchical Federated Learning (HFL) to predict plant health and optimize rice production. HFL enables distributed model training without sharing raw data, ensuring privacy and adaptability to local conditions. State of the Art & Research Gap Global advances in IoT, AI, and cloud computing have enabled real-time crop monitoring and disease detection using CNNs and Vision Transformers. Federated Learning further enhances privacy, but most implementations target well-connected environments. Rural Indonesia lacks solutions for low-bandwidth networks, heterogeneous data, and localized disease prediction. This gap motivates a system that is energy-efficient, privacy-preserving, and tailored for rice ecosystems . Objectives Develop RuralAI architecture based on HFL for rice health prediction. Deploy IoT sensors for soil moisture, temperature, EC, and NPK monitoring. Integrate predictive models into a farmer-friendly dashboard. Validate through field trials in Rice farm-Sidrap District South Sulawesi and collaborative testing in Australia. Methodology & Preliminary Findings Sensors collect soil and environmental data, processed via interpolation and rolling averages. LSTM models predict time-series trends, aggregated hierarchically (local → edge → cloud). A Grafana dashboard visualizes predictions for irrigation and disease control. Initial Sidrap data show soil moisture (29–31%) and N (306–335 mg/kg) within ideal ranges, but variability underscores the need for adaptive management. Prior HFL trials achieved low MSE in soil moisture prediction, confirming feasibility. Hierarchical Federated Learning in Action: Building Resilient Agriculture Future Direction: Resilient Cocoa Village Building on RuralAI, the next phase targets cocoa sustainability . The system will adapt HFL for predicting Phytophthora pod rot and Vascular Streak Dieback , integrate CNN-based lesion detection, and deploy biosensors for soil health. A cooperative dashboard will empower farmer groups, while genomic and climate data integration strengthens resilience. This expansion aligns with Indonesia’s cocoa revitalization strategy and global sustainability goals. Expected Outcomes Prototype RuralAI for rice and roadmap for cocoa. Improved irrigation and disease management. Capacity building for farmers and young researchers. Joint publication in Frontiers: Plant Science ."]

["Inoculum prevalence, virulence, and morphometric variation of Phytophthora palmivora recovered from soil across cocoa plantations in East Luwu, Indonesia", "2024", "Phytophthora palmivora is one of the most important pathogens affecting cacao production worldwide, particularly as the causal agent of black pod disease. Our research group investigates inoculum prevalence, virulence characteristics, and morphological diversity of P. palmivora populations associated with cacao-growing regions. Using soil baiting methods and selective media, isolates are routinely recovered and characterized through morphological observation of colony patterns and asexual structures. We also apply multivariate morphometric analyses, such as principal component analysis (PCA), to examine variation among isolates. Pathogenicity and virulence assessments are conducted through controlled inoculation on cacao pods, evaluating parameters such as disease severity, lesion development rate, and latent period. Our findings consistently show that P. palmivora populations exhibit diverse morphotypes and varying degrees of virulence, with some isolates showing low or no pathogenicity while others cause rapid disease progression. Soil consistently serves as an important reservoir of inoculum in cacao plantations. Overall, this research contributes to a better understanding of P. palmivora population structure, pathogenic potential, and epidemiological significance, supporting the development of improved disease management strategies for cacao farmers."]

["Molecular identification of fungal pathogens associated with pod rot disease of cocoa in South Sulawesi", "2023-2024", "Cacao pod rot caused by Phytophthora species remains one of the most destructive diseases limiting cacao production worldwide. However, recent studies have highlighted the occurrence of other fungal taxa, including Lasiodiplodia species, which are typically endophytic but can shift to pathogenic lifestyles under stress conditions. With the increasing impact of drought and other climate change–related factors over the past decade, the biological behavior and pathogenic potential of Lasiodiplodia spp. may be changing, possibly influencing their role in pod rot development. Therefore, this study was undertaken to identify the fungal pathogens associated with cacao pod rot in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, using morphological and molecular characterization, and to evaluate their pathogenicity and symptom development through Koch’s postulates and detached pod assays."]

["Analysis of Symptom Development of Cocoa Pod Rot (Phytophthora palmivora) Under Different Paranet Shade Densities", "2024", "As a C3 crop, cacao requires specific microclimatic conditions for optimal growth, including adequate shade to regulate light intensity. The recommended shade level for cacao is generally 60–80%. However, excessive shade increases humidity around the pods, creating favorable conditions for cocoa pod rot caused by Phytophthora palmivora , a major constraint in cacao production. Because shade can both support plant growth and promote disease development, understanding the effects of different artificial shade densities on pod rot is essential. Objectives. This study aimed to determine the effects of varying artificial shade densities on the development of cocoa pod rot symptoms. Methods. A Randomized Block Design (RBD) was used with five artificial shade density treatments: 0% (no shade), 30%, 50%, 65%, and 80%. Each treatment was replicated three times. Disease development was assessed visually for four weeks after inoculation, and symptom progression was quantified using the ImageJ application. Results. Artificial shade density significantly influenced the development of cocoa pod rot. Higher shade densities (50%, 65%, and 80%) accelerated symptom progression, while lower shade levels (0% and 30%) slowed lesion development. Conclusion. Although shade is necessary for cacao growth, high shade densities can intensify the spread of cocoa pod rot due to the humid microclimate they create. Disease development tended to slow at an optimal shade density of around 30%."]

["Institutional Analysis of Beef Cattle Agribusiness in Supporting Beef Self-Sufficiency in Barru District", "This activity aims to analyze the role of beef cattle agribusiness institutions in supporting the achievement of beef self-sufficiency in Barru District. Analysis is conducted using descriptive and qualitative approaches to understand the linkages between institutions and the role of regulations and policies in supporting self-sufficiency. This activity will also evaluate the support provided by local governments in strengthening agribusiness institutions. ["Strategies for Strengthening Beef Cattle Partnership Institutions in South Sulawesi Province", "This activity aims to strengthen partnership institutions in beef cattle business in South Sulawesi through collaboration between farmers, government, financial institutions and related industries. ["Implementation of Biosecurity on Beef Cattle Farms in Luwu District", "This activity aims to improve the application of biosecurity in beef cattle farming in Luwu District to prevent the spread of disease and improve livestock health. Biosecurity includes prevention, control and monitoring of potential disease risks that could threaten beef cattle populations. The main activities include training and counseling farmers on the basic principles of biosecurity, such as cage sanitation, feed management, disease vector control, and the use of personal protective equipment. In addition, periodic livestock and environmental health audits are conducted to detect the potential spread of disease early. Facilitation of procurement of tools and materials for the implementation of biosecurity, such as disinfectants, body temperature measuring instruments, and livestock health facilities is also carried out to support this program. This activity is complemented by strengthening the livestock health recording and reporting system to facilitate disease detection and countermeasures. Through this activity, it is hoped that farmers in Luwu District can understand the importance of biosecurity in maintaining beef cattle health and increasing livestock productivity in a sustainable manner."]

["Model of profit sharing system in partnership between universities and cattle farmers based on local wisdom in Enrekang Regency.", "This activity aims to build a local wisdom-based partnership model between universities and cattle farmers in Enrekang Regency with a mutually beneficial profit-sharing system. Within this framework, universities provide training and counseling to farmers on modern livestock technology that is in accordance with the principles of local wisdom, such as sustainable utilization of surrounding natural resources. This partnership model involves equitable profit sharing, with calculations based on each party\\'s contribution to livestock management, operational costs, and production output. The university will conduct research to identify appropriate solutions in livestock management that can be applied by farmers, including in the aspects of feed, animal health, and environmental management. In addition, the implementation of this activity also includes the application of local wisdom in livestock management, such as the utilization of local plants for animal feed and the principle of mutual cooperation in cattle raising. With this profit-sharing system, it is expected that there will be an increase in livestock productivity, farmer welfare, and sustainable preservation of local wisdom."]

["Supply Chain Study of Buffalo Livestock to Fulfill the Needs of Traditional Feasts of the Toraja Community", "This activity aims to analyze the supply chain of buffalo cattle used in Toraja traditional feasts. The main focus is to understand the distribution process of buffalo cattle from farmers to end consumers, as well as the factors that influence the availability and price of buffalo cattle in the local market. The first step in this activity is to survey buffalo farmers, traders and transportation service providers to identify the stages of livestock distribution. Next, the marketing system, the influence of cultural, economic and social factors in determining prices and demand patterns during certain seasons, especially before major traditional events, will be analyzed. In addition, this activity will also evaluate challenges in the supply chain, such as logistical constraints, feed supply uncertainty and price fluctuations that can affect the sustainability of livestock supply. The results of this study are expected to provide recommendations for more efficient buffalo supply chain management that supports the smooth supply of livestock for traditional feasts without compromising farmer welfare and production sustainability."]

["Beef Cattle Farmers\\' Behavior towards Foot and Mouth Disease Outbreaks in Bone District, South Sulawesi", "This activity aims to analyze the behavior of beef cattle farmers in Bone Regency related to handling Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) outbreaks. The main focus of this activity was to identify farmers\\' knowledge, attitudes, and actions in dealing with FMD outbreaks and the factors that influence their decisions in managing livestock health. The activity begins with a survey of beef cattle farmers in several sub-districts in Bone Regency to gather information on their understanding of FMD, including symptoms, prevention and treatment of the disease. In addition, this activity will evaluate farmers\\' responses to government and animal health officials\\' recommendations for dealing with outbreaks, as well as their level of compliance with biosecurity and vaccination policies. Qualitative and quantitative approaches will be used in this study to analyze the data obtained, as well as identify the barriers farmers face in implementing preventive measures. The results of this activity are expected to provide insights into farmer behavior, and suggest more effective communication and education strategies to improve the response to FMD outbreaks in Bone District."]

["Risk Analysis and Critical Points of Aflatoxin-Producing Fungal (AFM1) Contamination in Fresh Milk and Dangke Cheese in Enrekang Regency", "Using HACCP principles, all processing is carried out to prevent contamination of Dangke cheese at all critical control points. The raw milk was sourced from clean farms in the first phase of the study, where no Aspergillus flavus was detected on dairy farms in Enrekang Regency. Processing is also carried out with good sanitation and hygiene to prevent contamination by Aspergillus flavus, which can produce aflatoxins harmful to human health. Feed and food contamination by toxigenic fungi and their aflatoxins is one of the main threats to animal and human health worldwide and in the agricultural and industrial sectors. This study evaluated the contamination magnitude by Aspergillus species in dairy farms, aflatoxin AFB1 in cow feeds, and aflatoxin AFM1 in milk and local cheese (Dangke). One hundred twenty-two swabs from farms, 12 roughage feeds, 16 concentrated feeds, 39 fresh cow milk, and six cheese samples were analyzed for Aspergillus spp., AFB1, and AFM1 contamination. Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus niger were detected in 13.93% and 7.38% of the swab samples, respectively. The roughage feeds showed low levels of AFB1, detected in 8.33% with contamination of 7.32 µ/kg, while concentrated feed was detected in 37.5% of specimens, with contamination levels of 27.8 µg/kg. Aflatoxin AFM1 was detected in raw milk samples and represented approximately 69.2% of samples, with a mean of 7.31 µg/kg. All local cheese samples were free of AFM1. There were critical points regarding HACCP inside the farms, which play significant roles in contamination by fungi and aflatoxins. Fungal contamination and aflatoxins pose dangerous public health problems to humans, especially infants and older people. Therefore, monitoring programs for mycotoxins are critical in reducing contamination."]

["FUNCTIONAL PASTEURIZATION COW MILK PROTOTYPE (SUKISA)", "Demand for functional food products continues to rise in line with growing public awareness of the importance of a healthy lifestyle and disease prevention. Cow's milk is a highly nutritious food source with significant potential for development as a functional product. However, in Indonesia, the use of milk as a functional product is still limited to large-scale industries. Innovation in milk processing, including functional pasteurization, rich in bioactive compounds, such as antioxidants and non-viable probiotics, is urgently needed to address the community's nutritional challenges while providing added value for local farmers. This research aims to develop a prototype of functional pasteurized cow's milk (SUKISA) formulated using natural bioactive ingredients and low-temperature pasteurization technology. This product is expected to have nutritional stability, adequate shelf life, and sensory characteristics acceptable to consumers, while also providing functional benefits such as increased immunity. The methods used include the formulation of fresh milk raw materials with the addition of bioactive compounds (e.g., local plant extracts), a low-temperature pasteurization process, and analysis of physicochemical characteristics, antioxidant activity, and organoleptic testing. Evaluations are conducted to obtain an optimal formulation with the best quality and stability. This research is at Technology Readiness Level (TKT) 6, where the system prototype has been tested in a relevant environment. The primary output of this research is a SUKISA prototype model, along with technical recommendations for its production process. With an upstream-downstream approach and support from industry partners, this research is expected to encourage the development of high-value-added dairy products that are consumer-friendly, competitive in the market, and support the welfare of local farmers through the use of sustainable livestock products."]

["Innovation in making condensed milk from dangke whey through diversification of additional ingredients based on local products", "This study develops an innovation in producing condensed milk from dangke whey by diversifying additional ingredients sourced from local products. The approach is designed to enhance nutritional value, sensory quality, and the economic potential of dangke whey"]

["Study of the Characteristics of Halal Functional Kefir by Optimizing Fermentation and Heating Duration", "This study investigates the characteristics of halal functional kefir by optimizing fermentation and heating duration. The research aims to improve its physicochemical quality, functional properties, and compliance with halal standards"]

["High-Sales Empowerment of Dairy Cow Milk Consumers through MSME Management to Increase Economic Value with Diversification of Valuable Processed Products", "This research focuses on empowering dairy cow milk consumers through MSME-based management to enhance sales and economic value. Diversification into high-value processed products is promoted as a strategy to strengthen sustainability and competitiveness"]

["Standardization and Characterization of Processed Milk Product Suspesi from East Nusa Tenggara", "This study focuses on the standardization and characterization of dairy product suspensions from East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. The research aims to assess their physicochemical and microbiological properties to ensure consistent quality, safety, and potential functional benefits."]

["Exopolysaccharide (EPS) Production by Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp . bulgaricus starter fermented milk culture", "This study aims to evaluate EPS production by Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus ropy strain at various incubation temperature conditions."]

["Physicochemical and Activity Studies Antioxidants Pasteurized Milk with Addition Extract Leaf Matoa (Pometia pinnate)", "This study aims to obtain functional pasteurized milk with the addition of matoa leaf extract ( Pometia pinnata )."]

["Development Cheese Ripening Dangke for Downstream Products in Realizing National Food Independence", "Indonesia needs animal protein to increase national food security and resilience. One of the government\\'s policies in fulfilling national food needs is to improve the diversity of food consumption, including protein consumption. Dangke is a traditional cheese product from Enrekang, South Sulawesi, which is made from fresh milk curdled using papaya latex (Carica papaya). The target to be achieved in this study is to produce Dangke Cheese products and their diversification, which are downstream and applied to the industry managed by the Milk Processing Unit of the Faculty of Animal Science, Hasanuddin University as the forerunner of industry in supporting the Center of Excellence of the Faculty of Animal Science, Hasanuddin University in the Development of Animal Protein Products."]

["Scaling Up Cheese Prebiotics and Anti Cancer from Dangke as a Local Product Towards the Export Market", "The development of prebiotic cheese products is also one solution for utilizing milk production in South Sulawesi, considering there is no milk processing industry in this area. Therefore, cheese with several variants, functions as a functional food, and has a relatively long shelf life should be produced so that the product\\'s marketing is broader. This would seek market opportunities for export purposes and reduce cheese imports, thereby reducing the waste of foreign exchange, increasing the economy, and providing opportunities for developing the dairy industry in Indonesia."]

["Innovation in making functional cheese using coating edible whey based film Dangke combined with konjac flour and carrageenan", "The coating is needed to manufacture hard cheese to prevent the formation of a hard layer on the outside. So far, coatings made of wax have been used, which must be removed when the cheese is to be processed or consumed. If the wax is not removed and is eaten, it will cause health problems, so the coating material should be made of edible materials, such as honey wax. However, making cheese in large quantities causes constraints on raw materials, such as honey wax, and its price is relatively high. Therefore, in this study, edible film coating material was made from whey, a by-product of cheese making. Whey is a by-product of dangke processing and is also obtained from the cheese-making industry after separating casein and fat during milk sedimentation. Whey is one of the materials that can be used as an edible film. Edible film is a thin layer that coats food products (coating) that can be consumed with the coated product. Processing edible film made only from whey will produce less good edible film characteristics, such as not being transparent, easily brittle, and inflexible. The characteristics of a good edible film are transparency, flexibility and not easily brittle. Konjac flour and carrageenan are polysaccharides that improve the characteristics of edible film. The purpose of this study was to determine the characteristics of the edible film made from dangke whey, such as dissolution time, tensile strength, elongation, thickness, gelation time, and water vapor transmission rate (WVTR) with a combination of konjac flour and carrageenan as a hard cheese layer"]

["Innovation using fermented milk culture starter exopolysaccharide ropy strain producing strains (EPS) to produce cheese functional", "Diversification of cheese for health purposes, such as functional cheese for food as prebiotic and anti-cancer food, needs to be done to increase the utility value of the product. Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus strain ropy is one of the lactic acid bacteria that produces polysaccharides excreted outside the cell, called exopolysaccharides (EPS). EPS can be used as a food additive (stabilizer, binder, and increase the viscosity and rheometric of yoghurt. Our previous research showed that EPS from Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp bulgaricus is an antitumor and can inhibit and kill tumor cells, anti-cholesterol, and other health benefits. This research will be conducted by performing ripening techniques on cheese, diversifying South Sulawesi Traditional Cheese (Dangke) with inoculation of Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus. The purpose of this study is to produce new cheese variants from the modification of traditional Dangke cheese, which are functional cheeses, as well as to extend the shelf life of the product and make this product an original Indonesian cheese."]

["Strengthening Campus Educational Tourism for commercialization product Functional milk", "This program is a dairy product commercialization program that collaborates with the industry to develop products produced by the laboratory."]

["Characteristics of Dangke Cheese with inoculation Lactococcus starter culture lactis subsp . lactis 0086, coating and ripening", "Lactobacillus lactis is one of the starter cultures for fermented cheese. This study aims to see the potential of Dangke cheese to be developed into hard and functional cheese."]

["Analysis Risk And Point Critical Contamination of Alphatoxin -Producing Fungus (AFM1) in Fresh Milk and Dangke Cheese", "Aflatoxins (AFs) are naturally toxic compounds produced by a specific type of fungi. They subsequently contaminate foods and animal feeds and are potentially carcinogenic to humans. However, when fungi produce AFB1 and animals digest contaminated feed, their liver metabolizes the AFB1 into hydroxylated aflatoxin AFM1, which is secreted into milk if the animal is milking. This study aims to control the possibility of contamination and the risk of aflatoxin in raw milk materials and Dangke cheese products during the processing of Dangke cheese."]

["Study of Exopolysaccharides from Bacteria Fermented Milk Culture Starter Isolated from Dangke and Its Potential as an Antitumor", "Dangke is one of the typical foods of Enrekang Regency, South Sulawesi, made from fresh cow or buffalo milk. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are found in fermented milk starter cultures, such as those used in making dangke. LAB has an important role in the fermentation process as a starter culture that provides a distinctive taste, aroma, and texture to the final product and provides various health benefits. The types of LAB commonly used as starter cultures in fermented milk are Streptococcus lactis , Str. diasetilactis , Str. cremoris , Str. durans and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subs. bulgaricus . In addition, LAB is a microorganism that has the potential to produce exopolysaccharides, which play an important role in fermented milk products through their gel-forming and thickening properties. Exopolysaccharides (EPS) are polymers produced by microorganisms such as bacteria that have promising health potential, including their activity as antitumors. However, not all types of LAB can produce EPS. Therefore, it is necessary to conduct a study to isolate bacteria from the starter culture of fermented milk dangke, identify and characterize the EPS produced, and evaluate the potential of EPS as an antitumor. This study is expected to be a comprehensive reference for future EPS development. This study was conducted for 3 years, where; in the 1st year, the isolation and characterization of starter culture bacteria from dangke will be carried out; in the 2nd year, the extraction/purification and characterization of EPS will be carried out, and in the 3rd year the evaluation of EPS antitumor activity will be carried out through in vitro and in vivo tests. In addition to the final report, this study is expected to be able to produce publications in 3 reputable international journals and participate in the International Seminar."]

["Effect of curdlan, a bacteria polysaccharide on rheological properties and microstructure of acid milk curd by lactic acid fermentation", "Curdlan is an Exopolysaccharide produced by Alcaligenes faecalis var. myogenesis, which is a homopolysaccharide. In this study, curdlan was used as a stabilizing agent for yogurt, and its physicochemical and microstructural properties were characterized using a Scanning Electron Microscope."]
