["Policy Entrepreneurship Analysis in Food Security Policy Networks in Poor Communities in South Sulawesi Province", "2023", "This study aims to analyze the role of policy entrepreneurship in food security policy networks targeting poor communities in South Sulawesi Province. Food security in marginal areas is often influenced not only by the availability of resources, but also by the effectiveness of policy actors in building strategic connections, creating policy opportunities, and encouraging innovation in the context of structural and institutional limitations. Policy entrepreneurs are positioned as agents of change who are able to bridge interests between stakeholders in complex and dynamic policy networks. This study uses a qualitative approach with a case study design in several poverty pockets that have community-based food security policy interventions. Data collection techniques were carried out through in-depth interviews with key actors, field observations, and policy document reviews. The analysis was carried out to identify strategies, network capital, and policy window moments utilized by policy entrepreneurs in influencing the policy process. The results of this study are expected to contribute to strengthening the design of food security policies that are more inclusive, network-based, and responsive to the local conditions of poor communities in South Sulawesi."]

["Strengthening Local Food Security Governance: Analysis of Institutional Entrepreneurship in the Implementation of Food Security Policy in South Sulawesi Province", "2023", "This study aims to analyze the strengthening of local food security governance in South Sulawesi Province through an institutional entrepreneurship approach. Food security is a strategic issue that is not only related to the availability and access to food, but also reflects the capacity of local institutions in building a resilient and sustainable system. In this context, institutional actors who are entrepreneurial (institutional entrepreneurs) play an important role in driving change, creating policy innovation, and strengthening cross-sector collaboration. Using an exploratory qualitative approach, this study examines the dynamics of food security policy implementation in several districts/cities in South Sulawesi that have different geographical and socio-economic characteristics. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, observations, and document studies, then analyzed thematically to identify intervention patterns, adaptation strategies, and the key roles of local actors in designing and navigating food security policies. The results of this study are expected to be able to formulate a participatory local food security governance model based on institutional innovation, as well as enrich the treasury of public administration studies in the context of sustainable development in the regions."]

["Adaptive Capacity Model of Local Institutions in Empowerment-Based Poverty Alleviation Policies in Coastal Areas Through Utilization of Local Potential in South Sulawesi Province", "2023", "This study aims to formulate a model of the adaptive capacity of local institutions in supporting empowerment-based poverty alleviation policies in coastal areas of South Sulawesi Province through the utilization of local potential. The background of this study is based on the fact that poverty alleviation policies in coastal areas often face implementation challenges due to the limited capacity of local institutions in responding to local socio-economic and environmental dynamics. In this context, the adaptive capacity of local institutions is key to ensuring that policies are effective and in accordance with the needs of coastal communities. This study uses a qualitative approach with a case study design on several local institutions in coastal areas that have different social characteristics and economic potential. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participatory observations, and documentation studies, then analyzed thematically to identify dimensions of adaptive capacity including regulatory, structural, human resources, collaborative networks, and community participation aspects. The results of this study are expected to produce a conceptual model that can be used as a reference in designing responsive empowerment policies based on local potential. This model also contributes to strengthening inclusive development governance in coastal areas."]

["Strengthening Local Food Security Governance: Analysis of Institutional Entrepreneurship in Food Security Policy Implementation in South Sulawesi Province.", "Strengthening local food security governance requires the involvement of strategic actors who are able to drive institutional change through their roles as institutional entrepreneurs. This study examines how agents of change in South Sulawesi Province shape, modify and direct food security policy practices through institutional innovation and collaborative networks. The focus is on the dynamics of transforming structures and norms that influence successful policy implementation at the local level. An analytical approach to institutional entrepreneurship is used to explore the strategies, resources and contexts that support adaptive and sustainable institutional change. The findings of this study are expected to enrich academic discourse and policy practice in the field of locally-based food security."]

["Analysis of Indigenous People in Collaborative Governance for the Implementation of the “Cas Kampung” Education Program in Merauke District", "This research analyses the role of indigenous people in the collaborative governance framework for the implementation of the “Cas Kampung” education program in Merauke district. The study examines how local actors, including indigenous communities, local government and education institutions, interact to build effective collaboration to improve access to and quality of local wisdom-based education. Emphasis is placed on the dynamics of indigenous peoples\\' participation as active subjects in program governance, as well as the challenges of integrating traditional values in the formal education system. This research is part of a doctoral completion program conducted by students and under the direct supervision of Prof. Dr. Alwi as Promoter. The results of this study are expected to provide theoretical and practical contributions in the development of inclusive collaborative models for the context of education in indigenous territories."]

["Policy Entrepreneurship Analysis in the Food Security Policy Network for the Poor in South Sulawesi Province", "This study aims to analyze the role of policy entrepreneurship in the food security policy network targeting the poor in South Sulawesi Province. The focus of the study is on identifying key actors, policy advocacy strategies, and interaction dynamics that influence the process of policy formulation and implementation at the local level. This study places policy entrepreneurs as catalysts of change in the context of social inclusion-based food security governance. This research is part of the Fundamental Research program funded by BIMA Kemenristekdikti, which aims to encourage the development of contextual-based science relevant to national development needs."]

["Local Governance Network in Order to Improve Food Security Policy Performance: Case Study of Food Security Policy Implementation Network in South Sulawesi Province", "This research examines the dynamics of the local governance network in the context of food security policy implementation in South Sulawesi Province. The main focus is on analyzing the network of cross-sector actors involved in the process of policy formulation and implementation, as well as the patterns of collaboration between institutions that affect the effectiveness of the policy. This study aims to identify key factors that support and hinder the performance of food security policies through a policy network approach. Using a qualitative case study approach, this research is expected to make theoretical and practical contributions towards strengthening local governance in the food sector."]

["Integrated Lower Level Bureaucracy Capacity Development Model in Food Diversification Policy Implementation in South Sulawesi Province", "This research project represents a doctoral-level scholarly endeavor aimed at addressing the institutional and administrative challenges associated with the implementation of food diversification policies in Indonesia, specifically within the context of South Sulawesi Province. The title reflects a comprehensive study undertaken by a doctoral student to develop a model that enhances the operational capacity of lower-level bureaucratic structures, which often serve as the frontline implementers of government policies. The core objective of this research is to design an integrated capacity development model tailored for local and sub-national bureaucratic actors, thereby improving their effectiveness in executing food diversification strategies. This initiative is particularly important given Indonesia’s ongoing efforts to ensure food security, reduce dependency on rice as the staple food, and promote the consumption of alternative and locally available food sources. By focusing on lower-level bureaucracies, the study seeks to identify key institutional barriers, capacity gaps, and inter-organizational coordination issues that hinder policy implementation. Furthermore, the research aims to contribute both theoretically and practically by offering a model that aligns with the socio-cultural and administrative dynamics of South Sulawesi, ensuring that food diversification policies are not only designed but also executed effectively at the grassroots level."]

["Bridging the Welfare Gap: Why Location Still Matters in Social Assistance", "2026", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Apr 14 2026/GMSC/ – Access to social welfare programs remains uneven between peri-urban and rural communities in Indonesia. A recent study found that residents in peri-urban areas often perceive welfare assistance as more effective due to better infrastructure, easier access to information, and closer proximity to public services, while rural communities continue to face barriers such as distance, limited connectivity, and fewer service facilities. The findings underline that reducing poverty requires not only strong policies, but also fair and inclusive delivery systems that reach citizens in every location."]

["Rethinking Poverty: Why Local Capacity Holds the Key to Sustainable Change", "2026", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Apr 15 2026/GMSC/ – Poverty alleviation is increasingly understood as a question of local capacity rather than just financial support. A recent global study highlights that effective poverty reduction depends on how well institutions, communities, and resources work together at the local level. The findings show that stronger governance systems, community networks, and adaptive capacity play a crucial role in responding to crises and sustaining development outcomes, emphasizing that ending poverty requires integrated and context-specific approaches rather than one-size-fits-all policies."]

["When Class Shapes Democracy: Why Some Citizens Trust Government While Others Protest", "2025", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Oct 28 2025/GMSC/ – Social class continues to shape how citizens engage with democracy in many developing countries. A recent comparative study of Indonesia and Bangladesh found that wealthier groups are more likely to participate through formal political channels such as elections and party activities, while lower-income communities often turn to protests or grassroots action when they feel excluded. This divide highlights that unequal access to political participation remains a major challenge, showing that stronger democracy depends not only on institutions, but also on reducing social inequality."]

["Digital Government, Real Trust? How Technology Is Reshaping Citizen Participation in Indonesia", "2025", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Dec 17 2025/GMSC/ – Digital transformation is changing how citizens interact with government, but it does not automatically increase public participation. A recent study in Gowa Regency, Indonesia, found that while digital public services improve efficiency, transparency, and trust in government, citizen engagement through online platforms remains relatively low. The findings highlight a “participation paradox,” where higher trust does not always lead to active involvement, emphasizing that inclusive design, digital literacy, and responsive governance are essential to turning technological progress into meaningful democratic participation."]

["When Land Shapes Democracy: Why Rural Inequality Influences Political Participation in Indonesia", "2025", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Mar 25 2025/GMSC/ – Economic inequality in rural communities continues to influence how citizens participate in democracy. A recent study published in Frontiers in Political Science found that farmers with greater access to land, education, and economic resources were more likely to participate in formal political activities such as elections and village meetings. In contrast, small-scale farmers and landless laborers tended to rely more on informal political participation, including community discussions and direct engagement with local officials. The findings from Gowa Regency, Indonesia, highlight that reducing rural poverty and expanding equal access to resources are essential steps toward building more inclusive democratic participation, particularly in support of SDG 1: No Poverty ."]

["Small Businesses, Big Impact: How MSMEs Drive Social Sustainability in Makassar", "2025", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Mar 6 2025/GMSC/ – Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) play a vital role in strengthening social sustainability in urban communities. A recent study in Makassar found that most MSMEs demonstrate strong commitment to social values such as fairness, community engagement, and trust-building, which support business resilience and local development. However, challenges remain in environmental practices and participation in policy processes, highlighting that sustainable growth requires not only economic performance but also stronger social and institutional support systems."]

["Empowering Change: How Local NGOs Are Shaping the Urban Middle Class in Makassar", "2025", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Jan 27 2025/GMSC/ – Local NGOs are playing an increasingly important role in empowering the urban middle class in Makassar, Indonesia. A recent study found that organizations such as AcSI and Dompet Dhuafa focus on political advocacy and economic support to strengthen the capacity of students, youth, and small business actors. While these efforts have improved skills, independence, and community engagement, challenges such as limited funding and uneven access remain, highlighting that sustainable development depends on strong partnerships between civil society and local communities."]

["Why Coastal Villages in Indonesia Need More Than Just Funds to Thrive", "2020", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia October 20 2025/GMSC/ – Governance challenges continue to shape development outcomes in Indonesia’s coastal villages. A recent study on village governance found that limited community participation and weak public accountability often hinder the fair distribution of village funds and decision-making processes. While village autonomy has increased under recent policies, power tends to remain concentrated in local elites, leaving many coastal residents—especially small-scale fishers—excluded from meaningful involvement. This situation underscores that achieving SDG 14 (Life Below Water) is not only about protecting marine resources, but also about strengthening inclusive and transparent governance at the local level."]

["New Roads, Same Journey: Why Migration Persists in Rural Indonesia", "2020", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia June 19 2020/GMSC/ – Rural development in Indonesia is not always reducing migration as expected. A recent study in two villages in Jeneponto found that despite increased village funding and infrastructure development, many residents continue to migrate to cities in search of stable livelihoods. Limited job opportunities, low agricultural productivity, and weak local governance remain key drivers of this trend. The findings highlight that achieving SDG 1 (No Poverty) requires more than physical development—it depends on inclusive governance, stronger local capacity, and sustainable economic opportunities that can truly improve rural livelihoods and reduce the need to migrate."]

["Community-Based Climate Change Adaptation: A Social-Ecological Resilience Model of Fishers on Barrang Lompo Island", "2025", "This report examines how coastal communities on Barrang Lompo Island respond to the growing social-ecological pressures caused by climate change. The study was motivated by the increasing vulnerability of small-island fishing households facing uncertain weather patterns, shifting seasons, more frequent extreme weather events, and the degradation of coastal ecosystems, particularly coral reefs. These changes have directly affected fish catches, increased the operational costs of fishing, and weakened the economic stability of local households. Using a qualitative approach, the research employed participant observation, in-depth interviews with fishers, and documentary analysis supported by secondary data from relevant agencies. The findings show that climate change has intensified seasonal uncertainty, increased the frequency of storms and extreme waves, and contributed to serious coral reef degradation. These environmental pressures have led to declining catches and income, longer fishing trips, and significantly higher operational expenses. In response, the community has developed a range of adaptive strategies, including livelihood diversification, spatial adjustments in fishing practices, the use of more adaptive fishing technologies, strengthening local institutions, and ecosystem rehabilitation efforts such as mangrove planting and coral conservation. Overall, the report argues that the social-ecological resilience of coastal communities on Barrang Lompo is shaped by the interaction of local knowledge, social capital, technological adaptation, and supportive policy measures. In a broader context, this research also contributes to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 13 (Climate Action) through strengthening local adaptive capacity, SDG 14 (Life Below Water) through the protection and rehabilitation of coastal and marine ecosystems, and SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) through efforts to sustain the livelihoods and economic resilience of small-scale fishing communities."]

["Ethnoecology of Communities Surrounding Karst Landscapes in South Sulawesi Province", "2025", "Karst ecosystems possess distinctive, unique, and specific natural resources that are not found in other ecological systems. These ecosystems play a vital role in supporting the livelihoods and cultural practices of surrounding communities. In South Sulawesi Province, such as the karst region within the Bantimurung Bulusaraung Ma’rupanne Biosphere Reserve, the interrelationship between humans and the karst environment has existed for thousands of years. This long-standing interaction has given rise to a wealth of local knowledge related to the management and sustainable use of natural resources in karst areas. However, to date, there is a lack of comprehensive scientific documentation regarding this local knowledge. Such information is crucial as a foundational database for sustainable karst ecosystem management and as a reference for policy formulation aimed at the preservation of these essential ecological areas. This exploratory research aims to: (1) collect data and information related to local knowledge (ethnobiology, ethnobotany, ethnoecology, and ethnoforestry) of communities residing near karst landscapes in South Sulawesi, and (2) assemble scientific collections of various types of natural resources utilized by these communities. Data collection on local knowledge and the types of natural resources used will be conducted through surveys, direct observation, and interviews. To assess the availability of these resources in their natural habitats, appropriate methods will be applied according to each taxon, including: Quadrant line methods for plant data, Line transects for mammals, Point count methods for birds, Pollard walk transects and traps for insects. Interview data will be analyzed descriptively. Ecological data on resource availability in natural habitats will be analyzed to determine density values, importance value indices, biodiversity indices, dominance indices, and species evenness indices. The final output of this research is expected to serve as a scientific database and reference for the sustainable management of karst natural resources, as well as a basis for community-based policy development for the conservation of essential karst ecosystems."]

["THE IMPACT OF TROPICAL CLIMATE CHANGE AND ECOLOGICAL ADAPTATION PATTERNS OF FARMERS (A Case Study on the Horticultural Development Center in Gowa Regency, South Sulawesi)", "2024", "Global, regional, and local climate change each exhibit distinct phenomenological characteristics. Consequently, their impacts on the horticultural sector, as well as the ecological adaptation patterns employed by farmers in response to these changes, are presumed to vary accordingly. This study aims to examine tropical climate change in South Sulawesi and analyze its effects on horticultural agriculture, particularly within the horticultural development center located in Gowa Regency, South Sulawesi. Furthermore, the research explores how horticultural farmers adapt ecologically to the impacts of tropical climate change. This study adopts a constructivist interpretive framework rooted in the case study tradition. The research begins with the purposive selection of the study location, the development of research instruments, the identification of data types and sources, and the determination of key informants using a snowball sampling technique. Data collection is carried out through a comprehensive approach, employing observation, in-depth interviews, documentation, and triangulation. Data analysis follows an integrated process consisting of data collection, data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The study concludes with a data validity check, involving credibility and reliability testing to ensure the accuracy and trustworthiness of the findings."]

["Analysis of the Potential of Massenrempulu Traditional Institutions in Supporting Village Welfare and Environmental Justice Programs in Enrekang Regency", "2024", "This research stems from the issue that the Maspul (Massenrempulu) people in Enrekang Regency remain relatively unknown and unrecognized as one of the ethnic groups in South Sulawesi, despite various anthropological, historical, and linguistic sources affirming their status as an ethnic group with a distinctive culture. Remarkably, several studies have revealed the richness of traditional institutions maintained and practiced by the numerous customary communities of the Maspul. This raises a key question: what roles do these traditional institutions play in sustaining the cultural systems that have been preserved over time? The long-term goal of this study is to enhance community welfare and promote productive, sustainable, and equitable forest management. The short-term objectives are: To identify the existing traditional institutions that persist among the three Maspul subethnic groups (Enrekang, Duri, and Maiwa); To analyze the structure and roles of these traditional institutions in operating local socio-cultural systems to manage socio-economic and forest resources in a productive, sustainable, and just manner; and To formulate programmatic ideas for improving welfare and achieving environmental justice through the synergy between local institutional functions and theoretical frameworks on institutional development. The mandatory outputs of this research include a publication in a Scopus-indexed international journal and an ethnographic book (as a teaching resource), both of which are currently in the submission and editing process, respectively. The research was conducted in three customary communities of the Maspul ethnic group in South Sulawesi, Indonesia: Kaluppini (Enrekang subethnic group), Orong, and Marena (both belonging to the Duri subethnic group). For comparative purposes, in-depth interviews and observations were also conducted in eight other customary communities: Patongloan, Uru, and Batunoni (Duri subethnic group); Bambapuang (a mixed community of Duri and Enrekang subethnic groups); and four communities within the Maiwa subethnic group (Pasang, Limbuang, Matajang, Tapong), all of which share relatively similar institutional structures and roles. This study adopts an ethnographic method and a qualitative approach, using data collection techniques such as in-depth interviews, systematic direct observations, secondary data collection, complemented by focus group discussions (FGDs) and data analysis. By applying key concepts including customary communities, traditional institutions, institutional roles, the operation of customary systems, and the productive, equitable, and sustainable management of customary land and forest resources—as well as a holistic definition of welfare—the positive roles of the three traditional institutions (Tau Aqpaq Kaluppini, Malepongna Bawangna Orong, and Sianene Marena) are analyzed in accordance with the research objectives. These institutions have been found to contribute positively to strengthening communal life, managing ancestral rice fields, and sustaining both the productive and protective functions of customary forests."]

["A HOUSEHOLD SURVEY ON MAPPING THE SOCIO-CULTURAL AND POLITICAL ASPECTS OF THE CORAL REEF RESTORATION PROJECT ON BONTOSUA ISLAND PHASE II", "2020", "The report titled “Household Survey on Mapping Socio-Cultural and Political Aspects of the Coral Reef Restoration Project in Bontosua Island Phase II” presents a comprehensive quantitative study conducted in collaboration between PT. Mars Symbioscience Indonesia, the University of Rhode Island (URI), and the Sociology-Anthropology Department of Universitas Hasanuddin. It explores the socio-economic, cultural, and political dynamics of Bontosua Island following the Phase I coral reef restoration, aiming to assess changes in livelihoods, community perceptions, and environmental sustainability. The study, based on household surveys, reveals that while most residents rely on fishing, they face challenges in income stability, access to clean water, education, and waste management. Despite limited awareness of ecological impacts, the community shows optimism about the future of coral reefs and expresses a desire for greater participation in marine resource governance. The report concludes with strategic recommendations to enhance community empowerment, environmental stewardship, and sustainable development in Bontosua."]

["Compilation of a Conflict-Prone Area Map for North Kalimantan Province", "2024", "The final report on the Conflict Vulnerability Mapping of North Kalimantan Province (2024) presents a comprehensive analysis of social conflict risks across five districts and one city. Using mixed methods and spatial analysis, the study identifies 34 conflict issues, with Nunukan classified as a red zone (high risk), Bulungan and Tarakan as yellow zones (moderate risk), and Tana Tidung and Malinau as green zones (low risk). Key conflict types include land disputes, political power struggles, ethnic and religious tensions, economic inequality, and border issues with Malaysia. The report emphasizes the importance of inclusive governance, legal recognition of indigenous land rights, intergroup dialogue, and participatory mapping to prevent and resolve conflicts. It also highlights strategic vulnerabilities in border areas, particularly in Nunukan, due to illegal trade, migration, and economic dependence on Malaysia."]

["STUDY OF TOURISM DEVELOPMENT POTENTIAL, ECONOMIC IMPACT, SOCIAL AND CULTURAL IMPACT AND INTEGRATION BETWEEN TRANSPORTATION MODES ON THE MAKASSAR-PAREPARE RAILWAY LINE", "2023", "This report presents a comprehensive study on the potential development of tourism, economic, social, and cultural impacts, as well as the integration of transportation modes along the Makassar–Parepare railway corridor in South Sulawesi. Conducted by Universitas Hasanuddin in collaboration with the Ministry of Transportation, the research analyzes community mobility patterns, readiness of local governments and residents, and the railway’s contribution to regional development. Using a mixed-method approach, the study surveyed 300 respondents across Maros, Pangkep, and Barru, revealing high public awareness of the railway, strong potential for tourism growth, and significant economic opportunities through improved connectivity. However, challenges such as infrastructure gaps, land acquisition conflicts, and limited public transport integration remain. The findings emphasize the need for inclusive planning, local workforce engagement, and strategic multimodal transport policies to maximize the railway’s benefits for sustainable development."]

["Inclusion and Exclusion: An Analysis of Beauty Brands’ Political Activism and Women with Disabilities", "Researcher: Tritia Kurniati (s1) Research Theme Description: The bodies and identities of women with disabilities are entitled to equal social acceptance without conditions; however, their existence is often exploited by the beauty industry. This study analyzes advertising campaigns from five beauty brands in Indonesia—Pond's, KULA, Scarlett, Luxcrime, and Wardah. The focus of this research lies in the disciplining of disabled bodies through two key aspects. First, persons with disabilities are reduced to inspiration porn , serving merely as objects of pity to evoke market sympathy. Second, they are expected to become aesthetic laborers, altering their appearance in order to have their existence validated. This study exposes the practice of woke-washing , in which brands actively display diversity for profit while neglecting to create structural change. This research aligns with the Disability Research Group (DRG) in challenging ableism and advocating for the bodily autonomy rights of persons with disabilities."]

["Dinamika Kontestasi Kuasa/Pengetahuan Partisipasi Politik Disabilitas Pada Pemilihan Gubernur dan Wakil Gubernur Sulawesi Selatan Tahun 2018-2024", "Researcher: Hasbullah (S3) Uraian Tema Penelitian: Meskipun regulasi kepemiluan hingga aspek teknisnya di Indonesia semakin inklusif namun tingkat partisipasi politik kelompok disabilitas justru mengalami penurunan. Hal ini tergambar dalam data hasil pemilihan Gubernur dan Wakil Gubernur Sulawesi Selatan Tahun 2024 justru mengalami penurunan jika dibandingkan dengan pemilihan pada tahun 2018: dari 54,28% turun menjadi 50,23%. Sementara pada aspek kepesertaan kedua pemilihan ini menunjukkan hasil serupa, yakni tidak ada disabilitas yang menjadi peserta. Penelitian ini berusaha menyelidiki akar hambatan serta tantangan yang dihadapi kelompok disabilitas dalam rangka merumuskan jalan perbaikan. Dengan menggunakan perspektif Foucaultian dan Axel Honneth, penelitian ini melihat dialektika setiap elemen dalam formasi diskursus disabilitas dalam konteks pilkada. Urgensi penelitian ini adalah mengisi kekosongan data empiris yang juga kuat secara teoritik berdasarkan perspektif sosiologi kritis. Relevan dengan DRG karena mengusung riset inklusif dan berpihak pada hak disabilitas untuk mendapat ruang hidup yang lebih adil."]

["Pembelajaran seksualitas sepanjang masa pada penyandang disabilitas: perspektif interseksional dan fenomenologis", "Researcher: Ida Ariaty Said (S2) Uraian tema penelitian Penyandang disabilitas berhak atas informasi seksualitas dan layanan kesehatan seksual, namun akses mereka terhambat stigma, tabu, dan minimnya pendidikan inklusif. Penelitian ini menggali bagaimana penyandang disabilitas belajar seksualitas sepanjang hayat dari keluarga, sekolah, teman, komunitas, media, dan pengalaman pribadi. Dengan perspektif interseksional, penelitian melihat irisan disabilitas, gender, kelas, daerah asal, dan agama. Urgensi: mengisi kekosongan data empiris di Indonesia. Relevan dengan DRG karena mengusung riset inklusif dan berpihak pada hak penyandang disabilitas atas tubuh dan pengetahuannya."]

["Perancangan Sistem Navigasi Kampus Inklusif Berbasis Teori Graf dan Algoritma A* dengan Bobot Aksesibilitas untuk Penyandang Disabilitas di Unhas", "Researcher: Junaidi (S1) Uraian Tema Penelitian: Penyandang disabilitas visual memiliki hak untuk mengendalikan tubuh mereka, tetapi hak mereka atas tubuh mereka sering kali dirampas oleh orang-orang terdekat mereka, termasuk keluarga mereka, karena stigma yang menganggap mereka tidak mampu mengurusi tubuh sendiri. Penelitian ini menggali bagaimana disabilitas visual memahami tubuh sendiri dan mempresentasikannya dengan atau tanpa campur tangan orang lain. Dengan perspektif interseksional, penelitian melihat irisan disabilitas, gender, kelas sosial, daerah asal, dan agama."]

["Pengalaman Tubuh dan Budaya Berpenampilan Disabilitas Netra", "Researcher: Tiara Ramadhani Sinjar (s1) Uraian Tema Penelitian: Penyandang disabilitas visual memiliki hak untuk mengendalikan tubuh mereka, tetapi hak mereka atas tubuh mereka sering kali dirampas oleh orang-orang terdekat mereka, termasuk keluarga mereka, karena stigma yang menganggap mereka tidak mampu mengurusi tubuh sendiri. The field studies the relationship between society and the environment, helping us understand why environmental problems occur and how societies can respond more effectively."]

["Basic research", "Basic research, or fundamental research, is the cornerstone of scientific discovery, driven by curiosity and a quest for knowledge. Unlike applied research, it focuses on understanding core principles, mechanisms, and processes that form the foundation of natural phenomena without immediate practical applications. In the context of waste management, basic research explores the fundamental behaviors of waste materials, degradation processes, and environmental interactions. For instance, studying the chemical composition and breakdown of organic waste provides critical insights into designing effective composting methods or bioconversion systems. Similarly, examining the environmental impact of different waste materials contributes to the development of environmentally friendly waste treatment technologies. Basic research also plays a pivotal role in understanding the socio-economic aspects of waste generation and management, guiding policies and innovations that align with sustainability goals. By advancing fundamental knowledge, basic research serves as the bedrock for applied research and technological innovation. It informs strategies that address global challenges such as urbanization, resource scarcity, and environmental degradation. Through rigorous investigation and collaboration, basic research bridges gaps in understanding, paving the way for transformative solutions in waste management and environmental protection."]

["A Cave That Remembers: What Leang Bulu Bettue Reveals About Humans in Sulawesi", "What if a cave could tell the story of human life for hundreds of thousands of years? Deep inside the limestone landscape of Maros-Pangkep, South Sulawesi, Leang Bulu Bettue offers something remarkably close to that. Beneath its surface lies a layered archaeological record that preserves evidence of human activity from the Pleistocene to the much more recent past. A major international research team has now documented this extraordinary record in the study “A near-continuous archaeological record of Pleistocene human occupation at Leang Bulu Bettue, Sulawesi, Indonesia.” Led by Basran Burhan and Adam Brumm, with researchers including Budianto Hakim, Iwan Sumantri, Suryatman, and many other Indonesian and international scholars, the study brings together years of excavation and scientific analysis. The researchers conducted multiple seasons of deep-trench excavation at the limestone cave and rock-shelter complex. Since investigations began in 2013, they have uncovered stratified deposits reaching approximately 8 metres below the present surface . The site is currently the only known location on Sulawesi with an archaeological sequence extending from the Middle and Late Pleistocene through to the Late Holocene. The deepest layers offer a glimpse into a very different Sulawesi. Evidence of animal butchery and stone-tool production, including a distinctive stone “pick,” dates to approximately 132,300–208,400 years ago . These findings indicate that humans—or earlier human relatives—were already using this landscape long before the emergence of the cultural world associated with later Homo sapiens . Then, around 40,000 years ago , the archaeological record changes dramatically. An earlier occupation phase, characterised by relatively simple cobble-based stone technology and animal remains dominated by dwarf bovids such as anoas, was replaced by a very different archaeological signature. The researchers identify this later phase as the first evidence at the site for artistic expression and symbolic culture . This transition raises a much bigger question: who were the people responsible for these changes? The researchers suggest that the sharp behavioural difference may reflect the replacement of archaic hominins by modern humans. However, they present this as a possibility rather than a definitive conclusion. The archaeological record provides an important new framework for investigating when different human populations arrived, lived, changed, and perhaps disappeared from Sulawesi. What makes Leang Bulu Bettue especially significant is therefore not a single artefact. It is the continuity of the archaeological record itself . Layer by layer, the cave preserves traces of changing technologies, environments, animals, and human behaviour. Together, these traces transform a limestone shelter into a long-term archive of human occupation in Wallacea. The discovery also highlights why protecting archaeological landscapes matters. The Maros-Pangkep karst is not simply a spectacular natural environment. Its caves contain irreplaceable evidence about the deep history of human life in Southeast Asia. This makes the research relevant to Sustainable Development Goal 15 (SDG 15): Life on Land , particularly the protection of terrestrial ecosystems and natural heritage. Conserving karst landscapes can simultaneously protect biodiversity, geological formations, and archaeological evidence that cannot be recreated once lost. Leang Bulu Bettue reminds us that Sulawesi's human story did not begin with written history. It reaches deep into the Pleistocene—preserved quietly in layers of sediment, stone, bone, and the traces of human activity. Sometimes, the oldest stories are not written in books. They are written in the ground. ["When Archaeologists Speak the Same Language: Building a Common Vocabulary for Indonesian Archaeology", "Archaeology is often imagined as a discipline of ancient objects, excavation sites, and discoveries buried beneath the ground. But behind every excavation is another essential tool: language . When archaeologists from different countries work together, even simple field instructions can become surprisingly complicated. A technical term that is familiar to an Indonesian archaeologist may not immediately carry the same meaning for an international researcher. The problem becomes even more important when research findings must later be communicated through international publications. A new article highlights a simple but practical way to address this challenge: creating a shared vocabulary between English and Indonesian for archaeological research. The article, titled “A Concise Indonesian/English Guide to Common Terms Used in Excavation and Archaeological Research,” was written by Yinika L. Perston and Suryatman . The authors recognize that international collaboration has played an important role in Indonesian archaeology for more than a century. As archaeological research becomes increasingly collaborative, clear communication between researchers becomes essential. Rather than presenting a complicated theoretical discussion, the article provides a basic list of translations for commonly used archaeological terms in English and Indonesian. These languages are currently among the most frequently used for archaeological research, fieldwork, and academic publications involving Indonesian archaeology. Why does such a list matter? Imagine a team preparing an excavation. Researchers need to describe soil layers, record archaeological contexts, identify finds, document features, and communicate observations. If members of the team use different terms for the same archaeological concept—or interpret the same term differently—small misunderstandings can affect field documentation and communication. A shared vocabulary can therefore function as more than a translation tool. It can become a bridge between researchers, students, field teams, and institutions . The need is particularly relevant for the next generation of archaeologists. Students entering archaeological fieldwork may encounter English terminology in international literature while using Indonesian terminology in classrooms, reports, and local research settings. Understanding the relationship between the two can make it easier to move between national and international research environments. The article also reminds us that language is part of the infrastructure of science. Archaeological discoveries may attract public attention, but reliable research depends on something much less visible: researchers being able to communicate accurately with one another. This perspective can be connected to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4): Quality Education . Building accessible bilingual resources can support students and researchers in developing the knowledge and communication skills needed to participate in archaeological research across linguistic and national boundaries. Ultimately, preserving archaeological knowledge is not only about protecting artifacts and excavation sites. It is also about ensuring that researchers can share, understand, document, and transmit that knowledge . Sometimes, strengthening archaeology does not require a new excavation or a sophisticated piece of technology. Sometimes, it begins with something much simpler: making sure everyone on the research team understands the same words. ["When a Forest Has Many Names: What Dayak Tunjung Vocabulary Reveals About a Changing Environment", "A forest is more than trees. For Indigenous communities, it can also be a living archive—holding knowledge about soil, plants, seasons, farming, and the gradual return of vegetation after a field has been cultivated. Sometimes, that knowledge is preserved not in written records, but in the words people use to describe the landscape around them. A study of the Dayak Tunjung community in East Kalimantan, Indonesia , shows why those words matter. The research, “Signifying the End of Swidden? An Analysis of Vocabulary of the Fallow Stage Among a Kalimantan Indigenous Group, Indonesia,” examines the vocabulary used to describe different stages of fallow land in traditional swidden agriculture. Conducted by Syamsul Rijal, Muhammad Hasyim, Lukman Lukman, and Ery Iswary, the study explores how language reflects changes in both ecological knowledge and the relationship between communities and their environment. The researchers conducted 16 semi-structured interviews and participant observation in Linggang Melapeh Village. Participants were selected across generations and occupations, allowing the researchers to compare how ecological vocabulary is remembered and used by different groups. The findings reveal an important generational difference. Older members of the Dayak Tunjung community still retain a detailed vocabulary associated with ecological succession and customary land management. These terms distinguish stages of fallow land and reflect observations accumulated through generations of interaction with the forest. Among younger generations, however, familiarity with some of these traditional terms is declining. At the same time, traditional agricultural cycles are changing, with increasingly shorter fallow periods. This is more than a change in vocabulary. The researchers describe the pattern as biocultural erosion —a process in which the loss of linguistic knowledge occurs alongside changes in ecological relationships and cultural practices. Land commodification and shifting livelihood strategies are among the pressures contributing to these transformations. The study offers an important reminder: when a word disappears, the knowledge behind that word may disappear with it. For this reason, protecting Indigenous languages is not only a matter of preserving cultural identity. It can also help safeguard ecological knowledge that has developed through long-term relationships with particular landscapes. The researchers call for efforts to revitalize Indigenous ecological narratives while strengthening Indigenous governance in conservation. They recommend approaches including education, participatory mapping, and culturally grounded policies that recognize local knowledge rather than treating conservation as something designed entirely from outside the community. This makes the research especially relevant to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 15: Life on Land , which promotes the protection and sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems. Indigenous ecological knowledge can contribute to this goal by offering locally grounded ways of understanding forests, land regeneration, and sustainable resource use. Ultimately, the Dayak Tunjung case shows that environmental change can sometimes be heard before it is seen. It may appear in the disappearance of a word, the shortening of a farming cycle, or the fading memory of how a forest regenerates. Protecting the forest, therefore, may also mean protecting the language that teaches people how to understand it. Article Information Article Title: Signifying the End of Swidden? An Analysis of Vocabulary of the Fallow Stage Among a Kalimantan Indigenous Group, Indonesia Authors: Syamsul Rijal, Muhammad Hasyim, Lukman Lukman, and Ery Iswary Journal: Forest and Society Publisher: Hasanuddin University Publication Date: 17 September 2025 Volume: 9 Issue: 2 Pages: 604–622 DOI: 10.24259/fs.v9i2.43632 Scopus EID: 2-s2.0-105027964454"]

["From Silent Readers to Digital Publishers: Why Social Media Ethics Matters", "Every day, millions of people scroll through social media, read comments, watch videos, share information, and express their opinions. But in the digital age, being an internet user means much more than simply consuming information. A person can read a message in the morning, create a response in the afternoon, and publish content to thousands of people by evening. This transformation raises an important question: when everyone can become a publisher, who is responsible for what gets published? The study “Netizens as Readers, Producers, and Publishers: Communication Ethics and Challenges in Social Media” by Burhanuddin Arafah, Muhammad Hasyim, and Herawati Abbas examines this question by looking at how netizens communicate and participate in public discussions on social media. The researchers used a descriptive qualitative approach, combining observations of comments on YouTube videos concerning corruption and immoral behavior with an online questionnaire. The questionnaire collected responses from 1,061 social media users , providing a broad picture of how people participate in digital communication. The findings reveal a digital environment with two very different sides. On one side, social media gives people an opportunity to express criticism, recommend positive changes, exchange ideas, and participate in public discussions. Some users employ respectful language and create content that encourages constructive dialogue. On the other hand, unrestricted expression can also produce harmful consequences. Some online discussions contain negativity, hostile responses, and hate speech , particularly when users react emotionally to controversial issues such as corruption and moral misconduct. The same platforms that allow constructive criticism can therefore also become spaces where harmful communication spreads rapidly. This is what makes the role of the netizen increasingly important. A social media user is no longer merely a reader. A comment can become a public statement. A repost can amplify information to thousands of people. A short video can influence public opinion. In other words, every user potentially participates in shaping the digital public sphere. The researchers therefore emphasize that participation comes with responsibility. Freedom of expression does not eliminate the need for ethical communication. Instead, the greater the ability to reach an audience, the greater the responsibility to consider the consequences of what is shared. This message is particularly relevant to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4: Quality Education . Education in the digital era should not stop at teaching people how to access information or operate technology. It should also equip them to evaluate information critically, communicate responsibly, respect others, and participate constructively in society. Digital literacy, therefore, is not simply about knowing how to use social media . It is also about understanding how our actions on social media affect other people . Ultimately, the study reminds us that the digital world is shaped not only by algorithms and technology, but also by everyday human choices. Every comment, post, reaction, and share contributes to the kind of public conversation we create. The question is no longer whether we have the right to speak. The more important question is: what kind of digital citizen do we choose to become? ["When Ancient Wisdom Meets Modern Leadership: Six Bugis Values for Better Leaders", "What makes someone a good leader? In modern discussions, the answer often revolves around competence, vision, innovation, and the ability to make decisions. But long before leadership became a subject of management studies, communities had already developed their own ideas about what makes a leader worthy of trust. Among the Bugis people of South Sulawesi, these ideas are preserved in local wisdom. A recent study, “The Values of Leadership in the Local Wisdom of the Bugis People,” explores how Bugis cultural values can provide principles for leadership, particularly in government. The study was conducted by Burhanuddin Arafah, Muhammad Hasyim, Herawaty Abbas, A. St. Aldilah Khaerana, and Takwa. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, the researchers examined literature on Bugis leadership values and gathered questionnaire responses to explore their implications for government leadership. At the heart of the study are six values: Lempu, Getteng, Ada Tongeng, Assitinajang, Acca, and Warani . Lempu refers to honesty. For a leader, honesty is more than telling the truth; it is the foundation for building public trust. Getteng , or firmness, highlights the importance of consistency and commitment in carrying out responsibilities. Then comes Ada Tongeng , meaning the use of right or truthful words. In leadership, words matter because public communication can shape trust, cooperation, and confidence. Assitinajang emphasizes appropriateness or fairness—the ability to act according to circumstances, responsibilities, and what is considered proper. The fifth value, Acca , represents wisdom and intelligence. A leader needs knowledge, but knowledge alone is not enough. It must be accompanied by the wisdom to understand situations and make appropriate decisions. Finally, Warani , or courage, reminds leaders that responsibility sometimes requires the willingness to make difficult decisions and stand by what is right. Together, these six values present leadership not simply as a position of authority, but as a matter of character . A leader is expected to possess knowledge and courage while remaining honest, fair, consistent, and responsible in communication. This perspective is particularly relevant in an era when leadership is increasingly judged not only by performance, but also by integrity and public trust. Local wisdom can therefore become more than a cultural inheritance. It can serve as a source of learning for younger generations about ethical behavior, responsibility, and civic leadership. This connects strongly with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4: Quality Education , particularly its broader emphasis on education that supports values, responsible citizenship, and lifelong learning. Cultural knowledge such as Bugis leadership philosophy can contribute to education by connecting contemporary leadership lessons with knowledge rooted in local communities. Ultimately, the study suggests that the wisdom of the past still has something to say about leadership today. Lempu, Getteng, Ada Tongeng, Assitinajang, Acca, and Warani offer a reminder that effective leadership is not only about what a leader can achieve, but also about who that leader becomes while serving others . ["When Translation Shapes Digital Literacy: Why Cultural Meaning Matters in Government Social Media", "A government message can be grammatically correct and still fail to communicate what it truly means. This becomes particularly important in today’s digital world, where governments increasingly use social media to communicate policies, public information, and services to younger generations. In a multilingual and culturally diverse country such as Indonesia, translating these messages is not simply a matter of replacing words from one language with another. Cultural meaning can shape how people understand, trust, and respond to information. A recent study explores this issue by examining how cultural nuances in the translation of Indonesian government social media content influence the digital literacy of young people . The research, titled “The Impact of Cultural Nuances in the Translation of Indonesian Government Social Media Content on the Digital Literacy of Young Generations,” was conducted by Burhanuddin Arafah, Herawaty Abbas, Muhammad Hasyim, Muhammad Ridha Anugrah Latief, and Taqdir . The researchers used a quantitative approach and collected data from 243 respondents aged 17–22 years through an online questionnaire. The study examined several interconnected factors, including cultural nuances, translation strategies, machine translation, socio-political context, message comprehension, and digital literacy. The findings offer an important lesson for digital communication: culture matters when people interpret information . The researchers found that cultural nuances positively influence young people’s comprehension of government messages. When translations preserve culturally meaningful expressions and contextual references, audiences are more likely to understand the intended message. Translation strategies, however, played only a limited mediating role. The research also highlights the growing influence of machine translation . Automated tools can make communication faster and more accessible, but they do not always capture the cultural and contextual meanings embedded in language. The study found that machine translation and socio-political context can significantly affect how young audiences interpret government messages. Another important finding concerns digital literacy itself. Young respondents generally demonstrated relatively strong abilities in areas related to digital ethics and safety , but their abilities in digital content creation and participation remained weaker . This distinction is significant. Being digitally literate is not only about knowing how to use technology safely. It also means being able to critically understand information, evaluate its meaning, and actively participate in the digital public sphere. The findings therefore suggest that government communication needs to move beyond linguistic accuracy. Effective digital communication should also consider cultural sensitivity, audience context, and the way young people interpret information . This perspective connects strongly with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4): Quality Education , particularly the goal of developing knowledge and skills that enable people to participate meaningfully in society. Digital literacy is increasingly part of that educational landscape. The study ultimately reminds us that translation is not merely a technical process. It is an act of interpretation. When government messages travel across languages and cultures, preserving meaning can help young people become not only safer digital users, but also more informed and active citizens. ["When a Wedding Ceremony Becomes a Classroom: The Cultural Knowledge Hidden in Tolaki Mekongga Ritual Speech", "A wedding ceremony is often remembered for its celebration, food, music, and gathering of families. But among the Tolaki Mekongga people of Southeast Sulawesi, a traditional wedding ritual can also function as a living classroom—where language teaches younger generations about respect, harmony, morality, and cultural identity. This is the central insight of a recent study examining Mowindahako , a traditional ritual speech practiced by the Tolaki Mekongga community in Kolaka, Southeast Sulawesi. The study, titled “Linguistic Units and Cultural Meanings in the Ritual Speech of Mowindahako Among the Tolaki Mekongga Ethnic Group,” explores how words, expressions, and patterns of speech used during the ritual carry meanings that extend far beyond ordinary communication. Conducted by Takwa, Burhanuddin Arafah, Muhammad Hasyim, Andi Muhammmad Akhmar, and Taqdir , the research uses a descriptive qualitative approach within the field of Cultural Linguistics. The researchers collected data through observation, audio recordings, interviews with customary leaders, and documentation of ritual speech. They then examined the language at several levels, from individual words and phrases to clauses, sentences, and complete discourse. The findings reveal that Mowindahako is characterized by repetition, rhythmic patterns, parallel expressions, and archaic forms of the Tolaki language . These features are not simply forms of artistic expression. They help give the ceremony its solemnity and reinforce the cultural meanings communicated through the ritual. Several important cultural symbols also appear in the speech. Kalosara , for example, represents unity, balance, justice, and moral order within Tolaki Mekongga customary life. Other symbols, including karambau and tawa-tawa , carry meanings connected to social, economic, and spiritual values. The ritual itself involves respected representatives of the families, including the tolea and pabitara , who deliver formal dialogue in Tolaki. Their speech is structured according to stages that include opening expressions of respect, dialogue and negotiation, closing statements, and a final affirmation or oath. Through these carefully structured exchanges, language becomes more than a tool for conveying information. It becomes a way of teaching culture . Values such as respect for elders, cooperation, honesty, social harmony, and balance are embedded within the words and performance of the ritual. In this sense, Mowindahako helps transmit cultural knowledge from one generation to another while strengthening the community’s collective identity. This finding is particularly relevant to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4): Quality Education , especially the broader goal of promoting education that values cultural diversity and lifelong learning. Education does not always take place in classrooms. It can also happen through ceremonies, stories, language, and everyday cultural practices. The study therefore reminds us that preserving a language means preserving much more than vocabulary. Within traditional speech, communities may store their history, ethics, worldview, and understanding of how people should live together. As globalization changes the way younger generations communicate, documenting and understanding ritual languages such as Mowindahako becomes increasingly important. A language can be a cultural archive—and sometimes, a wedding ceremony can be one of its most powerful classrooms. ["When a River Becomes a Story: How Cultural Narratives Create Memorable Tourism Experiences", "A journey through a geopark is rarely just about looking at mountains, rivers, or spectacular landscapes. Sometimes, what visitors remember most is the story they hear, the legend they encounter, or the cultural meaning they discover along the way. This idea is at the heart of a recent study exploring how cultural narratives can transform ordinary tourism activities into unique and memorable experiences . The study, titled “Cultural Narrative Tourism: Exploring Experience Unique and Memorable Tourist in Destination of Geo Park,” examines how visitors experience cultural narratives while exploring a geopark landscape characterized by karst mountains and rivers. Rather than viewing tourism only as sightseeing, the researchers highlight the importance of stories and cultural expressions in shaping how visitors remember a destination. The research was conducted by Muhammad Hasyim, Aqilah Nurul Khaerani, Farah Fadilah, and Wahyuddin . The researchers collected information directly from tourists through questionnaires and interviews at the tourism destination. Their focus was on how visitors expressed and remembered their experiences while engaging with the destination. One of the study’s central findings is that cultural narratives can become attractions in their own right . A boat journey through a river surrounded by karst landscapes, for example, is not simply a way to move from one point to another. When accompanied by cultural stories, myths, and local interpretations, the journey can become an experience that visitors find distinctive and memorable. This matters because tourism is increasingly about more than simply seeing a beautiful place. Visitors often seek experiences that feel meaningful, authentic, and different from everyday life. A landscape may attract people to a destination, but the stories connected to that landscape can influence what they remember after returning home. Cultural narratives can therefore serve as a bridge between place, people, and tourism experience . They can help visitors understand that a destination is not merely a collection of physical attractions but also a living cultural landscape shaped by memories, beliefs, activities, and local expressions. The findings also suggest an opportunity for destination development. By recognizing cultural narratives as part of the tourism experience, geopark destinations can create tourism products that are not solely dependent on scenery. Storytelling, interpretation, river journeys, and other culturally meaningful activities can add depth to the visitor experience while strengthening the identity of the destination. This perspective is particularly relevant to Sustainable Development Goal 8 (SDG 8): Decent Work and Economic Growth , which promotes sustainable tourism that creates jobs and supports local culture and products. When cultural narratives are responsibly incorporated into tourism, local knowledge and cultural expressions can become valuable components of the visitor economy. Ultimately, the research offers a simple but powerful reminder: people may visit a destination because of what they see, but they often remember it because of the stories they experience. For geoparks, protecting and interpreting those stories may be just as important as showcasing the landscapes themselves. ["Printing the Past: How 3D Technology Could Help Protect Sulawesi’s Ancient Rock Art", "What if one of the world’s oldest stories could be preserved without requiring everyone to enter the cave where it was painted? Deep inside the karst landscape of Maros-Pangkep, South Sulawesi, prehistoric rock art tells stories that have survived for tens of thousands of years. Among them is the remarkable hunting scene at Leang Bulu Sipong 4 , depicting human-like figures hunting wild pigs and dwarf bovids. Dated to at least 43,900 years ago, the artwork is considered the world’s oldest known narrative hunting scene. But preserving such ancient art is becoming increasingly difficult. Environmental deterioration, human activity, pollution, and other pressures threaten fragile cave surfaces and pigments. At the same time, allowing more visitors to access these sites can create additional conservation challenges. A new study proposes an innovative way to address this dilemma: 3D-printed replicas . The research, titled “3D-printed replicas for rock art preservation: A workflow development and fidelity assessment,” was conducted by Nur Ihsan, Yadi Mulyadi, Iswan Bintang, Aqilah NK. Latief, Khadijah Tahir Muda, Yusriana, Rustan Lebe, Moh Mochsen Sir, and Andi Jusdi . The researchers developed a workflow that combines photogrammetry, digital modelling, and consumer-grade 3D printing to reproduce large rock-art panels. Using Leang Bulu Sipong 4 as a case study, the team first digitally documented the cave wall and transformed the images into a three-dimensional model. The model was then divided into smaller sections and printed before being assembled into a half-scale, 1:2 replica . The result demonstrates that advanced heritage preservation does not always require expensive industrial technology. The researchers achieved geometric correspondence within 2.5% for overall dimensions , allowing the major motifs of the hunting scene to remain clearly recognizable. However, the study also found limitations. Fine surface textures and colour matching could not be reproduced perfectly because of the resolution of the printing process and surface finishing. Importantly, the researchers do not present the replica as a replacement for the original artwork. Instead, they describe it as a purpose-bound surrogate —a reproduction created for specific purposes such as museum exhibitions, education, research, and public interpretation. This distinction matters. A replica can increase public access while reducing the need for frequent visits to vulnerable archaeological sites. It can also provide opportunities for closer observation and hands-on learning without placing additional pressure on the original artwork. The approach contributes directly to Sustainable Development Goal 15 (SDG 15): Life on Land , particularly the broader goal of protecting terrestrial ecosystems and heritage landscapes. Conservation is not only about keeping ancient paintings in place; it is also about finding responsible ways for society to learn from and appreciate them. By connecting digital documentation with affordable physical reproduction, the study shows that technology can become a practical partner in heritage conservation. For regions with limited budgets, infrastructure, or site access, 3D printing may offer a new way to bring the stories of the past closer to people—while keeping the originals safely where they belong. Publication Date: 23 March 2026 Volume: 41 Article Number: e00526 DOI: 10.1016/j.daach.2026.e00526"]

["Beyond Accessible Trails: Rethinking Inclusive Tourism in Protected Rural Areas", "Tourism in protected rural areas is often associated with breathtaking landscapes, rich biodiversity, and opportunities to connect with nature. Yet, an important question remains: can everyone access, participate in, and benefit from these tourism experiences? A recent study highlights why inclusive tourism should go beyond simply building accessible facilities. The article, “Inclusive Tourism in Protected Rural Areas: A Systematic Review and Network Analysis,” examines how tourism destinations can balance accessibility, community participation, visitor management, and conservation. The study was conducted by Nur Adyla Suriadi, Arifuddin Akil, Amran Achmad, and Aqilah Nurul Khaerani Latif . Using bibliometric network analysis and a systematic literature review guided by PRISMA 2020, the researchers analyzed 498 publications indexed in Scopus and conducted an in-depth synthesis of 46 empirical journal articles . The findings reveal that research on inclusive tourism in protected rural areas has grown substantially, particularly between 2021 and 2024. However, the growth of research also points to persistent challenges. One of the most important issues is unequal accessibility . People with disabilities may continue to encounter physical and informational barriers even when tourism infrastructure has been improved. Accessibility, therefore, cannot be understood simply as the presence of ramps, pathways, or facilities. It also involves information, services, transportation, staff capacity, and the overall visitor experience. The study also emphasizes that inclusion must involve local communities . Tourism cannot be considered inclusive if residents are excluded from decision-making or do not receive a fair share of its economic, social, and cultural benefits. Meaningful participation, co-creation, and community engagement can strengthen perceptions of fairness while supporting the long-term legitimacy of tourism development. Another key finding is that infrastructure alone is not enough. Protected rural destinations require integrated visitor management, including interpretation, zoning, route management, appropriate access controls, and multi-stakeholder governance . These approaches can help destinations welcome visitors while maintaining ecological and conservation limits. The study therefore presents inclusive tourism as a shared management challenge rather than a single accessibility issue. Accessibility, community participation, governance, and conservation need to be addressed together. This perspective is closely connected to Sustainable Development Goal 15 (SDG 15): Life on Land , which promotes the protection and sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems. Making tourism more inclusive does not mean opening protected areas without limits. Instead, it means designing tourism systems that allow more people to participate while respecting the ecological boundaries of the places they visit. The research was published in Environmental and Sustainability Indicators , Volume 31, Article 101455, by Elsevier B.V. in September 2026 . The article is available as an open-access publication under a Creative Commons license, with DOI 10.1016/j.indic.2026.101455 . ["Forced into a meat grinder or defending their home country? The representation of ethnic Hungarian soldiers of Ukraine in the Hungarian press", "The research entitled “Forced into a Meat Grinder or Defending Their Home Country? The Representation of Ethnic Hungarian Soldiers of Ukraine in the Hungarian Press” examines how Ukrainian soldiers of ethnic Hungarian background are represented in the Hungarian media. The study is based on the situation of the ethnic Hungarian community in Ukraine, whose members have distinct cultural and historical identities while simultaneously holding Ukrainian citizenship. This situation becomes increasingly complex when some members of the community serve in the Ukrainian military during the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. The media plays an important role in shaping public understanding of events. News reporting does not simply present facts; it also involves the selection of particular words, sources, perspectives, and emphases. Therefore, the way ethnic Hungarian soldiers are portrayed in the media can provide insight into how their identity and position are understood within the context of the war. The title of the study presents two contrasting possible representations. The expression “forced into a meat grinder” portrays the soldiers as individuals placed in a dangerous and highly distressing wartime situation. This perspective emphasizes their vulnerability and the risks they face. They may be portrayed as individuals trapped in a conflict and forced to experience the consequences of an ongoing war. In contrast, the expression “defending their home country” offers a different perspective. From this viewpoint, ethnic Hungarian soldiers are presented as Ukrainian citizens fulfilling their responsibility to defend the country in which they live. Their Hungarian ethnic identity does not automatically determine their loyalty to another state. Cultural identity can coexist with Ukrainian citizenship and a sense of belonging to Ukraine. This issue of identity is particularly significant because many members of Ukraine’s ethnic Hungarian community live in Zakarpattia (Transcarpathia) , a region with strong historical and cultural ties to Hungary. The local population has developed a distinctive identity shaped by its language, traditions, and historical background. During the war, these characteristics have become important aspects of media coverage concerning ethnic Hungarian soldiers serving in the Ukrainian military. The study demonstrates that media representations of ethnic groups in situations of conflict can produce different meanings. A soldier may be portrayed as a citizen defending their country, as a member of a particular ethnic group, or as a victim of the conflict. The resulting representation depends largely on the narrative and perspective adopted by the media. Ultimately, the research highlights the close relationship between media, ethnic identity, and political conflict . Reporting on ethnic Hungarian soldiers in Ukraine is not solely about the war itself; it also involves broader issues of identity, nationalism, citizenship, and Hungary-Ukraine relations. Analyzing the Hungarian press is therefore important for understanding how a minority group is represented and how media narratives can shape public perceptions of that group's position within the conflict."]

["FRENCH COLONIAL CULTURAL HERITAGE IN VIETNAM", "This study examines various forms of heritage that emerged from the historical relationship between France and Vietnam during the colonial period. This heritage is not limited to historic buildings with European architectural styles, but also encompasses changes in urban planning, education, language, cuisine, and social life. Colonial heritage can therefore be understood as part of a historical process that contributed to shaping Vietnam’s development into the present day. French colonial rule influenced the development of several cities in Vietnam, particularly Hanoi and Saigon, now known as Ho Chi Minh City. During this period, urban development was directed toward supporting the needs of the colonial administration through the construction of administrative buildings, schools, hospitals, churches, post offices, roads, residential areas, and transportation infrastructure. Many buildings from this period have survived and remain part of Vietnam’s urban landscape. Their continued presence provides historical value while also contributing to the appeal of cultural tourism. Architecturally, colonial heritage reflects the introduction of European building concepts into an Asian environment. However, these concepts were not applied exactly as they were in France, as they had to be adapted to Vietnam’s tropical climate. This can be seen in the use of large windows, high ceilings, open spaces, and other elements designed to facilitate air circulation. This combination created a distinctive form of colonial architecture with its own identity in Vietnam. Today, some colonial buildings have been repurposed as offices, museums, cultural centers, educational facilities, and tourist attractions. French influence also extended beyond the physical environment. Interactions between Vietnamese society and French culture resulted in processes of cultural exchange and adaptation. Such influences can be found in education, language, cuisine, and patterns of urban life. Bánh mì , for example, demonstrates how culinary elements introduced during the colonial period were subsequently adapted by Vietnamese communities and transformed into a distinctly local food. Meanwhile, the use of the Latin-based writing system for the Vietnamese language through Quốc Ngữ became an important part of the development of communication and education in Vietnam. However, colonial heritage also needs to be understood critically. These legacies emerged within a context of colonial power involving complex social, political, and economic issues. Therefore, buildings and cultural traditions inherited from this period should not be viewed solely as symbols of progress, but also as reminders of the colonial experience and the Vietnamese people's struggle for independence. Ultimately, the study of French colonial cultural heritage helps reveal the complex relationship between the past and contemporary Vietnamese society. Preserving colonial heritage can serve as a means of maintaining historical memory while introducing its cultural significance to future generations. When developed within the context of cultural tourism, such heritage can provide an engaging way of learning about history, while ensuring that the experiences and perspectives of Vietnamese communities remain an essential part of how this heritage is interpreted and understood."]
