["Moringa and Royal Jelly: Local Nutrition for Better Birth Outcomes", "A healthy birth begins long before a baby is delivered. During pregnancy, the mother’s body provides the nutrients that support fetal growth, organ development, and readiness for life outside the womb. When maternal nutrition is not adequate, babies may face higher risks of low birth weight, shorter birth length, premature birth, and weaker early health. This is why safe and practical nutrition support during pregnancy remains an important public health priority. A scientific article entitled “Effect of Giving Moringa (Moringa oleifera) Leaf Extract Capsules Enriched with Royal Jelly to Pregnant Women on Birth Outcomes” discusses this issue through a study in Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. The article is listed in Gazzetta Medica Italiana - Archivio per le Scienze Mediche , under Edizioni Minerva Medica , with paper code Gazz Med Ital - Arch Sci Med-5827 . The attached manuscript shows the submission date as October 7, 2024 , and the article type as an Original Article . This study examined whether Moringa leaf extract capsules enriched with royal jelly, known as MRJ, could support pregnancy outcomes compared with multiple micronutrient supplementation, or MMS. The study was conducted in two sub-districts, Batui Selatan and Moilong. It was a follow-up cohort study from a previous pregnancy intervention. Pregnant women in the MRJ group received 500 mg capsules twice a day for 90 days, while women in the control group received MMS tablets once a day. The final sample included 21 mothers in the MRJ group and 25 mothers in the MMS group. Birth outcomes were obtained from medical records, including gestational age, APGAR score, birth weight, and birth length. The results showed that babies in both groups had generally good birth outcomes. The average gestational age was 38.95 weeks in the MRJ group and 39.52 weeks in the MMS group. The APGAR score, which reflects a newborn’s early condition after birth, was reassuring in both groups. Average birth weight was also normal, reaching 3267.38 grams in the MRJ group and 3280.00 grams in the MMS group. Birth length was 49.14 cm in the MRJ group and 48.88 cm in the MMS group. Although the differences were not statistically significant, these findings suggest that MRJ may provide birth outcomes comparable to MMS. This finding is meaningful because Moringa is a local plant rich in protein, vitamins, minerals, iron, calcium, and vitamin C. Royal jelly also contains nutrients and bioactive compounds that may support maternal health. Together, they may become a local nutrition-based option for pregnant women. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to improve maternal and newborn health. In conclusion, Moringa enriched with royal jelly may be a promising local supplement to support healthier pregnancies and normal birth outcomes, although further research with larger samples is still needed."]

["Gammara’Na: Bringing Nutrition Guidance Closer to Families in South Sulawesi", "Nutrition is one of the strongest foundations for a child’s future. During the first years of life, children need enough food, diverse nutrients, and regular growth monitoring to support their bodies and brains. When feeding practices are poor, children may become underweight, wasted, or stunted. These conditions can affect learning ability, immunity, and long-term productivity. For this reason, family nutrition support is an important part of child health programs. A published article entitled “The effect of nutritional assistance ‘Gammara’Na’ on food acceptance and nutritional status of children in South Sulawesi, Indonesia” provides important evidence on this issue. The article was published in Nutrición Clínica y Dietética Hospitalaria , Volume 45, Issue 1, pages 38–46, in 2025 , with DOI 10.12873/451nadimin . The article was received on 17 October 2024 and accepted on 3 December 2024 . It discusses how the Gammara’Na nutrition assistance program helped improve feeding practices and nutritional status among children in South Sulawesi. The Gammara’Na program was designed as a community-based nutrition support strategy in stunting-prone villages. The study used a pretest-posttest design without a control group and involved 114 villages and 2,148 families. For six months, Village Nutrition Assistants, known as TPGD, provided nutrition education and counseling to families. The assistance focused on infant and young child feeding, growth monitoring, and supplementary feeding. The findings showed encouraging changes. After the program, children’s feeding frequency increased by 12.1%. Dietary diversity increased even more, by 27.1%. Food acceptance, which reflects whether children receive meals frequently enough and consume diverse foods, improved by 25.3%. This means more families were able to provide children with better eating patterns after receiving direct assistance. The program also showed positive effects on nutritional status. The proportion of stunted children decreased by 5.4%. Wasting decreased by 1.2%, and underweight decreased by 2.6%. Children with good food acceptance also had better nutritional Z-scores than children with poor food acceptance. This finding shows that what children eat, how often they eat, and how varied their food is can influence their growth. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to improve child nutrition and reduce stunting. It also reminds us that nutrition programs should not only distribute food, but also educate, guide, and accompany families. When parents understand children’s nutritional needs, they can make better daily feeding decisions. This approach is especially relevant for vulnerable families who need practical advice that fits local food availability and daily household routines. In conclusion, the Gammara’Na program shows that village-level nutrition assistance can make a meaningful difference. Through counseling, home-based support, and growth monitoring, families can improve children’s diets and help them grow healthier. Strong community nutrition support can become a practical pathway to reduce stunting and build a healthier generation in Indonesia. Reference : DOI 10.12873/451nadimin Contact : Prof. dr. Veni Hadju, M.Sc., Ph. D +62811441803 phunhas@gmail.com"]

["Moringa and Royal Jelly: Natural Support for Stress During Pregnancy", "Pregnancy is a meaningful journey, but it can also bring emotional pressure. Many pregnant women experience changes in mood, sleep, energy, and confidence as their bodies adapt to pregnancy. When stress continues, it may affect both the mother and the developing baby. One biological sign of stress is cortisol, often known as the stress hormone. Managing stress during pregnancy is therefore not only about comfort; it is part of protecting maternal and infant health. A published article entitled “Moringa Leaf Extract Capsules Enriched with Royal Jelly on Cortisol and Stress” provides important evidence about this issue. The article was published in KEMAS: Jurnal Kesehatan Masyarakat , Volume 20, Issue 4, pages 705–714, in April 2025 , through the Universitas Negeri Semarang journal platform , with DOI https://doi.org/10.15294/kemas.v20i4.3578 . This study examined whether moringa leaf extract capsules enriched with royal jelly could help reduce cortisol and stress levels among pregnant women in Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi. The study used a single-blind randomized controlled trial design and was conducted from July to October 2023 in South Batui and Moilong Districts. A total of 61 pregnant women completed the study. The intervention group consisted of 31 pregnant women who received moringa leaf extract capsules enriched with royal jelly, while the control group consisted of 30 pregnant women who received multi-micronutrient supplements. Cortisol levels were measured using saliva samples, and stress levels were assessed using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales questionnaire. The results showed that both groups experienced improvement after the intervention. In the moringa and royal jelly group, cortisol levels decreased from 26.61 to 19.98. Stress levels also decreased from 18.68 to 15.90. The control group also showed reductions in cortisol and stress levels. However, when the changes between the two groups were compared, the difference was not statistically significant. This means that moringa leaf extract enriched with royal jelly produced results that were almost similar to multi-micronutrient supplements in this study. This finding is meaningful because moringa is a local plant that is already familiar in many Indonesian communities. Its leaves contain nutrients and bioactive compounds, including polyphenols, antioxidants, and gamma-aminobutyric acid, known as GABA, which may help calm the nervous system. Royal jelly also contains proteins, fatty acids, and other bioactive substances that may support the body’s response to stress and inflammation. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to improve maternal mental health and pregnancy care. It also reminds health workers that antenatal care should include not only physical examinations, but also attention to emotional well-being. In conclusion, moringa leaf extract enriched with royal jelly may become a promising local nutrition-based option to support pregnant women experiencing stress. With regular screening, counseling, and further research, natural products like moringa may help build healthier pregnancies and healthier babies. Reference : DOI https://doi.org/10.15294/kemas.v20i4.3578 Contact : Prof. dr. Veni Hadju, M.Sc., Ph. D +62811441803 phunhas@gmail.com"]

["Moringa and Royal Jelly: Helping Mothers Produce More Breast Milk", "Breastfeeding is one of the first and most important sources of protection for a baby. In the first months of life, breast milk provides energy, nutrients, and immune support that help infants grow and fight infection. However, many mothers face a common concern: feeling that their breast milk is not enough. This perception can reduce confidence and may lead to early use of formula or other foods before the baby is ready. A scientific article entitled “Potential of Moringa Leaf Extract (Moringa oleifera) Enriched Royal Jelly in Increasing Breast Milk Volume of Breastfeeding Mothers” discusses this important issue. The article is listed in Gazzetta Medica Italiana - Archivio per le Scienze Mediche , under Edizioni Minerva Medica , with paper code Gazz Med Ital - Arch Sci Med-5824 . The attached PDF shows the submission date as October 7, 2024 , and the article type as an Original Article . This study explored whether Moringa leaf extract enriched with royal jelly, known as MRJ, could help increase breast milk volume among breastfeeding mothers. The study was conducted in Batui Selatan and Moilong sub-districts, Banggai Regency, Indonesia, from April to July 2024. It used an analytical observational cohort design and involved 61 breastfeeding mothers who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The mothers were divided into two groups. The control group consisted of 28 mothers who consumed Multiple Micronutrient Supplement, or MMS. The intervention group consisted of 33 mothers who had consumed MRJ during pregnancy. Breast milk volume was measured after delivery during the mature milk period, between 14 days and three months postpartum. The researchers measured milk volume by comparing infant weight before and after breastfeeding. The results showed a meaningful difference between the two groups. Mothers in the MRJ group had a higher average breast milk volume than mothers in the MMS group. The average breast milk volume in the MRJ group was 850.5 ml , while the MMS group reached 666.9 ml . The difference was statistically significant, with a p-value of 0.04 . This means that Moringa leaf extract enriched with royal jelly may have potential to support higher milk production during lactation. This finding is important because Moringa is a local plant that is familiar in many Indonesian communities. Its leaves contain nutrients and bioactive compounds such as protein, vitamins, minerals, flavonoids, and phytosterols, which may help stimulate milk production. Royal jelly also contains nutrients and compounds that may support maternal metabolism and immunity. For health workers, this evidence can also enrich counseling during pregnancy and breastfeeding. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to improve maternal and infant health through better breastfeeding support. In conclusion, MRJ may become a promising local nutrition-based strategy to help mothers breastfeed more confidently and support healthier babies in early life."]

["Learning Through Videos: Helping Adolescent Girls Eat Better and Prevent Anemia", "Adolescence is a period of rapid growth, high curiosity, and preparation for adulthood. However, many adolescent girls still face nutritional problems, especially anemia. Anemia happens when the body does not have enough healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin to carry oxygen properly. As a result, girls may feel tired, weak, less focused, and less ready to perform well at school. A published article entitled “Nutrition education using video improves iron intake and dietary diversity among adolescents: a quasi-experimental study” provides an interesting solution to this problem. The article was published in Nutrición Clínica y Dietética Hospitalaria , Volume 45, Issue 2, pages 131–139, in 2025 , with DOI 10.12873/452kamil . The article was received on 10 March 2025 and accepted on 20 April 2025 . This study examined whether nutrition education videos could improve iron intake and dietary diversity among adolescent girls in Makassar, South Sulawesi, Indonesia. The study involved 69 adolescent girls from two senior high schools. The intervention group consisted of 34 students from SMAN 11 Makassar, while the control group consisted of 35 students from SMAN 8 Makassar. The intervention group received seven nutrition education videos based on the “Aksi Bergizi” program. These videos were delivered once a week for seven consecutive weeks through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, the control group received only one educational video from the Ministry of Health about anemia prevention. The video materials discussed practical topics such as anemia and iron, healthy breakfast, “Isi Piringku,” protein, vegetables and fruits, micronutrients, balanced nutrition, and food labeling. These topics are important because adolescent girls often have irregular eating habits, limited food variety, and low intake of iron-rich foods. The results showed that video-based nutrition education had a positive effect. In the intervention group, average iron intake increased from 5.33 to 9.70. Dietary diversity also improved, from 2.71 to 4.06. These changes were statistically significant. In contrast, the control group did not show the same level of improvement. This means that repeated and structured video education was more effective than a single video session. This finding is meaningful because videos are familiar, attractive, and easy to access for teenagers. When health messages are delivered through short and interesting videos, students may understand the information better and remember it longer. Nutrition education is not only about giving information; it is also about helping young people build healthier habits in their daily lives. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to prevent anemia and improve adolescent nutrition. It also supports SDG 4: Quality Education , because it shows how learning media can improve health knowledge and behavior. In conclusion, nutrition education through video can be a simple but powerful strategy to help adolescent girls eat better, consume more iron-rich foods, and build healthier futures."]

["Visoy: A Local Food Innovation to Help Pregnant Women Manage Stress", "Pregnancy is a time of hope, but it can also bring emotional pressure. Many women experience worry, fear, and stress as their bodies change and they prepare for childbirth. When anxiety continues for a long time, it may affect not only the mother’s mental well-being, but also the baby’s growth. One important biological signal of stress is cortisol, often called the stress hormone. A published article entitled “Alleviating Pregnancy-Related Stress: The Impact of Visoy, a Soybean–Sweet Potato Supplement, on Cortisol and Anxiety Levels” provides important evidence about a food-based approach to this issue. The article was published in Universal Journal of Public Health , Volume 13, Number 4, pages 1076–1082, in 2025 , through the HRPUB journal platform , with DOI 10.13189/ujph.2025.130430 . This study examined whether Visoy, a supplement made from soybean and purple sweet potato, could help reduce anxiety and improve cortisol regulation among pregnant women. The study involved 60 pregnant women aged 20–35 years who experienced mild to severe anxiety. They were divided into two groups: 30 women in the intervention group and 30 women in the control group. The intervention group consumed 80 grams of Visoy every day for 90 days, while the control group continued their usual diet without the supplement. Anxiety was measured using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 questionnaire, while cortisol levels were measured from saliva samples using the ELISA method. Visoy was designed as a nutrient-dense food additive. It combines soybean flour, which contains protein, iron, and isoflavones, with purple sweet potato flour, which is rich in anthocyanins, fiber, vitamin A, vitamin C, and antioxidants. These nutrients are important because they may help the body respond better to stress and support maternal health during pregnancy. This makes Visoy relevant for communities that need safe, affordable, and familiar food-based options. The findings were encouraging. After the intervention, 93.3% of pregnant women in the Visoy group had normal cortisol levels, compared with 66.7% in the control group. The average anxiety score also decreased more strongly in the intervention group, from 11.27 to 2.13. In comparison, the control group decreased from 11.33 to 5.80. These results suggest that Visoy may help pregnant women manage both physical and emotional signs of stress. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to improve maternal mental health and pregnancy care. It also shows that local food-based innovation can become a promising non-pharmacological strategy for supporting pregnant women. For health workers, this finding can enrich education during antenatal care, especially when discussing nutrition, emotional well-being, and practical daily food choices. In conclusion, Visoy offers a hopeful message: maternal health can be strengthened not only through medicine, but also through nutritious local foods. With further research, soybean and purple sweet potato may become part of broader prenatal care strategies to help mothers feel calmer, healthier, and better supported during pregnancy."]

["Moringa and Royal Jelly: Supporting Infant Growth from Pregnancy to Early Life", "A baby’s growth does not begin after birth. It starts much earlier, during pregnancy, when the mother’s nutrition helps shape the baby’s body, brain, and future health. Good nutrition during pregnancy is one of the most important foundations for preventing growth problems in early life, including poor weight gain, delayed development, and stunting. A scientific article entitled “Effect of Moringa Leaf Extract Capsule Enriched with Royal Jelly on Growth and Development of 0–3 Months Aged Infants” discusses this important issue. The article is listed in Gazzetta Medica Italiana - Archivio per le Scienze Mediche , under Edizioni Minerva Medica , with paper code Gazz Med Ital - Arch Sci Med-5825 . The attached PDF shows the submission date as October 7, 2024 , and the article type as an Original Article . This study examined whether Moringa leaf extract enriched with royal jelly, known as MRJ, could support infant growth and development during the first three months of life. The study was conducted in South Batui and Moilong Districts, Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. It followed mothers who had received nutrition supplementation during pregnancy and later observed their infants from birth to three months of age. A total of 63 mother-infant pairs were included. The intervention group consisted of 31 mothers who received MRJ, while the control group consisted of 32 mothers who received Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation, or MMS. Infant growth was assessed using several indicators, including weight-for-age, length-for-age, and weight-for-length. Infant development was measured using a developmental pre-screening questionnaire. These indicators are important because they help describe whether a baby is growing and developing according to age. The findings showed that both MRJ and MMS groups had generally good potential to support infant growth and development. For weight-for-age, there were significant differences between groups at one and two months, but not at birth and three months. For length-for-age and weight-for-length, most results showed no significant differences between the two groups. Infant development scores were also not significantly different between the MRJ and MMS groups. These results suggest that both supplementation approaches may provide useful nutrients for mothers and infants. Moringa is known as a nutrient-rich local plant containing vitamins, minerals, iron, calcium, and other important compounds. Royal jelly also contains protein, carbohydrates, lipids, and bioactive substances. Together, they may offer a local nutrition-based option to support maternal and infant health. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to improve maternal and child health and prevent early growth problems. In conclusion, strengthening maternal nutrition during pregnancy can become an important pathway to support healthier babies. Moringa enriched with royal jelly may serve as a promising local supplement, while further research can help clarify its long-term benefits for infant growth and development."]

["Healthy Teachers, Healthy Schools: Understanding Barriers to Balanced Nutrition", "Teachers are often seen as role models for students, not only in learning, discipline, and character, but also in daily health habits. In schools, teachers can influence how young people understand healthy eating and active living. However, teachers themselves also face busy schedules, work pressure, and daily routines that may make it difficult to follow balanced nutrition guidelines consistently. A published article entitled “Understanding Teachers’ Motivation and Barriers in Implementing Balanced Nutrition Guidelines in Indonesia: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective” discusses this important issue. The article was published in Media Publikasi Promosi Kesehatan Indonesia , Volume 8, Issue 9, pages 960–970, with the date of publication on 11 September 2025 . The article was published by the Faculty of Public Health, Universitas Muhammadiyah Palu , with DOI 10.56338/mppki.v8i9.7921 . This study explored how teachers practice balanced nutrition and what barriers prevent them from fully applying healthy lifestyle recommendations. The study used a qualitative approach through a Focus Group Discussion involving 11 teachers from a public senior high school in Makassar City, Indonesia. The discussion was guided by the ten key messages of the Indonesian Balanced Nutrition Guidelines. The researchers also used Self-Determination Theory, which explains that healthy behavior is influenced by motivation, autonomy, competence, and social support. The findings show that teachers understood the importance of balanced nutrition, but their daily practice was still limited. Many participants consumed vegetables only once a day and relied mainly on rice as their staple food. Protein sources such as fish and tempeh were consumed, but preparation time became a common obstacle. Some teachers skipped breakfast because it was not part of their habit. Others drank water only when they felt thirsty and avoided drinking too much because they did not want to urinate frequently during work. The study also found that social situations at school influenced eating behavior. For example, when colleagues brought fried snacks or sweet foods, some teachers felt uncomfortable refusing them because eating together was seen as a form of solidarity. Physical activity was also limited, mostly because teachers felt they had little time for structured exercise after work. These findings show that nutrition behavior is not only about knowledge. Even educated individuals may struggle to practice healthy habits when their environment, time, motivation, and social norms do not support them. Therefore, health promotion should not only give information, but also help people build confidence, create supportive routines, and make healthy choices easier in daily life. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially efforts to prevent non-communicable diseases through healthier eating habits and physical activity. It also connects with school-based health promotion, because healthy teachers can help build healthier school environments. In conclusion, improving teachers’ nutrition practices requires practical, realistic, and supportive strategies. When teachers are supported to eat better and live healthier, schools can become stronger spaces for health education and positive behavior change. Reference : DOI 10.56338/mppki.v8i9.7921 Contact : Prof. dr. Veni Hadju, M.Sc., Ph. D +62811441803 phunhas@gmail.com"]

["Behind the Care: Understanding Stress Among Schizophrenia Caregivers", "Caring for someone with schizophrenia is an act of love, patience, and responsibility. Yet behind this responsibility, many caregivers carry invisible emotional pressure. They may need to remind patients to take medicine, manage unpredictable symptoms, face community stigma, and still continue daily family duties. Over time, this situation can create stress that affects the caregiver’s own health and quality of life. A published article entitled “Determinant Factors of Stress in Caregivers of Patients With Schizophrenia: Cross-Sectional Study” brings attention to this often-overlooked issue. The article was published in JMIR Formative Research , Volume 9, article e70648, in 2025 , by JMIR Publications , with DOI 10.2196/70648 . The article was originally published on July 3, 2025 . This study explored the stress experienced by caregivers of patients with schizophrenia and identified the main factors that may increase or reduce that stress. The study was conducted from June to August 2024 at community health centers in Labakkang District, Pangkep Regency, South Sulawesi, Indonesia. It involved 110 female caregivers of people with schizophrenia. The researchers collected information using validated questionnaires and analyzed the data using chi-square tests and partial least squares structural equation modeling. This method helped explain how several factors, such as caregiving burden, stigma, knowledge, coping strategies, treatment nonadherence, and social support, were connected to caregiver stress. The findings showed that caregiver stress was common. More than half of the caregivers, or 53%, experienced mild stress, while 5% experienced severe stress. Many caregivers also faced a moderate caregiving burden, challenges with patient treatment nonadherence, limited knowledge about schizophrenia, and limited access to health information. These results show that caregiving stress does not come from one single cause. It is shaped by emotional, social, and practical challenges that happen together. Several factors were significantly related to caregiver stress, including age, education, caregiving burden, knowledge, coping strategies, treatment nonadherence, and stigma. The model also showed that caregiving burden, stigma, and limited knowledge were positively linked with higher stress. In contrast, social support had a strong protective role. This means caregivers who feel supported by family, community, and health services may be better able to manage stress. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , especially in improving mental health and supporting families affected by chronic mental illness. It also reminds us that mental health care should not focus only on patients. Caregivers also need education, counseling, social support, and community acceptance. For local health systems, this message is important because caregiver well-being can influence treatment continuity and patient recovery. In conclusion, caring for people with schizophrenia requires more than personal strength. It requires a supportive environment. By reducing stigma, improving caregiver knowledge, and strengthening social support networks, communities can help caregivers stay healthy while continuing to provide compassionate care for their loved ones."]

["Better Communication, Safer Pregnancy: Training Midwives to Support MMS Use", "Pregnancy is a critical period when mothers need the right nutrients to protect their own health and support the growth of their babies. One important strategy is Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation, or MMS. Unlike regular iron tablets, MMS contains a wider range of vitamins and minerals that can help reduce the risk of anemia and support better maternal and newborn health. However, supplements can only work well when pregnant women understand their benefits and use them correctly. A published article entitled “Interpersonal Communication Training as an Effective Strategy to Optimize Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS) Utilization in Preventing Maternal and Neonatal Deaths” discusses this issue. The article was published in Pharmacognosy Journal, Volume 17, Issue 4, pages 399–406, in July–August 2025, by Phcogj.Com, with DOI 10.5530/pj.2025.17.50. This study explored whether interpersonal communication training could improve midwives’ knowledge and skills in educating pregnant women about MMS. The study was conducted in Bone Bolango Regency, Gorontalo Province, in September 2024. It involved 74 coordinating midwives and village supervisors from nine health centers. The research used a quasi-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design. This means the researchers measured midwives’ knowledge before and after the training to see whether there was improvement. The training was designed to be practical and interactive. Midwives did not only receive classroom materials, but also participated in discussions, educational games, simulations, and direct field practice. One important part of the training was the interpersonal communication model based on listening, appreciating, and clarifying. Through this approach, midwives were trained to communicate with pregnant women in a more respectful and personal way. Instead of simply telling mothers what to do, midwives learned to listen to their concerns, respond with empathy, and explain MMS in language that is easier to understand. The results showed a clear improvement. Before the training, the average knowledge score was 10.80. After the training, it increased to 15.23. Statistical testing showed that this increase was significant, meaning the training had a real effect on improving midwives’ knowledge. The study also found that knowledge had a direct effect on skills, showing that better understanding can help midwives communicate more effectively in practice. This finding is important because many pregnant women may avoid supplements due to fear of side effects, misinformation, or lack of understanding. Midwives are trusted health workers, so their communication skills can strongly influence whether mothers accept and regularly consume MMS. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to reduce maternal and neonatal deaths and improve pregnancy care. It shows that improving health is not only about providing supplements, but also about strengthening the people who explain, guide, and support mothers. In conclusion, interpersonal communication training is a simple but powerful strategy. By helping midwives communicate better, health services can improve MMS use, strengthen antenatal care, and contribute to safer pregnancies and healthier newborns."]

["Building Village Teams to Fight Stunting in Batui Selatan", "Stunting is not only a problem of height. It reflects a long process in which children do not receive enough nutrition, health care, and protection during their most important years of growth. In Indonesia, reducing stunting requires more than health services alone. It needs coordination, village leadership, community participation, and clear teamwork from the national level down to families. A published article entitled “Barriers and Solutions to the Formation of Village Stunting Reduction Acceleration Teams (TPPS) in Batui Selatan Sub-District, Banggai District” discusses this important issue. The article was published in Community Practitioner, Volume 21, Issue 07, in July 2024, through the journal platform www.commprac.com , with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.13166261. The study explored why village-level Stunting Reduction Acceleration Teams, known as TPPS, had not yet been formed and what solutions could help villages establish them. The study was conducted for three months, from November 2023 to January 2024, in three villages in Batui Selatan Sub-district: Ombolu, Sinorang, and Bonebalantak. These locations were selected by considering nutritional status, geographical location, and ethnicity. The research used a qualitative design involving 15 informants, including village heads, village secretaries, PKK leaders, human development cadres, stunting cadres, family assistance team coordinators, and village midwives. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and analyzed using content analysis. The findings showed that most informants had heard about TPPS. However, all informants stated that TPPS had not yet been formed in their villages. Several barriers were identified. First, village governments had not received clear technical socialization on how to form TPPS. Second, some village stakeholders believed that existing teams, such as posyandu cadres, KPM, and family assistance teams, were already enough to handle stunting programs. Third, the formation of a new team was often associated with honorariums or incentives, while village funds were limited. Fourth, human resources were also limited, especially people with experience in health-related activities. To overcome these barriers, the researchers used a persuasive and informative approach. They explained that TPPS is not meant to replace existing teams, but to coordinate, strengthen, and evaluate stunting reduction efforts at the village level. They also clarified that TPPS membership could be voluntary and could involve people who were already active in village programs. Through this approach, TPPS was finally formed in Ombolu, Sinorang, and Bonebalantak villages. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve child health and reduce stunting. It also shows that health programs need strong local coordination. When village leaders, cadres, and communities understand their roles, stunting prevention can become more organized and effective. In conclusion, forming village TPPS is not only an administrative task. It is a community strategy to protect children’s growth, strengthen village health systems, and build a healthier future generation."]

["More Hemoglobin, More Energy: Why Anemia Matters for Adolescent Girls", "Adolescence is a time when young girls should have the energy to study, play, think clearly, and prepare for the future. However, many young girls silently struggle with anemia, a condition in which the body doesn't have enough hemoglobin to carry oxygen properly. When oxygen delivery is limited, the body may feel weak and tired, while the brain may struggle to focus and remember information. A published article titled \"Correlation Between Hemoglobin Levels, Physical Fitness, and Cognitive Scores in Adolescent Girls: A Cross-Sectoral Study in Banggai Regency, Indonesia\" draws attention to this issue. The article was published in the Journal of Pharmacognosy, Volume 16, Issue 2, in March–April 2024, by Phcogj.Com. The study explored how hemoglobin levels relate to physical fitness, cognitive abilities, and memory among adolescent girls in Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. This cross-sectional study involved 139 adolescent girls aged 12–18 from 13 junior and senior high schools in Banggai. Hemoglobin levels were measured using HemoCue, physical fitness was assessed through VO2max prediction using the Bleep Test, cognitive function was measured using the Culturally Fair Intelligence Test, and memory was assessed using the Intelligenz Structure Test. These measurements allowed the researchers to see not only whether the girls were anemic, but also how hemoglobin might relate to daily performance. The findings were significant. Overall, 58.3% of the students were anemic. Most had mild anemia, while some had moderate anemia. The average hemoglobin level was 11.6 g/dL. The study also found that hemoglobin was positively associated with physical fitness and memory. Girls with higher hemoglobin levels tended to have better VO2max scores, meaning their bodies can use oxygen more effectively during physical activity. Hemoglobin was also significantly associated with memory scores, suggesting that better blood health can support better learning capacity. This makes sense in everyday life. Hemoglobin acts like a delivery system, carrying oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body, including the muscles and brain. When hemoglobin levels are low, the body receives less oxygen. As a result, girls may tire more easily during exercise and may have difficulty concentrating in class. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being, specifically efforts to improve adolescent health and prevent nutrition-related problems. It also reminds schools, families, and health workers that anemia prevention is not just about avoiding disease. It is also about helping girls stay active, focused, confident, and ready to reach their potential. In conclusion, increasing hemoglobin levels among adolescent girls is an investment in their future health, education, and productivity. Regular checkups, nutrition education, iron-rich foods, and school-based health programs can help girls grow healthier, learn better, and live stronger lives. These steps are simple, but their impact can last for years."]

["Understanding Anemia among Adolescent Girls in Banggai", "Adolescence should be a time of energy, learning, and preparation for the future. However, for many girls, this period can be interrupted by anemia, a condition in which the body does not have enough healthy hemoglobin to carry oxygen. The symptoms may look simple, such as tiredness, weakness, dizziness, or difficulty concentrating, but the impact can affect school performance, physical fitness, productivity, and future pregnancy health. A published article entitled “Determinants of anemia among adolescents girls in district Banggai, Indonesia” highlights this important issue. The article was published in the International Journal of Public Health Science (IJPHS), Volume 14, Number 2, pages 1008–1014, in June 2025, through the IJPHS/IAESCore journal platform, with DOI 10.11591/ijphs.v14i2.23992. This study examined how common anemia is among adolescent girls in Banggai District and what factors are most closely related to it. The study used a cross-sectional design and involved 326 adolescent girls aged 12–18 years from junior and senior high schools in South Batui and Moilong Districts, Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi. Hemoglobin levels were measured using a HemoCue hemoglobinometer, while information on sociodemographic characteristics, nutritional status, and eating habits was collected using questionnaires and anthropometric measurements. The findings show that anemia remains a serious public health problem among adolescent girls in Banggai. Almost half of the respondents, or 48.8%, were anemic. Among those with anemia, 44.1% had mild anemia, 48.4% had moderate anemia, and 7.5% had severe anemia. The average hemoglobin level was 11.2 g/dL, indicating that many girls were below the normal threshold. The study also found that age and eating habits were the strongest determinants of anemia. Girls aged 15–18 years had a higher risk of anemia than younger girls. This may be related to rapid growth, menstruation, and increased need for iron and other nutrients during late adolescence. Eating frequency also mattered. Girls who ate only twice a day were more at risk than those who ate three times a day. This shows that anemia is not only a medical issue, but also a daily nutrition issue shaped by family routines, food availability, and adolescent behavior. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve adolescent health and prevent nutritional problems before they affect future mothers and children. It also reminds schools, families, and health workers that adolescent girls need regular nutrition education, healthy eating habits, and access to iron-rich foods. School-based programs can become an important entry point for screening, counseling, and encouraging girls to eat balanced meals every day. In conclusion, anemia among adolescent girls in Banggai needs serious attention. Simple actions such as improving meal frequency, strengthening school-based health education, and monitoring hemoglobin levels can help girls grow healthier, learn better, and prepare for a stronger future."]

["Posyandu Cadres: Local Guides for Healthier Toddlers in Banggai", "Early childhood is a short but decisive window for building a healthy future. In the first two years of life, toddlers need close growth monitoring, balanced food intake, and support from people around them. However, many mothers still face challenges in understanding growth charts, choosing nutritious foods, and responding early when a child’s weight or length does not increase as expected. This is where community health volunteers, known in Indonesia as Posyandu cadres, can play an important role. A published article entitled “The Effect of Posyandu Cadre Guidance on Mothers of Toddlers on the Nutritional Status of Toddlers in Luwuk Banggai District, South Batui District, Central Sulawesi Province” discusses this issue through a community-based intervention. The article was published in the Journal of Neonatal Surgery, Volume 14, Issue 28s, pages 676–682, in 2025. The article is available through the Journal of Neonatal Surgery platform and examines whether guidance from Posyandu cadres can help improve the nutritional status of toddlers aged 6–24 months in South Batui District, Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi. The study used a quasi-experimental design with intervention and control groups. Sixty mothers of toddlers participated, with 30 respondents in each group. The intervention group received assistance from trained Posyandu cadres, while the control group received only the first stage of cadre training without intensive mentoring. The programme was conducted in six villages from August to October 2024 . Cadres were trained and then involved in supporting mothers, especially in monitoring growth and encouraging better nutrition practices for toddlers. The findings show that cadre guidance made a meaningful difference. Toddlers in the intervention group experienced an increase in average body weight from 8.54 kg to 8.98 kg. Their average body length also increased from 72.20 cm to 72.63 cm. More importantly, the weight-for-length indicator improved significantly in the intervention group, showing better nutritional progress compared with the control group. These results suggest that mothers may benefit when cadres do more than weigh children; they also need to guide, educate, and accompany families. This result is important because Posyandu cadres are close to the community. They understand local conditions, meet mothers regularly, and can deliver health messages in a familiar way. When cadres are equipped with proper knowledge and mentoring skills, they can become a bridge between health workers and families. Their role can help mothers recognize nutrition problems earlier and improve daily feeding practices at home. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve child health and prevent malnutrition. It also shows that strengthening community-based health services can create practical solutions using existing local resources. In conclusion, Posyandu cadre guidance is a simple but powerful strategy. By empowering cadres and supporting mothers, communities can help toddlers grow healthier and build a stronger foundation for Indonesia’s future generation."]

["Moringa and Eggs: Simple Local Foods to Help Malnourished Toddlers Grow", "Malnutrition in toddlers is not only a matter of being underweight. It is a serious health problem that can affect growth, immunity, learning ability, and even survival. When a child does not receive enough nutrients, the body may not grow properly, making the child more vulnerable to infection and delayed development. For this reason, finding simple, affordable, and locally available foods is an important step in improving child nutrition. A published article entitled “Effects of Moringa oleifera Leaf Extract and Egg on Weight and Height Increase in Malnourished Toddler” discusses this issue through a nutrition intervention in Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. The article was published in Kesmas: Jurnal Kesehatan Masyarakat Nasional (National Public Health Journal), Volume 19, Issue 1, in 2024. The journal is available through the Universitas Indonesia ScholarHub platform. Based on the attached PDF, the article focuses on how Moringa leaf extract and eggs may help increase body weight and height among malnourished toddlers. The study was conducted from July to October 2023 in Moilong District and South Batui District, Banggai Regency. It used a true experimental design with a pretest-posttest control group. A total of 60 toddlers aged 6–59 months with poor nutritional status participated in the study. The intervention group received 500 mg of Moringa leaf extract per day plus one chicken egg weighing 45 grams, while the control group received one chicken egg weighing 45 grams per day. The intervention was carried out for 12 weeks. The findings showed that both groups experienced significant improvements in body weight and height after the intervention. In the intervention group, toddlers gained an average of 2.06 kg in body weight and 1.57 cm in height. In the control group, toddlers gained an average of 1.76 kg in body weight and 0.90 cm in height. Although the increase was higher in the group receiving Moringa leaf extract and eggs, the difference between the two groups was not statistically significant. These findings are meaningful because Moringa and eggs are familiar foods for many Indonesian families. Moringa leaves contain protein, vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, calcium, iron, and amino acids that support growth and body function. Eggs are also a high-quality source of animal protein, which is essential for muscle, bone, and brain development. Together, these foods offer a practical nutrition option that can be promoted in community-based health programs. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve child health and reduce the burden of malnutrition. It shows that local foods can contribute to better nutrition when used consistently and supported by health education. In conclusion, Moringa leaf extract and eggs may help improve the growth of malnourished toddlers. This local food-based approach can become an accessible strategy to support healthier children and build a stronger future generation."]

["Moringa and Royal Jelly: A Local Nutrition Innovation for Healthier Births in Indonesia", "A healthy baby does not begin at birth. Growth starts much earlier, during pregnancy, when the mother’s body provides oxygen, nutrients, and protection for the fetus. When nutrition during pregnancy is not adequate, babies may face a higher risk of being born too early, having low birth weight, or experiencing other health problems. This makes maternal nutrition an important public health issue, especially in communities where access to diverse and nutritious food may still be limited. A published scientific article entitled “Effect of Moringa Oleifera Plus Royal Jelly Capsules in The Gestation Age and Placenta Weight of Newborns in Indonesia” provides useful evidence on this issue. The article was published in Pharmacognosy Journal, Volume 16, Issue 5, September–October 2024, by Phcogj.Com, with DOI 10.5530/pj.2024.16.192. This study explored whether capsules containing Moringa oleifera plus royal jelly, known as MRJ, could help support gestational age and placental weight among newborns in Indonesia. The study was conducted in Banggai District, Central Sulawesi Province. It involved 160 pregnant women from two sub-districts. One group received MRJ capsules, while the comparison group received Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation, or MMS. Both groups consumed one capsule or tablet every day for six months. Researchers monitored the mothers regularly and measured pregnancy outcomes after delivery, including gestational age and placental weight. Moringa is a familiar plant in many Indonesian communities. Its leaves contain important nutrients, including iron, vitamins, calcium, fiber, and natural antioxidants. Royal jelly is also known for its nutritional value. Together, these ingredients may offer a local and non-pharmacological option to support pregnancy health. In this study, no pregnant women reported side effects such as allergies or diarrhea, showing that the intervention was well tolerated. The results showed that the average gestational age in both groups was similar, around 39 weeks. This is a positive finding because babies born around this period are generally considered mature and have better readiness to live outside the womb. However, the MRJ group showed a higher average placental weight than the MMS group. The average placental weight in the MRJ group was 507.62 grams, while in the MMS group it was 464.19 grams. After considering maternal body mass index, this difference remained significant. The placenta is often called the baby’s lifeline in the womb. It helps deliver oxygen and nutrients from the mother to the fetus. A healthier placenta may support better fetal growth and reduce the risk of adverse birth outcomes. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially the effort to improve maternal and newborn health. It shows that local nutrition resources, when tested scientifically, can contribute to safer pregnancies and healthier births. Although further research is still needed, Moringa oleifera plus royal jelly offers a promising pathway for strengthening maternal nutrition and protecting the next generation in Indonesia."]

["Moringa and Royal Jelly: Local Nutrition for Healthier Newborns in Central Sulawesi", "Every baby’s growth begins long before birth. During pregnancy, the mother’s body becomes the first home, food source, and protection system for the developing baby. When a pregnant woman does not receive enough nutrients, the baby may face a higher risk of low birth weight, poor growth, and other health problems after delivery. For this reason, improving maternal nutrition is one of the most important steps in building a healthier generation. A published article entitled “Effect of Moringa Leaves Podwer Enriched with Royal Jelly on the Anthropometric Measurements of Neonates in Central Sulawesi, Indonesia” highlights this important issue. The article was published in the International Journal of Medical Toxicology & Legal Medicine, Volume 27, Number 5, in 2024, through the journal platform ijmtlm.org, with DOI 10.47059/ijmtlm/V27I5/028. This study examined whether Moringa oleifera leaves enriched with royal jelly, known as MRJ, could support newborn growth among pregnant women in Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. Moringa is already familiar in many Indonesian communities. It is often planted around houses and is known as a nutrient-rich local plant. Its leaves contain protein, vitamins, calcium, iron, and natural antioxidants. Royal jelly is also known for its nutritional potential. When combined, these two ingredients may provide a natural and practical supplement to support pregnancy health. The study involved 160 pregnant women who were divided into two groups. The intervention group received two MRJ capsules every day, while the comparison group received one Multiple Micronutrient Supplement, or MMS, tablet every day. The intervention was carried out for six months. Researchers then measured the newborns’ birth weight, birth length, head circumference, and chest circumference. The results showed that babies born to mothers who consumed MRJ had a higher average birth weight than those in the MMS group. The average birth weight in the MRJ group was 3174.81 grams, while the MMS group was 3073.40 grams. This difference remained significant even after the researchers considered maternal body mass index. Meanwhile, babies in the MMS group had a slightly longer average birth length. Head circumference and chest circumference were relatively similar between the two groups. These findings show that local nutrition-based supplementation may become an important part of maternal and child health efforts. Birth weight is not just a number; it reflects how well a baby grows in the womb and may influence health in early life. By using local resources such as Moringa, communities may have more accessible options to support healthier pregnancies. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve maternal and newborn health. It also shows that scientific research can transform local food knowledge into evidence-based public health innovation. In conclusion, Moringa enriched with royal jelly offers a promising non-pharmacological approach to support newborn growth. Further studies are still needed, but this research gives an important message: healthier babies can begin with better nutrition for mothers."]

["From Moringa Leaves and Eggs to Better Nutrition for Toddlers in Banggai", "Early childhood is a golden period for growth. At this age, children need enough energy, protein, vitamins, and minerals to build strong bodies, active minds, and better immunity. When toddlers do not receive diverse and nutritious foods, they can become undernourished. This condition may make them more vulnerable to illness, slow growth, and long-term developmental problems. A published article entitled “Effect of Moringa (Moringa oleifera) Leaf Extract and Egg Feeding on Diet in Undernourished Toddlers” highlights a simple local nutrition approach. The article was published in Community Practitioner, Volume 21, Issue 06, in June, through the journal platform www.commprac.com , with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.12205214. The study focused on undernourished toddlers in Moilong and Batui Selatan sub-districts, Banggai District, Indonesia. The research used a true experimental design with a pretest-posttest control group. A total of 60 toddlers aged 6–59 months completed the study. The intervention group received 500 mg of Moringa leaf extract per day and one egg weighing 45–50 grams per day. The control group received one egg per day. The intervention was carried out for three months, and the children’s diet was assessed using a Food Frequency Questionnaire. The findings showed that adding Moringa leaf extract to egg feeding improved several parts of the toddlers’ diet. In the intervention group, the score for animal side dishes increased from 1.10 to 1.57. The score for vegetables and fruits also increased from 1.57 to 1.87. These improvements were statistically significant. Meanwhile, staple foods and plant-based side dishes did not show significant changes. This means that the combination of Moringa and eggs had a stronger effect on improving diet quality, especially in foods that provide important nutrients for growth. This result is meaningful because both Moringa and eggs are familiar and accessible in many Indonesian communities. Moringa leaves contain protein, fiber, vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients that can support child health. Eggs are also a high-quality source of animal protein and are relatively easy to prepare for young children. When combined, they may become a practical nutrition strategy for families, health workers, and community-based nutrition programs. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve child health and reduce undernutrition. It also connects with the broader goal of building healthier communities through local food resources. Instead of relying only on expensive or hard-to-access products, communities can use familiar foods that are already part of daily life. In conclusion, the study shows that Moringa leaf extract combined with eggs may help improve dietary patterns among undernourished toddlers. With proper education, regular monitoring, and family support, this simple local food approach can contribute to healthier children and a stronger future generation."]

["Moringa Leaf Tea: A Local Drink to Help Adolescent Girls Fight Anaemia", "Adolescence is a time of rapid growth, learning, and preparation for adulthood. For girls, this period requires enough nutrients to support body development, school performance, and future reproductive health. One of the most common nutrition problems in this age group is anaemia, a condition that can make girls feel weak, tired, less focused, and more vulnerable to health problems. A published article entitled “The intervention of moringa leaf tea in the ‘Nutritious Action’ programme on the nutritional status and haemoglobin levels in adolescent girls” discusses a school-based nutrition solution for this issue. The article was published in Nutrición Clínica y Dietética Hospitalaria, Volume 46, Issue 1, pages 318–324, in 2026, with DOI 10.12873/461nawaliah. The study was conducted among adolescent girls in Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. This research compared two approaches in the “Aksi Bergizi” or Nutritious Action programme. The intervention group received 2.5 grams of moringa leaf tea once a week for 12 weeks. The control group received one Multiple Micronutrient Supplement tablet once a week for the same period. Nutritional status was assessed using BMI-for-age Z-scores, while haemoglobin levels were measured using capillary blood samples. The results showed that moringa leaf tea produced stronger improvements than the micronutrient supplement group. After 12 weeks, the moringa leaf tea group had a greater increase in nutritional status, with a mean change of +1.15 SD, compared with +0.50 SD in the control group. Haemoglobin levels also increased more in the moringa leaf tea group, rising by +1.6 g/dL, while the supplement group increased by +0.9 g/dL. These findings indicate that moringa leaf tea had a meaningful effect on improving adolescent girls’ nutritional condition and blood health. This result is important because moringa is a local plant that is easy to find in many Indonesian communities. Moringa leaves contain iron, vitamin C, protein, folic acid, and other nutrients that help support haemoglobin formation. Vitamin C also helps the body absorb iron better, making moringa leaf tea a promising natural option to help prevent anaemia. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve adolescent health and reduce anaemia among girls. It also shows that school-based nutrition programmes can use local food resources as practical and sustainable solutions. Beyond individual health, this finding also encourages schools, health workers, and families to value local food wisdom. By turning moringa into a regular school nutrition option, communities can support anaemia prevention using resources that are familiar, available, and culturally acceptable. In conclusion, moringa leaf tea may become an affordable and effective local nutrition strategy for adolescent girls. When combined with health education and regular school-based programmes, this simple drink can help build healthier, stronger, and more productive young women in Indonesia."]

["Moringa and Royal Jelly: Supporting Mothers to Breastfeed Successfully", "Breastfeeding is one of the first protections a baby receives in life. During the first six months, breast milk provides complete nutrition, supports growth, strengthens immunity, and helps protect infants from diseases such as diarrhea and pneumonia. Yet, many mothers struggle to maintain exclusive breastfeeding because they worry that their milk is not enough. This concern often leads to early introduction of formula or other foods. A published article entitled “Moringa oleifera Leaf Supplementation during Pregnancy Improves Six-Month Breastfeeding Outcomes: A Randomized Controlled Trial in Banggai, Indonesia” provides valuable evidence on this issue. The article was published in Universal Journal of Public Health, Volume 13, Number 5, pages 1170–1180, in 2025, through the HRPUB journal platform, with DOI 10.13189/ujph.2025.130508. The study examined whether Moringa oleifera leaf supplementation enriched with royal jelly during pregnancy could improve breastfeeding success six months after childbirth. The research was conducted in South Batui and Moilong subdistricts, Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. It followed mothers who had participated in a previous double-blind randomized controlled trial during pregnancy. The intervention group received one capsule of Moringa Royal Jelly, or MRJ, every day from the second trimester until delivery. Each capsule contained 490 mg of dried Moringa leaf powder and 10 mg of royal jelly. The control group received a multi-micronutrient supplement, known as MMS. At six months postpartum, 88 mothers and infants were included in the follow-up analysis. The findings showed that mothers in the MRJ group had better breastfeeding outcomes. Exclusive breastfeeding at six months was higher in the MRJ group, reaching 52.4%, compared with 32.6% in the MMS group. Although this difference was not statistically significant, the breastfeeding success score was significantly higher among mothers who consumed MRJ. The MRJ group reached an average score of 95.00, while the MMS group reached 90.71. This result is important because breastfeeding success is not only about producing milk. It also reflects the baby’s comfort after feeding, feeding frequency, the mother’s confidence, and signs that the baby is satisfied. Moringa is a local plant known for its rich nutrients, including iron, calcium, vitamin C, protein, fiber, and bioactive compounds. It is also traditionally recognized as a natural galactagogue, meaning it may help support breast milk production. Because Moringa grows in many Indonesian communities, this approach is also practical, familiar, and easier to connect with local maternal health programs. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve maternal and infant health. In conclusion, Moringa enriched with royal jelly may become a promising local nutrition strategy to help mothers breastfeed successfully. With further support from health workers and community programs, this natural intervention can contribute to healthier mothers, stronger babies, and better early-life nutrition in Indonesia."]

["Posyandu Cadres: Local Guides for Healthier Toddlers in Banggai", "Early childhood is a short but decisive window for building a healthy future. In the first two years of life, toddlers need close growth monitoring, balanced food intake, and support from people around them. However, many mothers still face challenges in understanding growth charts, choosing nutritious foods, and responding early when a child’s weight or length does not increase as expected. This is where community health volunteers, known in Indonesia as Posyandu cadres, can play an important role. A published article entitled “The Effect of Posyandu Cadre Guidance on Mothers of Toddlers on the Nutritional Status of Toddlers in Luwuk Banggai District, South Batui District, Central Sulawesi Province” discusses this issue through a community-based intervention. The article was published in the Journal of Neonatal Surgery, Volume 14, Issue 28s, pages 676–682, in 2025. The article is available through the Journal of Neonatal Surgery platform and examines whether guidance from Posyandu cadres can help improve the nutritional status of toddlers aged 6–24 months in South Batui District, Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi. The study used a quasi-experimental design with intervention and control groups. Sixty mothers of toddlers participated, with 30 respondents in each group. The intervention group received assistance from trained Posyandu cadres, while the control group received only the first stage of cadre training without intensive mentoring. The programme was conducted in six villages from August to October 2024. Cadres were trained and then involved in supporting mothers, especially in monitoring growth and encouraging better nutrition practices for toddlers. The findings show that cadre guidance made a meaningful difference. Toddlers in the intervention group experienced an increase in average body weight from 8.54 kg to 8.98 kg. Their average body length also increased from 72.20 cm to 72.63 cm. More importantly, the weight-for-length indicator improved significantly in the intervention group, showing better nutritional progress compared with the control group. These results suggest that mothers may benefit when cadres do more than weigh children; they also need to guide, educate, and accompany families. This result is important because Posyandu cadres are close to the community. They understand local conditions, meet mothers regularly, and can deliver health messages in a familiar way. When cadres are equipped with proper knowledge and mentoring skills, they can become a bridge between health workers and families. Their role can help mothers recognize nutrition problems earlier and improve daily feeding practices at home. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve child health and prevent malnutrition. It also shows that strengthening community-based health services can create practical solutions using existing local resources. In conclusion, Posyandu cadre guidance is a simple but powerful strategy. By empowering cadres and supporting mothers, communities can help toddlers grow healthier and build a stronger foundation for Indonesia’s future generation."]

["Understanding Anemia among Adolescent Girls in Banggai", "Adolescence should be a time of energy, learning, and preparation for the future. However, for many girls, this period can be interrupted by anemia, a condition in which the body does not have enough healthy hemoglobin to carry oxygen. The symptoms may look simple, such as tiredness, weakness, dizziness, or difficulty concentrating, but the impact can affect school performance, physical fitness, productivity, and future pregnancy health. A published article entitled “Determinants of anemia among adolescents girls in district Banggai, Indonesia” highlights this important issue. The article was published in the International Journal of Public Health Science (IJPHS), Volume 14, Number 2, pages 1008–1014, in June 2025, through the IJPHS/IAESCore journal platform, with DOI 10.11591/ijphs.v14i2.23992. This study examined how common anemia is among adolescent girls in Banggai District and what factors are most closely related to it. The study used a cross-sectional design and involved 326 adolescent girls aged 12–18 years from junior and senior high schools in South Batui and Moilong Districts, Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi. Hemoglobin levels were measured using a HemoCue hemoglobinometer, while information on sociodemographic characteristics, nutritional status, and eating habits was collected using questionnaires and anthropometric measurements. The findings show that anemia remains a serious public health problem among adolescent girls in Banggai. Almost half of the respondents, or 48.8%, were anemic. Among those with anemia, 44.1% had mild anemia, 48.4% had moderate anemia, and 7.5% had severe anemia. The average hemoglobin level was 11.2 g/dL, indicating that many girls were below the normal threshold. The study also found that age and eating habits were the strongest determinants of anemia. Girls aged 15–18 years had a higher risk of anemia than younger girls. This may be related to rapid growth, menstruation, and increased need for iron and other nutrients during late adolescence. Eating frequency also mattered. Girls who ate only twice a day were more at risk than those who ate three times a day. This shows that anemia is not only a medical issue, but also a daily nutrition issue shaped by family routines, food availability, and adolescent behavior. This article supports SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, especially efforts to improve adolescent health and prevent nutritional problems before they affect future mothers and children. It also reminds schools, families, and health workers that adolescent girls need regular nutrition education, healthy eating habits, and access to iron-rich foods. School-based programs can become an important entry point for screening, counseling, and encouraging girls to eat balanced meals every day. In conclusion, anemia among adolescent girls in Banggai needs serious attention. Simple actions such as improving meal frequency, strengthening school-based health education, and monitoring hemoglobin levels can help girls grow healthier, learn better, and prepare for a stronger future."]

["Building a Healthy Work Culture to Mitigate Fatigue in Aircraft Maintenance Engineers", "Aircraft Maintenance Engineers (AMEs) play a crucial role in ensuring aircraft remain airworthy, but their demanding responsibilities also make them highly vulnerable to work fatigue. Research highlights several contributing factors, including individual characteristics such as age and marital status, physical and mental workload, quality of sleep, nutritional status, and lifestyle habits like smoking. The 24-hour rotating shift system further intensifies this pressure, especially when not balanced with proper health management. To address these challenges, it is essential to foster a healthy work culture supported by a strong safety culture within aviation organizations. Companies should not only focus on operational targets but also prioritize employee well-being through effective workload management, promotion of healthy living practices, and provision of social support systems. By implementing comprehensive fatigue management strategies, organizations can safeguard both the well-being of AMEs and the ultimate priority of the aviation industry: passenger safety."]

["Building a Healthy Work Culture: Strategies to Reduce Work Stress Among Aircraft Maintenance Engineers", "Work-related stress is a common issue faced by professionals with high levels of responsibility, including Aircraft Maintenance Engineers (AMEs) who play a vital role in ensuring flight safety. A quantitative approach was employed using standardized instruments, including the Job Stress Questionnaire from NIOSH, the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) , and the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS-21) . The findings indicate that work stress among AMEs is influenced not only by job-related factors but also by individual characteristics and the level of social support available. These results highlight the importance of fostering a healthy work culture and strengthening a safety culture as key strategies to mitigate work stress. Through the implementation of comprehensive stress management practices, organizations can enhance the well-being of AMEs while ensuring that flight safety remains the top priority."]

["The Influence of Noise on Work Productivity Through Work Stress and Work Fatigue as Intervening Variables Among Apron Workers at Sultan Hasanuddin Airport Makassar", "According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2010), approximately 1 in 5 people (or 100 million citizens) in the European Union are exposed to harmful noise levels. ["Community-Based Infectious and Non-Communicable Disease Control Assistance Program", "Public Health in the Oil and Gas Industry: The Case of PT Pertamina Hulu Mahakam Public health is one of the crucial aspects that must be considered in the development of large-scale projects, including oil and gas projects.
