["Why Quality Matters for Insured Patients in Indonesian Hospitals", "2024", "Having health insurance is often seen as a guarantee of better healthcare. But is access alone enough? A recent study reveals that even insured patients may not always receive the quality of care they deserve. The article titled “Healthcare Quality Received by Insured Patients in Two Indonesian Regional Public Hospitals” , published in the journal Public Health of Indonesia by Sage in June 2024, explores this important issue . The study analyzed hospital data from 2019 to 2020 to evaluate how well insured patients were treated in two regional public hospitals in Indonesia. At first glance, the findings seem reassuring. Most patients were discharged with a doctor’s approval, and hospital stays generally followed expected durations. However, a deeper look reveals several hidden problems that affect healthcare quality. One major concern is the variation in length of hospital stay among patients with the same diagnosis. Some patients stayed longer than necessary, while others were discharged too early. This inconsistency suggests that care is not always standardized. In healthcare, consistency is critical—patients with similar conditions should receive similar treatment plans. Another important issue is the rate of hospital readmission within 30 days . Ideally, this rate should be very low, indicating that patients were properly treated before discharge. However, the study found that readmission rates in both hospitals exceeded the recommended standard. This means some patients had to return to the hospital shortly after leaving, which may indicate incomplete treatment or poor follow-up care. The study also highlights that more than 60% of patients were treated in third-class wards. This reflects the reality that most insured patients come from lower-income groups. While Indonesia’s national health insurance system (BPJS) has improved access to healthcare, ensuring equal quality across all patient groups remains a challenge. These findings are closely connected to SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , which emphasizes not only access to healthcare but also the quality and safety of services. Providing insurance is an important step, but it must be accompanied by high-quality care that is safe, effective, and consistent. So, what is the solution? The researchers recommend implementing Integrated Clinical Pathways (ICP) . This approach standardizes patient care by outlining clear steps for diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. By using ICP, hospitals can reduce unnecessary variations in care, shorten hospital stays, and lower readmission rates. In addition, better coordination among healthcare professionals—especially nurses, doctors, and administrators—is essential. Strong teamwork ensures that patients receive continuous and well-planned care from admission to discharge. In conclusion, this study reminds us that healthcare is not just about access, but also about quality. Insurance alone cannot guarantee good outcomes if the care provided is inconsistent or incomplete. To truly achieve SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , Indonesia must focus on improving the quality of healthcare services for all patients, regardless of their economic status."]

["Title: Seconds Matter: How Smart Triage Can Save Lives in Indonesian Emergency Rooms", "2024", "When someone arrives at the emergency room, every second counts. But what if the system that decides who gets treated first is not working as well as it should? This is where triage comes in—a process that determines which patients need immediate care and which can safely wait. A study titled “Evaluation of the Emergency Severity Index Triage for Improving Emergency Room Services Quality in Indonesian Hospital” , published in the journal Public Health of Indonesia by Yayasan Cipta Anak Bangsa (YCAB) on August 20, 2024, takes a closer look at how this system works in Indonesian hospitals . The research examined 100 patients in emergency departments and evaluated how well the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage system was implemented. This system classifies patients into five levels based on the severity of their condition and the resources they need. Ideally, it ensures that critically ill patients are treated immediately, while less urgent cases wait their turn. The findings are both encouraging and concerning. On one hand, hospitals already have adequate facilities and infrastructure to support triage. Response times were generally within acceptable standards, meaning patients were not left waiting too long for initial assessment. In fact, patient satisfaction was quite high—reaching 92%, especially in areas like empathy and assurance from healthcare workers . However, the study also revealed a major challenge: a shortage of nurses . In both hospitals studied, the number of nurses was below the required standard. This imbalance can lead to fatigue, slower decision-making, and potential risks for patients. Even the best system cannot function properly without enough trained professionals to run it. Interestingly, the study found that the triage system itself was not directly linked to patient satisfaction. Instead, satisfaction was more influenced by how patients were treated—through communication, empathy, and professionalism. This highlights an important truth: healthcare is not just about systems and protocols, but also about human connection. This issue directly relates to SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being , which aims to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all. Efficient triage systems help reduce waiting times, prevent complications, and improve survival rates. At the same time, ensuring enough trained healthcare workers is essential to achieving this goal. So, what can be done? The study recommends increasing both the number and competence of nurses in emergency departments. Regular training, better workforce planning, and continuous evaluation of triage practices are key steps forward. By strengthening both the system and the people behind it, hospitals can provide faster, safer, and more effective care. In the end, triage is more than just a sorting system—it is the frontline of emergency care. When done right, it can save lives. When overlooked, it can cost them. Indonesia’s journey toward better emergency services reminds us that improving healthcare is not just about technology or infrastructure, but about ensuring the right care reaches the right patient at the right time."]

["Half of Oncology Nurses Lack the Skills to Care for a Dying Patient’s Soul And That’s a Problem We Can Fix", "2018", "When a patient is diagnosed with end-stage breast cancer, medicine can only do so much. At some point, the goal shifts from curing the disease to easing the journey. In those final months, patients often need not another drug, but someone who can sit with them in their pain, acknowledge their fears, and support their sense of meaning and purpose. That is what spiritual care is all about. And according to a study at one of Indonesia’s leading cancer hospitals, many nurses are not yet equipped to provide it. Researchers from Universitas Hasanuddin surveyed 24 nurses in the Oncology Department of Dr. Wahidin Sudirohusodo Hospital in Makassar using a validated tool called the Spiritual Care Competency Scale (SCCS). The scale assesses six areas: assessing and implementing spiritual care, professionalising that care, personal support and counselling, referrals, attitudes toward patients’ spirituality, and communication. The findings were striking: 50 percent of nurses scored in the ‘low competence’ category. Only 25 percent reached a high level. The encouraging part: nurses scored highest in communication and attitude the warmth and compassion are already there. What is missing are formal skills, such as how to assess a patient’s spiritual needs or refer them to appropriate religious and counselling resources. The data also reveal a clear driver of this gap: training. Nurses who had attended chemotherapy training showed higher spiritual care competence, while those with no training at all were the most likely to score poorly. Why does this matter beyond the hospital? Because spiritual care is not a luxury it is a proven component of quality healthcare. Patients who receive spiritual support experience less anxiety and depression, better social support, and longer survival periods. When spiritual needs go unmet, research shows that medical costs at the end of life increase two to three times. This is both a human and an economic problem. This challenge connects directly to Sustainable Development Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-Being) , which calls for universal access to quality health services including for patients at the end of life. Achieving SDG 3 means going beyond physical treatment to address the psychological and spiritual dimensions of care, especially for the most vulnerable. Nurses are on the front line of this mission. The path forward is clear. Hospitals and nursing schools must integrate spiritual care into standard training and continuing professional development. Dr. Wahidin Sudirohusodo already has the foundation a palliative care programme and partnerships with religious leaders. The next step is ensuring every oncology nurse has both the heart and the competence to walk alongside a patient in life’s most difficult moments. Breast cancer does not end when treatment stops. The quality of a patient’s final days is shaped not only by medical skill, but by the human presence of those who care for them. Investing in nurses’ spiritual care competence is investing in dignity and every patient deserves that. ["When Recovery Costs More Than Treatment: The Hidden Financial Burden of Drug Use", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Oct 12, 2026 /BERG/–For families supporting someone affected by drug use, recovery can bring hope. But it can also come with difficult questions: Who will pay for rehabilitation? What happens when someone loses a job? And how can a household rebuild when everyday expenses keep rising? These questions are at the heart of Household economic burden, rehabilitation affordability, and recovery reintegration among people affected by drug use in South Sulawesi, Indonesia , a study by Sudarianto Sudarianto, Sukri Palutturi, and Hasmin Hasmin. The research appeared in the Journal of Substance Use and Addiction Treatment , published by Elsevier Inc. , and was first published online on 4 October 2026 . Although it is assigned to the journal’s 2027 volume, the online publication date marks its first public release. The researchers surveyed 59 people in Makassar and Sidenreng Rappang, South Sulawesi, between October 2025 and February 2026. Participants included people with experiences of drug use or recovery, family members, and affected community members. They described how drug-related circumstances had affected work, income, household spending, and the ability to pay for treatment. The figures tell a troubling story. Average reported monthly income was approximately 2.66 million Indonesian rupiah before drug-related involvement, compared with 1.55 million rupiah at the time of the survey. That is a difference of about 1.11 million rupiah per month. Meanwhile, nearly 90% of respondents said household expenses had increased. Paying for rehabilitation was another challenge. Families were the main source of funding for 59.3% of respondents, while 55.9% reported difficulty covering rehabilitation costs. Two-thirds also reported having experienced unemployment or job loss following drug-related involvement. Five respondents said family assets had been sold to meet related expenses. Behind each statistic is a practical concern. A household may need to choose between transportation to treatment, food, school supplies, and other essentials. Even when rehabilitation services exist, families may struggle to afford the journey through recovery. This makes the findings especially relevant to Sustainable Development Goal 1 (SDG 1): No Poverty . Poverty reduction is not only about earning more money. It also means protecting vulnerable households from financial shocks that can push them deeper into hardship. The study suggests that recovery support should go beyond clinical care. Affordable rehabilitation, job training, employment opportunities, community support, and targeted financial assistance could help people rebuild their lives without leaving families to carry the full burden. Importantly, this was a small survey based on people's recollections, not a representative study of all South Sulawesi households. It cannot prove that drug use caused the reported income decline. Still, it raises a powerful public question: If a person completes treatment but returns to unemployment and financial hardship, how sustainable can recovery be? Helping people recover means caring for their health and giving their families a fair chance to recover financially, too. ["Why Poverty Is More Than Low Income: The Hidden Role of Everyday Financial Decisions", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sept 13 2026 /BERG/–Poverty is often explained through low wages, unemployment, limited access to education, weak infrastructure, or inadequate social protection. These factors are fundamental. Yet poverty also has a household-level dimension: how families plan, spend, save, and respond to financial pressure can influence how deeply economic hardship affects them. This issue is examined in the scientific article “ Model Testing and Contribution of Antecedent Variable to Absolute Poverty: Low Income Family Perspective in Indonesia ” , published in Sustainability by MDPI, Basel, Switzerland , on 19 April 2023 . The study involved 201 low-income households from Makassar, Jeneponto, Selayar Islands, Bone, North Luwu, and North Toraja in South Sulawesi. The researchers focused on two ideas: short-term vision and uncontrolled consumption . Short-term vision refers to thinking mainly about immediate needs, with limited attention to saving or financial planning. Uncontrolled consumption includes unplanned purchases, spending based on desires or prestige, and spending that can exceed available income. The study found that short-term thinking was strongly associated with uncontrolled consumption. In turn, uncontrolled consumption was positively associated with absolute poverty. The statistical model also showed that uncontrolled consumption partly explained how short-term thinking was related to deeper poverty. This does not mean that poverty is simply the result of poor personal choices. Low-income families often make decisions under severe constraints. Limited income, unstable employment, weak access to clean water, education, healthcare, sanitation, and secure housing all remain central dimensions of poverty. In fact, the study itself measured poverty using several of these basic-needs indicators. The findings connect directly with Sustainable Development Goal 1 (SDG 1: No Poverty) . Ending poverty requires both structural support and stronger household resilience. Government assistance, jobs, education, social protection, and infrastructure remain essential, but financial literacy and household-level planning can complement these measures. One practical lesson is that poverty programmes may become more effective when they include simple and respectful financial education. Families can be supported to distinguish needs from wants, plan spending, manage debt, and prepare for periods when income falls. The study also warns that such interventions should avoid paternalism and should recognise the strengths, realities, and priorities of low-income households. The broader message is that poverty reduction works best when public policy and household capability are strengthened together. Structural opportunities create room to improve lives, while better planning can help families use limited resources more securely. ["Better Training, Better Teachers: Why Creative Teaching Needs More Than Workshops", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sept 13 2026 /BERG/–Teacher training is often seen as one of the easiest ways to improve education. Schools organise workshops, teachers attend professional development sessions, and certificates are issued. But does participation in training automatically make teaching more creative? A recent study from Indonesia suggests that the answer is no. The scientific article behind this popular piece is “ Strategic Management of Training Processes to Improve Teacher Quality and Creativity in Educational Institutions ” , published in the International Journal of Educational Management by Emerald Publishing Limited in 2026 . The study surveyed 615 teachers from public and private schools in South Sulawesi to examine how training management, teacher quality, and teaching creativity are connected. The main finding is simple but important. Well-managed training was strongly associated with better teacher quality, and better teacher quality was strongly associated with more creative teaching. However, training management itself did not have a significant direct relationship with teaching creativity. Instead, its influence operated through teacher quality. This means that sending teachers to workshops is not enough. What matters is whether professional development actually strengthens their teaching skills, classroom experience, professional knowledge, and ability to respond to learning challenges. The study therefore views teacher development as a continuous cycle rather than a one-time event. Schools should first identify teachers’ needs, design relevant programmes, provide good-quality training, and then continue with coaching, mentoring, professional learning communities, lesson study, and classroom-based evaluation. This has a direct connection with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4: Quality Education) . Quality education depends heavily on teachers who can adapt, solve classroom problems, and design learning experiences that respond to students’ changing needs. Professional development therefore becomes meaningful when it improves what teachers can actually do in the classroom. The findings also challenge a common way of evaluating teacher training. Schools often count how many teachers attended a programme or completed a course. A better question is: what changed afterward? Did teachers become more confident? Can they design lessons differently? Are they better able to solve classroom problems? Can they generate several approaches when one teaching strategy does not work? For school leaders, this means professional development should continue after the training room empties. Coaching, peer discussion, protected time for professional learning communities, classroom observation, and opportunities to experiment can help teachers convert new knowledge into better teaching practice. The broader lesson is clear: creative teaching does not emerge simply because teachers attend more training. It grows when schools turn professional development into sustained teacher capability. ["Digital Skills Without Expensive Internet: A Better Way to Reach Coastal Youth", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sept 13 2026 /BERG/–For many young people, digital skills are becoming essential for finding work, starting a business, and continuing education. Yet learning digital skills is not equally easy for everyone. In low-income coastal communities, young people may have motivation but still face simple barriers: no personal smartphone, expensive data, weak internet coverage, and training that does not match local livelihood opportunities. A recent study from South Sulawesi explores how these barriers can be addressed. The scientific article behind this popular piece is “ Designing Contextual Digital-Skills Training for Low-Resource Communities: Evidence from Coastal Youth in South Sulawesi ” , published in Information Development by SAGE Publications Ltd and first published online on 23 January 2026 . The study examined coastal youth in Makassar, Pangkep, and Bulukumba. Through 30 interviews and focus group discussions, researchers found that digital inequality is not only about internet access. Many participants relied on shared or borrowed phones, while high data costs, weak connectivity, and low confidence in online learning remained important obstacles. The youth were not simply asking for more technology. They wanted practical skills connected to real income opportunities. Digital marketing, tailoring, food businesses, and motorcycle repair were among the skills most often mentioned. They also preferred training that was affordable, close to their communities, practical, and followed by mentoring or equipment support. From these findings, the study proposes three practical ideas. First, training content should match local livelihood opportunities. Second, learning should involve trusted local actors such as youth organisations, community leaders, NGOs, and mentors. Third, training should use low-bandwidth and offline-first methods, including short learning modules and simple WhatsApp or SMS follow-ups. This connects directly with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4: Quality Education) , especially SDG 4.4 , which calls for more young people and adults to gain relevant skills for employment, decent jobs, and entrepreneurship. Quality education should therefore not be measured only by whether training exists. It should also consider whether disadvantaged learners can realistically access, complete, and use that training. The wider lesson is important. Digital inclusion does not mean simply giving people internet access. It means designing learning around the realities of people’s lives. ["Can Stronger Family Ties Help Families Escape Poverty? Lessons from Indonesia", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sept 13 2026 /BERG/–Poverty is often discussed in terms of income, jobs, subsidies, and access to public services. These factors are certainly important, but they do not tell the whole story. Inside many households, everyday decisions about spending, saving, sharing resources, and helping relatives can also shape how families cope with financial hardship. A study from Indonesia explores this less visible side of poverty. The scientific article behind this popular piece is “ Religious-Based Family Management and Sustainable Household Consumption: Evidence from Indonesia ” , published in the International Journal of Sustainable Energy Planning and Management by Aalborg University Open Publishing on 9 September 2025 . The research involved 325 low-income households across Makassar, Jeneponto, Selayar, Bone, North Luwu, and North Toraja in South Sulawesi. The study examined two important ideas. The first is Religious-Based Family Management , or RBFM, which refers to the way religious values influence household decisions, discipline, patience, responsibility, and the management of limited resources. The second is Silaturahim Quality , which reflects the strength of emotional, material, and practical support among family members, relatives, neighbours, and communities. The results showed that stronger religiously guided family management was associated with lower absolute poverty. It was also linked to stronger silaturahim , while better-quality social relationships were themselves associated with lower poverty. In simple terms, families appeared to become more resilient when personal discipline was combined with reliable social support. Why might this matter? A household facing financial pressure may not always have access to formal credit, insurance, or government assistance. In these circumstances, trusted social networks can provide practical help through food sharing, informal loans, information, emotional support, childcare, job referrals, and other forms of mutual assistance. The study suggests that these informal systems may act as an additional safety net when formal support is limited. This finding has a direct connection with Sustainable Development Goal 1 (SDG 1: No Poverty) . Ending poverty requires more than increasing income. It also requires stronger household resilience, access to basic services, social protection, and mechanisms that help vulnerable families cope with economic shocks. However, the study should not be interpreted to mean that religion alone can eliminate poverty. Structural factors such as employment, education, healthcare, clean water, housing, and economic opportunity remain essential. Indeed, the study measures poverty across several of these dimensions. The broader lesson is that poverty reduction works best when formal programmes and community strengths support each other. Financial assistance, education, and social protection can become more effective when they also recognise trusted local networks and culturally meaningful forms of mutual support. ["Training Is Not Enough: How Knowledge and Soft Skills Make Health Workers Perform Better", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sept 13 2026 /BERG/–Hospitals and public health facilities often invest heavily in staff training. New procedures are introduced, clinical knowledge is updated, and employees attend workshops designed to improve performance. But an important question remains: does attending training automatically make health workers perform better? A recent study from Indonesia suggests that the answer is more complicated. The scientific article behind this popular piece is “ Training Effectiveness and Health-Worker Performance: The Roles of Knowledge Management and Soft-Skill Competence ” , published in the International Journal of Health Care Quality Assurance by Emerald Publishing Limited . The article was published online on 14 April 2026 . The study examines how training becomes connected to health-worker performance through knowledge management and soft-skill competence. The online publication date is independently indexed as 14 April 2026. The findings show that effective training is positively associated with better knowledge management, stronger soft skills, and higher health-worker performance. More importantly, the indirect pathway from training through knowledge management and soft skills was stronger than the direct relationship between training and performance. What does this mean in everyday healthcare? Training becomes more useful when employees do not simply remember what they learned but also share, store, discuss, and apply that knowledge. Simple practices such as updating standard operating procedures, discussing cases with colleagues, conducting short after-action reviews, and sharing lessons from problems can help turn individual learning into organisational learning. Soft skills are another essential part of this process. Communication, teamwork, problem-solving, adaptability, and empathy can influence how healthcare workers interact with colleagues and patients. These skills help teams coordinate work, respond to difficult situations, and provide more patient-centred services. Technical competence remains important, but technical knowledge alone may not guarantee reliable care if staff cannot communicate clearly or work effectively together. This has a direct connection with Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being) . Achieving better health outcomes requires not only medicines, equipment, and infrastructure but also capable health workers who can learn continuously and translate knowledge into dependable daily practice. For healthcare managers, the message is practical. Training should not end when the workshop closes. Facilities can support knowledge sharing through brief peer-learning sessions, updated SOPs, structured handovers, and regular reflection on cases or incidents. Managers can also reinforce communication and teamwork during routine supervision. Ultimately, improving healthcare performance is not simply about providing more training. It is about creating an environment where knowledge is shared and soft skills are practised every day. When learning becomes part of routine work, training has a greater chance of contributing to more reliable, respectful, and responsive healthcare. ["When Coastal Voices Are Heard: Why Participation Needs Visible Action", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia, Sept 13 2026 /BERG/–Living by the sea means depending on more than fish, boats, and good weather. Coastal communities also depend on public services, permits, local programmes, and decisions made by government institutions. But what makes people trust these institutions and continue participating in local decision-making? A recent study offers an important answer. The scientific article behind this popular piece is “ Trust, Participation and Street-Level Bureaucracy: Interpreting Service and Governance Experiences in Coastal Indonesia ” , published in Frontiers in Political Science by Frontiers Media SA on 22 May 2026 . The research explored coastal communities in Makassar, Pangkep, and Bulukumba in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, drawing on the experiences of fishers, traders, processing workers, household caregivers, young people, community leaders, government actors, and other local stakeholders. One message from the study is especially clear: simply inviting people to meetings is not enough. Participation becomes meaningful when citizens can see what happens after they speak. People value forums that are easy to reach, clearly explained, focused on practical issues, and followed by visible government action. When proposals are recorded, responsibilities are clear, and officials provide updates, people are more likely to regard participation as worthwhile. Trust works in much the same way. Coastal residents do not appear to judge government only by promises. They look at whether officials listen, explain limitations honestly, respond to concerns, and follow up on previous discussions. Repeated meetings without visible results can produce “meeting fatigue,” while clear communication and tangible follow-up can encourage people to engage again. Yet participation does not take place under equal conditions. Fuel and travel costs, unstable seafood prices, limited internet access, low digital literacy, and difficulties accessing training or microfinance can prevent some residents from benefiting fully from government programmes. Women, youth, and small-scale livelihood actors may face additional barriers. These findings have a strong connection with Sustainable Development Goal 14 (SDG 14: Life Below Water) . Protecting marine resources is not only about ecosystems. Sustainable coastal management also requires communities that can participate in decisions affecting fishing, livelihoods, coastal development, and access to public support. Local knowledge becomes more useful when governments create channels where citizens can speak and receive meaningful responses. The lesson is simple: good coastal governance needs more than public meetings. It requires communication, accountability, accessible services, responsive frontline officials, and continued dialogue. When people can see that their voices lead to understandable decisions and practical follow-up, participation can become a bridge between coastal communities and more sustainable governance. ["Training That Works: Why Better Teams Need More Than a Classroom", "MAKASSAR, Indonesia Sept 13 2026 /BERG/–Workplace training is often treated as a simple formula: send employees to a course, improve their skills, and expect better performance. Yet real workplaces are more complicated. A recent study from Indonesia shows that training can matter greatly, but not always in the direct way managers expect. The scientific article behind this popular piece is “ The Role of Training Effectiveness in Enhancing Team Performance: Mediating Effects of Diversity Management and Teamwork Quality ” , published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications by Springer Nature on 14 July 2026 . The study examined 215 employees in an Indonesian state-owned enterprise and explored how training, diversity management, teamwork, and team performance are connected. The most interesting finding is that effective training did not directly improve teamwork quality. Instead, training was associated with stronger diversity management, which was then linked to better teamwork, and better teamwork was associated with higher team performance. In other words, a training programme may give employees useful knowledge and skills, but those gains are more likely to become visible in team results when the workplace also gives people a fair voice, respects differences, encourages feedback, and creates room for cooperation. This finding matters because organisations often focus on the training event itself: the trainer, the materials, the schedule, or the certificate. The study suggests that what happens after training may be just as important. Employees need opportunities to practise what they have learned, work with colleagues from different backgrounds, communicate openly, and feel safe when sharing ideas. A one-off workshop is unlikely to transform teamwork if daily routines still discourage participation or if some voices are ignored. This message connects directly with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4: Quality Education) . SDG 4 is not only about schools and universities; it also promotes lifelong learning and the development of relevant skills. In the workplace, quality learning should therefore go beyond transferring technical knowledge. It should help people apply skills, participate confidently, learn from others, and contribute to inclusive and productive teams. For managers and public organisations, the practical lesson is clear: training should be designed as part of a broader organisational process. Follow-up coaching, inclusive leadership, fair treatment, open communication, and opportunities for teamwork can help turn learning into everyday behaviour. When employees see that learning is supported by the organisation and connected to inclusive practices, training becomes more than a short course. It becomes a pathway toward stronger collaboration and better collective performance. The study reminds us that people do not perform better simply because they have attended training. They perform better when learning is supported by a workplace where differences are respected, teamwork is practised, and new skills can be used in real situations.
